"There are others like us now," she said, still not meeting my eyes. "Others who manifested during the Breach. They're gathering. You need to come with me before—"

"No." The word came out sharp and clear despite my racing pulse. "I'm done with this crazy shit. I have a job. A life. Whatever happened last night was an anomaly, and I'm going to get it sorted through official channels."

Lysandra finally turned back to face me, and the pity in her expression scared me more than anything else.

"Official channels?" She laughed bitterly. "Mara, you think the County General administration doesn't know exactly what happened? That the city council isn't already meeting right now to decide what to do about you?"

She stepped out into the hallway, then paused at the threshold.

"You have twenty-four hours before they make contact,"

* * *

I stood there in my cramped apartment bathroom, still reeking of cedar from the shift at County General, when I heard the knock.

Not at the door—that came later. First was three sharp raps against the toilet tank, followed by a woman's voice cutting through the thin walls like smoke through a keyhole.

"Commander Vance. We need to talk."

The smell hit me next. It wasn't the antiseptic tang I'd been scrubbing from under my fingernails for twenty minutes. This was different—like ozone after lightning, but wrong somehow. Chemical. Fear made it taste metallic on my tongue.

I opened the bathroom door to find her standing in my living room.

She looked wrong too. Not just because she wore a floor-length coat that shouldn't fit in my shoebox apartment, or because her dark skin seemed to drink the predawn light instead of reflecting it. It was her eyes—they had this quality like she was seeing the room behind mine, overlapping realities stacked on top of each other.

"My name is Lysandra Vance," she said, and the way she said *Vance* made something cold slither down my spine. "We don't have much time."

"You're not my sister." The words came out before I could stop them. Years of running trauma calls had taught me to read people fast—family resemblance isn't just blood, it's bearing, carriage, the set of someone's shoulders. This woman carried herself like someone who'd learned violence as a second language.

A bitter smile crossed her lips. "No. But I knew your father."

The sirens were already building outside, their sound climbing up from the South Side streets like a wounded animal. 6 AM meant shift change at the precinct houses, trucks rumbling toward the Pulaski Skyway. Normal morning sounds that suddenly felt like countdown timers.

"Your father was Elias Morvain," Lysandra continued, watching my face like a hawk. "And you are his daughter, whether you know what that means yet or not."

My hands found the countertop behind me. Paramedic training kicked in—I catalogued exits: window, door, the knife block by the stove. The cedar smell mixed with that ozone stink, making my head swim.

"That's insane." My voice sounded hollow. "I'm nobody's daughter but mine own."

"Not according to the Bureau of Arcano-Telluric Control." She moved closer, and I caught it then—a faint mark on her wrist, scars arranged in patterns that hurt to look at directly. "They're forming right now, Mara. Piecing together the old networks, the telluric lines that run beneath this city's infrastructure. They call themselves BATC now, corporate-speak for something older and far more hungry."

She pulled a phone from her coat—one of those ancient Nokia bricks, the kind we used before smartphones turned everyone into walking surveillance devices. The plastic was worn smooth, scratched along one edge.

"This is a burner. No tracking, no metadata. Memorize the number." Her grip tightened as she held it out. "When they come—and they will come—they'll offer you everything. A position, authority, uniforms that glow with borrowed power. Don't take them."

"They?" The word came out strangled.

"The High-Spire Elves mostly." Lysandra's expression darkened. "Already flocking to the BATC banner like moths to flame. They want control of the Undercity, want to build their spires on foundations soaked in human suffering. And they need people like you to make it look legitimate."

"I don't know what you're talking about." But even as I said it, I felt the lie twist in my chest. Didn't I? Hadn't there always been moments during calls when reality seemed thin? When I could *feel* the wrongness seeping up through asphalt cracks?

"You have your father's gift," Lysandra said quietly. "The ability to touch the wounded and pull them back from death's threshold. To feel the vital currents running through living things." She reached out, and I flinched—I couldn't help it—but her fingers just brushed my wrist, finding the pulse point. "They'll dress it up as medical skill, supernatural talent. Tell you it's your birthright to serve."

Thunder rumbled outside, though the sky had been clear moments ago.

"Here's what they won't tell you: Your father made a choice thirty years ago. Chose love over duty, chose to walk away from whatever ancient bloodline he descended from." Her eyes met mine, and for the first time I saw something like pain there. "That choice cost him everything. Cost our family everything."

"But it gave you life." She pressed the phone into my palm, closed my fingers around it. "And now that life is in danger, Mara Vance. The moment BATC realizes who you are—who your *father* was—they will conscript you. Use you. Break you open and harvest whatever power runs in Morvain blood."

The footsteps came then—heavy, synchronized, echoing in the hallway outside. Professional. Measured. Coming toward my door.

"They're already here." Lysandra moved to the window, threw the latch. "Listen to me carefully: Trust no one in a suit. Hide anything that smells of lilac or cedar or any scent that marks you as different. And when they knock—and they will knock—remember that you have a choice Elias never got."

A fist pounded on my front door. Three sharp raps, authoritative and unmistakable.

"Bureau of Arcano-Telluric Control," a smooth voice called out, corporate-friendly despite the early hour. "Open up, Ms. Vance. We just need to ask you some questions about your recent performance at County General."

Lysandra turned back to me, her expression apologetic and fierce all at once. "I'm sorry about this. About all of this." Then she was gone, dropping through the window onto the fire escape with barely a sound.

I stood there holding the burner phone, its plastic warm from her grip, listening to those footsteps circle around to block the fire exit. The ward she'd cast on my door was already fading—I could see it breaking apart like smoke, revealing the cheap wood underneath.

Another knock, harder this time.

"We know you're in there, Commander. Please make this easy on everyone involved."

---

## CHAPTER 6: THE CORPORATE DRAFT

The fluorescent lights overhead flickered—again—casting everything in County General's ER in stuttering shades of green and white. I'd lost count of how many times I'd watched them die and reboot since midnight. Three? Four?

My Nextel buzzed. Another run, another breach victim, another body for the triage system that was already drowning. But instead of moving toward ambulance bay three, I stayed put, watching the circus unfold before me.

The waiting room had transformed into something straight out of a fever dream. Two weeks post-Breach and Newark still hadn't figured out how to process what happened when those telluric mains ruptured beneath Neon Hollow. Now the city was packed with walking contradictions—humans who'd been touched by whatever the hell poured through the crack in reality and came out changed. Some for better. Most for worse.

The suits moved through it all like they owned the place.

And maybe they did now.

"Commander Vance?"

I turned. A woman in a charcoal pencil skirt stood there, tablet in hand, her aura reeking of ozone and something colder—corporate ambition, maybe, or the kind of calculated ruthlessness that smelled faintly of iron and fresh ink. BATC. Bureau of Arcano-Telluric Control. The acronym tasted bitter on my tongue even thinking it.

"I'm not interested," I said flatly.

She smiled—a perfect, practiced thing that didn't reach her eyes. "Ms. Vance, you're a Commander-level paramedic. Your bio-resonance readings are off the charts. We've been monitoring your—"

"That's a hard pass."

"What if I told you we could triple your salary? Quadruple it. Private medical suite, research access to treatments that can actually stabilize the caseload you're dealing with here." She gestured around the ER where an Orc was screaming as a doctor tried to set his compound fracture without proper sedation. "Does this look like stabilization to you?"

My jaw tightened. Behind her, another BATC recruiter had cornered a newly transformed Elf—a former investment banker from Sterling Manor whose left arm had sprouted translucent crystalline structures along his veins during the Breach. He looked terrified but also... calculating. Like he was already doing the math on whether selling himself to these people would be worth it.

"They're drafting everyone who looks corporate-friendly," I observed quietly.

"We're providing opportunities for high-value assets to contribute to societal reconstruction."

"By stealing them from their families while they're still bleeding out in emergency rooms?" I stepped closer, my own white-lilac scent cutting through the ozone-tainted air between us. "I've seen what happens when people sign those NDAs. They disappear into BATC facilities. Nobody hears from them again except for press releases about how much they're contributing to the greater good."

Her smile never wavered. "Is that what you think is happening?"

"I know what I see." My hand went to my pager. Another buzz. Another run. "Now if you'll excuse me, I have actual patients to treat."

I pushed past her toward ambulance bay three, but I could feel her eyes burning into my back. The BATC was building something down at Newark Bay—massive new facilities constructed at impossible speeds using construction crews that worked eighteen-hour shifts fueled by whatever miracle chemical cocktail kept them going. They called it progress. Looked more like a cage being built around everything the Breach had touched.

My paramedic partner, Chen, was waiting by the ambulance when I arrived.

"You okay?" she asked, loading an IV kit into the vehicle.

"Peachy," I lied, sliding into the passenger seat as dispatch crackled over the radio about a collapsed building near the Kearny Marshes and multiple casualties with telluric burn symptoms.

Behind us, County General's ER continued its grim dance of trauma and triage while the suits picked through the wreckage looking for anyone who might help them build whatever dystopian future they were engineering.

The city was changing faster than anyone could keep up with.

And I was pretty sure we were all just along for the ride whether we liked it or not.

* * *

I jumped, my hands instinctively flaring with a soft, pure white-lilac light that smelled of fresh cedar. The bio-ward illuminated the dark corner of the hallway where I had retreated to catch my breath.

Standing in front of me was a BATC recruiter. This one wasn't human. She was a High-Spire Elf, her sharp features framed by a severe bob cut, her eyes a piercing, calculating gray. She held an open IBM ThinkPad, the screen glowing with my personnel file.

"Easy on the light show, Vance," the elven woman said, her voice a smooth, flat North Jersey drawl. "I'm Agent Thorne. BATC Internal Affairs. I've been reviewing the security footage from New Year's Eve. You restarted a flatlining cardiac patient using an unregistered psychogenic bio-ward while Rig 42 was dead in the water."

"I was trying to save his life," I said defensively, my cedar-scented magic dimming but not vanishing. "I didn't ask for this magic. It just... happened when the shockwave hit."

Thorne snapped the ThinkPad shut. "Nobody asked for it. But you have it. And more importantly, your weave is clean. Do you know how rare that is? Half the medics in this city who awakened are accidentally cooking their patients from the inside out because they panic and their magic turns to microwave radiation. Your aura is stable."

"What do you want?" I asked, crossing my arms.

"I'm drafting you into Aegis," Thorne said flatly. "It's BATC’s new medical-tactical responder cohort. The city is a powder keg. The cops don't know how to arrest an Orc who can punch through a 1999 Crown Vic engine block, and the regular paramedics can't triage a Dwarf whose blood has turned to liquid bismuth. We need medics who can stitch a chest closed with magic before the patient bleeds out in a gutter. Aegis gets the best gear, the best armor, and the authority to police the metahuman spectrum."

The fluorescent lights overhead flickered, casting erratic shadows across the linoleum floor. Through the thin walls, I could hear the sounds of County General's ER—a symphony of suffering that had only intensified since January first. Screams. Coughing. The mechanical hiss of ventilators fighting losing battles against lungs filled with telluric residue.

"And if I say no? If I stay here?" I asked, though I already knew the answer was written on Thorne's face.

"Then you'll burn out in six months," she replied coldly. "County General is bankrupt. The city is going to cut their funding. Aegis is the only way you actually save lives on a macro scale. We give you the resources. You give us your talent. It’s basic economics."

I looked down the hall at the overwhelmed nurses and the dying patients. A young Latino orderly was crying in the corner, his arms covered in mysterious purple burns from trying to stabilize a woman whose body had started crystallizing from the inside out. The smell of ozone and fear hung thick in the air, mixing with antiseptic and fresh blood.

My white-lilac light pulsed gently around my hands—patient, clean, pure. A stark contrast to the chaos bleeding through every surface of this hospital.

"I need to see it," I said quietly. "The work you're talking about. Before I commit."

Thorne's expression didn't change, but there was the barest hint of respect in her eyes. She gestured toward the exit. "Follow me. But keep that ward leashed, Vance. We're going somewhere you don't want to be flashing magic like a kid with firecrackers."

She led me outside into the January cold. The Newark night air hit me like a slap—the temperature had dropped twenty degrees since last week, part of the weather weirdness everyone was calling "the Cascades." My breath fogged as we walked across the parking lot toward a sleek black Suburban parked away from the other vehicles.

"This is a mobile command unit," Thorne explained as she opened the side door. Inside, the vehicle was nothing like any ambulance or rescue truck I'd ever seen. Banks of monitors lined one wall, all displaying different feeds: police scanners, satellite imagery, what looked like thermal vision of moving targets scattered across a map of North Jersey.

At the center console sat another agent—a human this time, middle-aged, wearing tactical gear that looked more like something Navy SEALs would use than anything BATC had deployed before the Breach. He glanced up at us briefly, his eyes sharp behind wire-rimmed glasses.

"Agent Vance, meet Specialist Chen," Thorne said. "He runs our triage matrix for Sector Seven. You wanted to see the work? This is where it starts."

Chen turned his monitor toward me. The screen showed a live feed of some kind of disturbance—flashing lights, people running. The audio crackled with panicked voices.

"Three hours ago, there was a metahuman fight in a bodega on South Street," Chen said clinically. "Two Orcs and a Troll went berserk over a poker game. Six civilians injured, two critical. Standard response time for EMTs? Forty-seven minutes. Too long when you're bleeding out from impact trauma that shattered your femur into dust."

He switched feeds. Now the screen showed the same scene, but from a different angle—higher resolution, enhanced. I could see figures moving with supernatural speed, their heat signatures burning bright against the cooler nighttime background.

"Aegis team responded in eight minutes," Chen continued. "Medical tech named Rodriguez. She's not even fully awakened herself yet—the magic just started manifesting last week—but she has basic regeneration weaves. Pulled all six victims clear. Stitched three of them closed right there on site using bio-accelerated sutures."

"What about the other three?" I asked.

"The two criticals died anyway," Chen admitted without emotion. "The third lost both legs. But they were alive. They got fighting chances they wouldn't have had waiting for standard ambulances." He looked at me directly. "That's what we do, Commander Vance. We save lives that would otherwise be statistics."

Thorne stepped closer. "The question is whether you want to be the statistic-taker or the life-saver."

I stared at the monitors, watching the aftermath unfold through various camera angles. Police were securing the scene now. News helicopters circled overhead. And somewhere in that chaos, a medic named Rodriguez was probably getting debriefed, her hands still shaking from the adrenaline of keeping six dying people alive while monsters fought around them.

My white-lilac light flickered gently at my fingertips. Pure. Clean. Powerful enough to restart hearts and mend wounds that conventional medicine couldn't touch.

"When do I start?" I asked.

Thorne's lips quirked into something almost resembling a smile. "Tomorrow morning. 0600 hours. Sterling Manor base. Pack light—we'll issue your equipment there. And Vance?"

"Yes?"

"

* * *

I stared at the blinking green text on the Nokia's cracked LCD screen, watching the letters dance in the fluorescent hell of the County General locker room. CODE 3. AEGIS DEPLOYMENT. SECTOR 4.

The words sat there like a death sentence wrapped in corporate branding.

Behind me, Agent Thorne hadn't made it to the door yet. I heard her Nextel crackle to life, her voice cutting through the stale air. "Copy that. Vance is en route. ETA five minutes."

She turned, her dark eyes catching mine with something between pity and professional detachment. "Sector Four is downtown Newark. Federal Plaza area. You'll need your kit from Sub-Station Seven first—" She paused, glancing at my half-packed belongings scattered across the bench. "You can grab what you need later. The city doesn't wait for anyone to say goodbye."

My hands were shaking. Not from fear—from adrenaline, from the bone-deep knowledge that everything had just shifted into high gear. I'd signed the contract ten minutes ago. Ten *minutes*. And now they were throwing me into the deep end with weights tied around my ankles.

"What's the situation?" I asked, already moving toward the door.

Thorne followed close behind as we descended the emergency stairwell, our footsteps echoing off concrete painted institutional gray. "Telluric breach at an underground parking structure beneath the federal building. Three casualties, unknown number of metahuman transformations. Civilian response units are overwhelmed." She pulled open the basement exit, revealing the January night air biting cold against my face. "This is why BATC exists now, Vance. This is what your signature bought you."

We emerged into the County General lot where two black BATC SUVs idled, their engines rumbling like caged beasts. The lead vehicle's passenger door hung open, waiting. Unlike the battered Ford ambulances I'd ridden out of this hospital a hundred times before, these vehicles gleamed with fresh paint, reinforced bumpers, and telluric-absorbent plating I could see even in the dim lot lighting.

I climbed inside. The interior smelled wrong—new vinyl, ozone filters, and something else underneath it all. Something electric and hungry. A driver I didn't recognize nodded once, his hand already on the gear shift. Through the bulletproof glass, I watched Thorne climb into the second vehicle.

The Nokia vibrated again in my palm. Another message: COORDINATES UPDATED. PROCEED WITH CAUTION. SECTOR 4 RESTRICTED ACCESS.

Restricted access meant the Breach was bad enough that civilian authorities had been pushed out entirely. It meant whatever had torn through the telluric veil down there had made the federal government hand over jurisdiction to a corporation that existed for less than a month.

My old paramedic bag sat in that box upstairs, filled with gauze and epinephrine and bandages that couldn't do shit against whatever we were heading toward. But in the back of this SUV, mounted between the seats, I saw my new kit. A medical case built from composite materials, equipped with arcano-stabilization fields and weapons-grade restraint systems.

I touched the cold metal of the case and felt nothing but certainty. Whatever Commander Mara Vance had been before midnight on New Year's Eve—before the world split open and let the other side pour through—that woman died two weeks ago along with everything normal about existence.

The SUV lurched forward onto Lesh Street, tires screaming as we cut through Newark's grid toward Federal Plaza. Through the windshield, I caught glimpses of the city's new reality: boarded-up buildings marked with BATC containment symbols, military police checkpoints, civilians clutching protection charms sold by street vendors who'd learned the new currency overnight.

And everywhere, bleeding off the transformed metahumans like stink, that goddamn ozone static. It crawled up my nose, scratched at my throat, made my teeth ache. But beneath my white-lilac cedar wards—the ones that had somehow stayed pure through the whole nightmare—I felt protected.

The city was burning from the inside out, and I'd just signed up to be a fireman carrying gasoline.

We hit the Pulaski Skyway entrance hard, and the driver killed his lights entirely. We became a ghost in the darkness, racing toward Sector Four while downtown Newark lit up with emergency vehicle flashes below us like dying stars.

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE FIRST THREE LAWS

The second drill was worse.

We were paired up for combat scenarios—dummy targets rigged to fire rubber bullets at variable speeds while we tried to maintain active wards under stress. The warehouse reeked of ozone and fear-sweat as recruits scrambled to shield themselves and their partners.

"Vance! You're with Chen!" Instructor Graves barked.

Chen was a thin kid from Elizabeth, newly awakened with a water-manipulation talent that made him nervous as hell around liquids. We took positions behind our concrete barricades as the training dummies across the range powered up, red targeting lasers sweeping the area.

"You feel that?" I whispered to Chen, my hands already beginning the psychic reach for my ward. "Before you even cast, your heartbeat's racing. Slow it down."

But he couldn't. I smelled it rising—the acrid tang of adrenaline mixed with copper. His concentration was already fracturing.

"Three seconds!" the range master called out.

I deployed my bio-ward first, the white-lilac sphere expanding around both of us just as rubber rounds began peppering our position. Each impact against the barrier sent ripples through the field, but it held, steady and pure.

Then Chen panicked.

His water spell erupted in a desperate spray instead of controlled manipulation—the scent shifted instantly to burnt sugar and iron filings. Three shots got through his compromised defense, one stinging my forearm hard enough to bruise.

"Dammit!" Chen cursed, his face flushed with shame.

Graves was on us immediately. "You see that, Vance? Your partner loses focus, your ward's integrity drops by what, twenty percent?"

I touched my bleeding arm. "Closer to thirty, sir. The emotional bleed created a weak point in my coverage."

"This is why Aegis units train together for months before deployment," Graves said, his voice sharp but not cruel. "Because when Miller's fear makes his shield shatter or Chen's panic creates gaps in your coverage, people die. Real bullets, real blood, real bodies hitting the floor."

He made us run the drill seven more times. By the seventh iteration, my arms were shaking from maintaining active wards while managing both my own mental state and compensating for Chen's leaking emotional resonance. The smell of cedar and lilacs in my personal spell-scent was getting strained, mixing with traces of my own exhaustion—that metallic taste of pushing too hard.

But we didn't get hit again.

* * *

The January wind cut through the alley like broken glass. Mara pulled her EMT jacket tighter around herself, though it did little against the cold that seemed to seep straight through concrete and bone alike.

"Recruit Vance. Kaelen." The voice came from behind them—sharp, clipped, with the distinct accent of someone who'd spent too many years in the military before the Awakening. Sergeant Rask stood at the mouth of the alley, arms crossed over a chest that had seen combat in places no one talked about anymore. Her eyes scanned the huddled recruits like she was inventorying ammunition. "Break's over. You've got five minutes to finish your coffee and get your asses back inside for Phase Two."

Torque grunted something unflattering under his breath but stubbed out what remained of his Marlboro against the brick wall. The ember hissed as it hit the wet pavement.

Mara drained the last of her burnt coffee—warm now, which was an improvement—and followed the others back through the warehouse doors. The sudden warmth inside hit like a slap, making her skin tingle.

Phase Two training took place in the main bay, where BATC had converted half a city block into simulated urban environments. Rubble-strewn streets, overturned vehicles, fake blood splashed across cracked pavement. The smell of ozone hung heavy in the air—that particular electric tang that meant telluric lines were active nearby.

"Listen up!" Sergeant Rask's voice echoed off corrugated metal walls. She stood on a platform elevated five feet above ground level, giving her a perfect view of all twenty-three recruits in Aegis Cohort Seven. "What you're about to learn is called psychogenic resonance. It’s why we screen casters for mental stability. Why we check your emotional baseline every morning before live fieldwork."

She hopped down from the platform with practiced ease. "Magic isn't just energy, people. It's *you*. Your fear, your anger, your joy—it all gets baked into the spell-scent you leave behind. And in this line of work?" Her eyes locked onto Mara specifically. "That scent can mean the difference between coming home and ending up in a body bag."

A recruit two rows back—a lanky kid who couldn't have been older than nineteen—raised his hand tentatively. "Sergeant, what exactly do you mean by 'scent'? Like, literally?"

Rask's expression didn't change. "Exactly literally, Private. Casters bleed psychic residue. We call it the scent because that's the closest approximation most humans can understand." She pulled out a small silver device from her belt—the same kind Mara had seen medics use at County General for reading stress hormones. "This is an emotional spectrometer. Telluric sensitivity is built-in now, thanks to the Breach, but the basic principle hasn't changed since they invented these things back in '99."

She held it up to inspect it under the fluorescent lights. "White means clean. Neutral. Controlled. Anything else..." Rask's jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. "...means you're compromised."

Torque shifted his weight beside Mara, arms crossed even more tightly now. His beard twitched with barely suppressed irritation.

"Commander Vance." Rask tossed the spectrometer directly at her without warning. Mara caught it reflexively, feeling its weight settle into her palm like ice. "You're up first. Show them how a professional handles telluric diagnostics."

Mara stared down at the device, watching as a thin blue indicator light flickered to life along its edge. The screen displayed a simple color gradient: pure white at one end, bleeding through pastels—cream, ivory, pale yellow—before diving into darker territory. Crimson. Rust-brown. Black.

Her hands trembled slightly—not from fear, she realized, but from the unfamiliarity of holding technology designed specifically for this new world order where magic was just another utility to be monitored and controlled.

"Just... breathe normal," Rask instructed. "The spectro reads your baseline psycho-emotional state and cross-references it against your telluric signature. Should take about three seconds."

Mara pressed her thumb against the activation plate on top of the device.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then the screen bloomed with data:

**SUBJECT: VANCE, M. (CMD)**
**CLASSIFICATION: HUMAN PRIOR-AWAKENING**
**TELLURIC SENSITIVITY: MODERATE**
**EMOTIONAL BASELINE: STABLE**
**SCENT SIGNATURE: WHITE-LILAC / CEDAR**

Below that, in smaller text, a single word:

**PRISTINE**

A few recruits muttered amongst themselves. Torque's expression softened marginally, though he still looked skeptical.

Rask gave a curt nod of approval. "See? That's what clean looks like." She gestured to the readout. "Lilac means you're operating under calm focus. Cedar means you've got that EMT mindset—that clinical detachment thing paramedics are trained for. Combined, it keeps your spell-work untainted."

* * *

The afternoon sun cuts through the grimy warehouse windows, painting bars of yellow across concrete littered with shell casings and spent spell components. My tactical vest still smells like ozone and dust—Briggs' blood, mostly.

"Vance. My office. Now." Captain Graves' voice crackles through my headset before I can even help the Orc sit up properly. His shoulder is already swelling into a nasty purple bruise beneath the sealed flesh, but he'll live.

I leave Briggs with another medic and make my way through the maze of plywood corridors, boots echoing on wet concrete. The other recruits give me space—the kind of distance you give someone who just pulled off something spectacular or completely fucked up. With the Brass, it's usually both.

Graves' office is a converted storage room, walls covered in incident reports and a massive city map studded with red pins marking gang territories. The Elven High-Spire supervisor from earlier sits in the only visitor chair, his white suit somehow still immaculate despite standing over our kill-house disaster. He doesn't introduce himself when I enter.

"You have exceptional discipline," he says, his accent clipped and old-money British. His eyes are pale gray, the kind that don't quite focus on you when they look. "That level of emotional control is... rare."

"Thank you, sir." I stand at attention because Graves taught me never to relax around High-Spire brass, no matter how friendly they seem.

He waves a dismissive hand. "Not a compliment, Commander Vance. It's an observation. One that raises questions." He stands, circling me slowly. "Most casters bleed their emotions into everything they do. Anger makes fire spells hotter, fear makes kinetic blasts unstable. The weave reflects what's inside."

"I understand, sir."

"Do you?" He stops directly in front of me, close enough that I can smell expensive cologne underneath his crisp cedar scent. "Your output was pure. Sterile. Like you'd never experienced genuine emotion in your life. That's not natural for a human. Especially not one raised in Newark Bay."

My jaw tightens involuntarily. The muscle twitches—the first crack in my composure since entering this room. I feel Graves' eyes drilling into the back of my skull, but I keep mine forward.

"That's classified, sir."

A smile ghosts across his lips. Not friendly. "Everything is classified now, Commander. Your entire cohort has been flagged for accelerated training. Effective immediately, you're being transferred to Sub-Station Seven." He hands me a folder thicker than my hand. "Read it. Don't discuss it with anyone. And Vance?"

"Yes, sir?"

"The Third Law exists for a reason." His voice drops lower. "Emotionless precision is beautiful to watch. But when things get truly desperate, when the choice is between mission success and watching your friends die..." He leans closer. "Pure control breaks faster than anything else. Remember that when you're holding together under fire."

He leaves. Just walks out without another word, leaving me standing there with Graves staring at the floor behind his desk.

"You heard everything," I say quietly.

"Every fucking word." Graves lights a cigarette even though it's against regulations in the office. "Sub-Seven is where they send the assets they plan to burn through fast. You just got put on the express lane, Mara."

I open the folder. The first page is my new assignment orders: Counter-Insurgency Unit, Aegis Division, direct report to High-Spire Command. Below that, a list of names—operatives I'll be working with. Most are marked with red flags.

"Who am I hunting?" I ask.

Graves exhales smoke toward the ceiling. "Not who. What. They found something in the Kearny Marshes last week. Something that shouldn't exist according to every magical theory we have." He taps ash onto the incident map. "It's already killed seven field agents. The brass wants it contained before it reaches Newark proper."

"What is it?"

His eyes meet mine, and for the first time since I've known him, I see genuine fear. "That's the problem, kid. We don't know yet. But whatever it is, it's learning how to hide from our psychometric scanners by mimicking clean emotional signatures."

White-lilac and cedar.

The scent of my bio-ward floods my senses uninvited, and suddenly I understand what the Elven supervisor meant about pure control breaking faster than anything else.

Because if something can mimic what I am?

Then I'm going into those marshes blind.

---

## CHAPTER 8: BLACK-IRON COUGH

The rain hammered down like bullets against my tactical helmet as I sprinted across the collapsed tenement site. Miller's boots splashed beside me, both of us hauling medical gear that felt heavier than it should. The acrid stench of crushed brick and something worse—something organic and wrong—filled my lungs with each breath.

"Commander Vance! Over here!" A firefighter waved frantically from behind a towering pile of twisted rebar and pulverized concrete. His face was blackened with soot, eyes wide with the kind of terror that comes from watching people die who shouldn't be dying.

I dropped to one knee beside the first casualty. She couldn't have been more than thirty, maybe a tenement worker or someone's mother. Her left leg was pinned under three thousand pounds of debris, but she was conscious—her eyes tracking me with desperate hope even as blood bubbled at the corner of her mouth.

"Not yet," I whispered, placing my palm flat against her forehead. "Hold on."

The familiar warmth started in my core, that liquid light I'd learned to summon during the Breach years. It flowed up through my arm like molten gold, pooling where flesh met flesh. Usually, this is where the healing begins—the cells remembering their original blueprint, the tissue knitting itself whole. But tonight, something fought back.

It felt like touching an oil slick made of shadow. My magic rippled against an unseen barrier in her lungs, sliding off like water on glass. When I pushed harder, concentrating until sweat beaded on my temples, I caught a glimpse of what was wrong: dark, viscous sludge moving through her bronchial tubes, thick as motor oil, *alive* in some terrible way.

"What the fuck..." Miller had dropped to his knees beside me, running his scanner over the woman. The readout flickered red. "Commander, her vitals are collapsing. Pulmonary edema, but the scanner says... it says there's foreign matter in her system. Like she inhaled something that won't let go."

A coughing fit wracked the woman's body. What came out wasn't just phlegm and blood. It was black. A dense, tarry substance that steamed slightly when it hit the rain-soaked pavement, dissolving slowly into the gutters like chemical waste.

"More casualties incoming!" Another firefighter appeared, dragging a young man by the arms—couldn't have been more than nineteen, face pale as bone. His breathing was ragged, desperate. "Found him in the basement. Said three others still down there with him."

I transferred my hand from the first victim to the second, desperately trying to maintain both threads of healing energy. The same resistance greeted me. This time I focused on it, really looked at it with my magical sight instead of just trying to push through.

The sludge moved with purpose. Not random contamination, but something directed, almost intelligent. Each particle seemed to carry a tiny fragment of intent—not human, not even close to anything I'd encountered during the Breach. This felt older, colder, like touching sedimentary rock that remembered prehistoric nightmares.

"You're losing them," Miller said quietly. His voice carried no blame, just the flat statement of fact that paramedics learn to live with.

My jaw clenched so hard it hurt. Every instinct screamed at me to pour more power into the spell, to overwhelm whatever this corruption was with sheer force of will. But I could feel it already—the drain on my reserves, the way pushing harder made the resistance stronger, like trying to hold back an ocean with your bare hands.

"Triage line! Now!" The command came from one of the senior medics, a grizzled veteran named Kowalski who'd been running field operations since before the Breach. "We've got six confirmed dead, twelve critical. Sort them!"

Around us, the scene had grown into organized chaos. Police were setting up barricades while firefighters continued pulling bodies from the wreckage. The smell of ruptured gas lines mixed with smoke and rain, creating an atmosphere thick enough to taste. Above it all, the strobing lights continued their hypnotic rotation—blue and white against red and amber—a Technicolor nightmare painted across the tenement's skeletal remains.

I pulled my hand away from both victims, watching as their conditions immediately began deteriorating without my magic holding back the darkness in their lungs. The first woman's eyes widened in panic as she realized what was happening.

"I'm sorry," I told her, meaning it down to my bones. "Hold on. I need... I need to figure out what we're dealing with."

Miller caught my eye, his expression unreadable behind his respirator mask. He understood. We couldn't heal what we didn't understand.

The radio crackled again: *"Aegis Actual to Unit 4. How many wounded? Repeat, how many metahuman casualties?"*

I looked around at the growing line of stretchers, at the faces twisted in pain or frozen in death, at the black sludge staining the pavement like oil spills. Whatever had caused this collapse, whatever had contaminated these people's lungs with something that resisted divine healing...

It wasn't over.

And I had no idea what we were going to do when the next wave came.

* * *

I grabbed my med kit and yanked out a syringe, jabbing it into the toddler's thigh without hesitation. Pure adrenaline—nothing fancy, just what I needed to keep his heart pumping while I figured out what the hell was happening inside him.

"Commander!" Miller's voice cut through the chaos around us. "We got three more incoming! Building two is collapsing!"

I ignored him, focusing on the Orc boy in my arms. His tiny chest continued its desperate struggle for air, each breath producing another wet, rattling sound that made my stomach turn. I pressed my hands against his ribs again, letting the healing current flow deeper this time.

The white-lilac light surged into his lungs, and I felt it immediately—that same sickening resistance, like pushing through molasses made of broken glass. Except underneath that physical sensation was something else. Something wrong. The contaminant wasn't just matter; it had a texture to it, an almost intentional malevolence. It resisted my magic with what felt like awareness.

"Fuck," I muttered, watching the boy's lips turn a deeper shade of blue.

Behind me, I heard the distinctive crackle of a structural collapse followed by screaming. More casualties. Always more casualties. But if I couldn't figure out how to treat this, then every single one of them would die the exact same way—their lungs filling up with whatever poison had turned the South Side's dust into something that could kill a kid faster than any building collapse.

I pulled back, looking down at the child's face. His mother was still screaming somewhere behind me, but her voice sounded distant now, muffled by the pounding of blood in my ears. I checked his pulse—weak, erratic, fading fast.

The black phlegm on the pavement caught the emergency lights from the surrounding vehicles, making it look like oil shimmering across water. Except oil didn't sizzle when it hit rain. And oil definitely didn't feel like it was actively fighting my healing magic, trying to choke this kid to death while I held him.

"What are you?" I whispered, looking at the substance.

Then the toddler's eyes rolled back and he stopped breathing entirely.

"Dammit!" I slammed my hands back onto his chest, forcing more power into the bio-ward. The white-lilac light flared brighter, intense enough that I saw Miller flinch back. My magic smashed against the dark barrier inside his lungs, and for just a second—a fraction of a heartbeat—I thought I broke through.

But then the resistance pushed back harder, and pain lanced through my own chest cavity like someone had driven a spike between my ribs.

I gasped, my concentration breaking. The light flickered out.

The toddler's body went limp in my arms.

"No." The word came out as barely more than a whisper. "No, no, no."

I placed two fingers against his throat, searching desperately for a pulse that wasn't there anymore.

* * *

The coughing started before we even cleared the rubble field.

I knelt beside the first victim—middle-aged human woman, maybe fifty, with gray streaking through her brown hair and dirt ground deep into the creases of her palms. Her breathing came in wet, labored gasps, each exhale producing a thick rattle like marbles tumbling down a metal chute.

"Ma'am, I need you to take slow breaths for me," I said, one hand already reaching for my stethoscope. "Can you tell me when this started?"

She couldn't answer. Instead, she coughed—a violent, wracking spasm that doubled her over. When it subsided, she spat onto the cracked asphalt between us.

My eyes locked on what hit the ground.

Black-iron flecks, sizzling against the cold February air. The same goddamn substance I'd seen coating the inside of that collapsed basement support column. Only this wasn't oxidized steel. It moved with wrongness, writhing across the pavement like oil on water before fading to rust-brown.

"The whole building's got it," someone croaked from the triage line forming behind me. I glanced up to see another patient—a Dwarven man with soot-stained hands and a broken forearm splinted with torn fabric. His breath came in metallic hacks, and when he opened his mouth to speak more, I caught the glint of black residue coating his tonsils. "Thought it was just damp. We all thought—"

His words dissolved into another fit of coughing.

I stood abruptly, my boots crunching over debris as I moved down the line. Victim after victim showed the same symptom: that distinctive rattling cough, those dark speckles in their throats, the way their lungs sounded like they were filled with gravel and tar.

This wasn't respiratory distress. Not exactly. This was something worse.

"Vance!" My radio crackled—Substation Seven dispatch, voice tight with urgency. "We've got reports of similar incidents spreading through Neon Hollow. Tenement collapse at Seventh and Marston, another at Kearny Road. All showing identical symptoms."

My jaw clenched hard enough to ache. Spreading. Systemic. Deliberate.

I knelt beside an elderly human man—grandfather type, face lined with decades of hard living, eyes glazed with pain and confusion. He coughed weakly, unable to clear whatever was clogging his airways.

"Sir, I need you to breathe for me," I said softly, pulling out my trauma shears. The standard protocol wouldn't work here. This wasn't a simple obstruction or infection. This was... I didn't even have a name for what this was yet.

I pressed my palm against his chest, feeling the labored rise and fall, and reached for the Fourth Law. Warmth built between my fingers—not the clean white-gold of healing, but something darker, more primal. My magic had saved lives in County General ER a thousand times before. But this...

The moment my intent touched his lungs, I felt it: resistance. A cold, heavy sludge that pushed back against my will like thick mud against a shovel blade. Black-iron contamination saturating lung tissue, binding with cellular structure, refusing to be cleansed by pure therapeutic intention.

He coughed again, and I saw blood flecked with those same metallic particles.

Behind me, more victims were arriving via stretcher and ambulance. The coughing chorus grew louder, more desperate. Dozens of people, all showing the exact same symptom.

All poisoned by the same source.

I pulled my hand back from the old man's chest, my breath coming hard through my teeth. The black-iron residue coating his airway wasn't just physical matter. It was corrupted telluric energy—ground magic twisted into something toxic, pumped directly into the South Side water supply.

Someone was poisoning us. Methodically. Deliberately.

And I was on the front lines with no way to stop it.

---

## CHAPTER 9: THE REYES CROSSING

The tent flaps burst open, revealing two figures—one tall and lean, the other shorter and stockier. Both moved with the careful tension of people who'd learned violence young.

"Ma'am!" The taller one shoved his way through, eyes scanning the triage area until they locked onto Elena. His voice carried an edge of desperation that didn't match his hardened demeanor. "Where's Danny?"

Elena's fierce expression softened immediately. "Cole." She stepped around Mara without a backward glance. "He's home with the fever. I came when I heard about the collapse."

"That was hours ago," Cole shot back, running a hand through short dark hair. "His temperature was 104 when I left. I need to get back."

"You should never have left him alone," Elena said sharply, though there was concern underneath. She grabbed a fresh set of gloves from a supply box. "Go sit. I'll finish here."

"He needs medicine," Cole insisted. Behind him, his companion—a stocky man with a scarred face and nervous energy—shifted from foot to foot, casting wary glances at the other patients.

"I know what he needs," Elena snapped back. "Now GO SIT before I stitch you down to a cot just for something to do."

Cole opened his mouth to argue, then seemed to deflate slightly. He jerked his head toward his friend, and both moved to a row of empty cots near the tent's edge. The stocky one sat heavily, elbows on knees, while Cole remained standing, radiating barely-contained anxiety.

Mara watched them, noting how the ambient temperature around Cole seemed noticeably colder than the rest of the tent. A fine mist began forming in the air near his hands.

"Stop staring and help me move this patient," Elena muttered beside her, already lifting one end of a gurney.

The work continued relentlessly—stitches, dressings, IV lines. Around midnight, a commotion erupted outside. Shouts. Then gunfire—three sharp cracks that made several patients flinch.

"Gang territory dispute," Elena said flatly, not looking up from an injection she was preparing. "The Vipers and the Iron Saints are fighting over whatever scraps they can find in the rubble. Happens every night now."

Through the tent opening, Mara caught glimpses of flashlight beams cutting through darkness, men running between collapsed buildings. The Vipers wore red bandanas. The others were harder to distinguish.

"We need security in here," Mara said, reaching for her radio.

"You think your corporate guards will come into the South Side?" Elena laughed bitterly. "Half of them are afraid we'll bite. The other half are paid off by the gangs anyway."

A woman at the far end of the triage area suddenly screamed. Blood bloomed across her chest—not from gang violence, but from the black veins spreading up her neck like parasitic roots. Another Breach-related infection.

Elena was there instantly, pushing aside two younger medics. "Back! Everyone back!" She grabbed scissors and began cutting away the woman's clothes with brutal efficiency. "Mara! Get me the containment field equipment!"

But when Mara turned toward their supply station, she found Cole Reyes standing there instead of where he'd been sitting. His hands were clenched into fists, frost forming on his knuckles, spreading up his forearms in delicate crystalline patterns. His breathing came hard and fast.

"Easy," Mara said carefully, holding out her hands. "I know you're scared about your brother. But I need you to calm down before—"

"I'm fine," Cole cut her off, voice strained. He deliberately opened his hands, and the frost sublimated into a cold mist that drifted upward like smoke.

* * *

The tent flaps parted, and a young man stepped inside, carrying a battered, unconscious Gnome over his shoulder.

He was twenty-one years old, tall and broad-shouldered, wearing a heavy canvas Carhartt jacket stained with motor oil and concrete dust. His face was smeared with grease, his dark eyes hard and unreadable. As he walked past me, I felt an unnatural chill in the air—a sudden, sharp drop in the ambient temperature that made my breath plume slightly in the humid tent.

It was a nascent telluric aura. Dead-silent, zero-remorse frost-cobalt. It wasn't fully formed yet, but the raw, freezing anger radiating off him was palpable.

"Cole," Elena said, her harsh demeanor instantly softening as she rushed forward. "Put him on cot three."

Cole Reyes gently laid the Gnome onto the canvas cot. He reached into his pocket, the heavy clink of wrenches sounding against the fabric, and pulled out a rag to wipe the blood from the Gnome's face.

"Found him pinned under a radiator on the second floor," Cole said, his voice a low, gravelly baritone that perfectly matched the gritty 2000s cadence of the South Side. "Leg's crushed. But he's breathing."

Elena quickly began assessing the Gnome. "Are you hurt, Cole? You shouldn't be digging in that rubble without a hardhat."

"I'm fine, Ma," Cole said, stepping back. He looked exhausted, the weight of the city already settling heavily on his young shoulders. "I need to get back to the apartment. Danny's coughing again. It's worse tonight. That black sludge is coating the inside of his throat."

Elena closed her eyes for a brief second, a flash of pure agony crossing her face. "Give him the expectorant from the blue bottle. I'll be home as soon as I can."

Cole nodded. He turned to leave, his eyes briefly locking onto me. He took in my pristine tactical gear, the glowing Aegis badge, and the soft white-lilac light still lingering on my fingertips. His expression didn't change, but the temperature around him seemed to drop another degree. He didn't say a word to me. He just turned and walked back out into the freezing rain.

The flaps settled behind him with a wet rustle. The tent suddenly felt warmer.

"Pay him no mind," Elena muttered without looking up from the Gnome she was stabilizing. Her hands moved with practiced efficiency—checking pulse points, examining the extent of injuries beneath torn clothing. "Cole's been carrying the world since he was sixteen. Now it's Danny's turn to weigh on him."

She glanced at me then, those sharp eyes missing nothing. "You're new. Fresh from Academy. I can smell the soap on your uniform." She jerked her chin toward the unconscious Gnome. "This one needs transport. Leg's shattered below the knee. Internal bleeding we can't stop here. You got an ambulance?"

"Yes, Commander. Two blocks north."

"Then move it. And take Cole with you when you go. The boy needs to see someone who isn't drowning in this mess." She paused, adding quietly, "He thinks he's strong enough to carry us all. Prove him wrong."

I was already moving, radio crackling at my belt as I requested immediate extraction coordinates. The Gnome's breathing was shallow, ragged. Time-sensitive. My EMT training kicked in, years of field work overriding the strange encounter with Cole Reyes.

But even as I worked, calculating IV drip rates and oxygen flow, part of my mind kept replaying that frost-cobalt aura. Nascent. Raw. Untrained. A young man barely holding his telluric powers in check while the entire South Side collapsed around him.

I pushed through the tent flaps into the chaos of the collapse zone. The rain had intensified, turning the rubble into a slurry of concrete and rebar. Emergency lights painted everything in sickly yellows and reds. Somewhere in the distance, a building groaned—a deep, structural death rattle that made my teeth ache.

Cole was nowhere to be seen.

* * *

The tent's fluorescent lights flickered once, twice, then steadied as power returned from the generator. Through the canvas walls, I could see Cole's silhouette receding into the darkness beyond our perimeter, moving with that same mechanical precision he'd shown with the engine.

Elena emerged from surgery, face streaked with blood—not all of it patient's—and fatigue written in every line of her body. "Mara. We need to talk about the Gnome."

I turned from watching Cole disappear into the rain-soaked night. "Is he stable?"

"He'll live." She grabbed my arm, pulling me toward the far corner where our supplies were stored. Her voice dropped to barely a whisper. "But I did a full tox screen while we had the equipment running. Every single person from that building—every one—has elevated levels of heavy metals in their system. Lead, mercury, cadmium."

"The black-iron water," I said.

She nodded sharply. "And it's been going on for months. Maybe years." Elena pulled out a crumpled paper from her scrubs—a printout from the analyzer. The numbers were damning. "This isn't accidental contamination. This is systematic poisoning."

My mind raced back to what Cole had said. *They're the ones dumping it.* Had he known? How long had the Reyes family been living with this knowledge?

"We have to report this," I said. "Immediately. BATC needs to—"

"BATC?" Elena cut me off, her eyes flashing. "Mara, you've been working this side of Newark for three years now. When has that agency ever done anything but whitewash corporate negligence?"

"But it's our job to report—"

"It's our job to save lives tonight." She gripped my shoulder hard enough to hurt. "After that, we figure out how to actually make things change. Not just file a report that gets filed away in some bureaucrat's office."

The generator coughed outside, steady and reliable. Somewhere in the tent behind us, the Gnome was waking up to a life with permanent nerve damage. Danny Reyes was at home with fluid in his lungs. And I stood there holding evidence of a crime so vast it made my stomach turn.

Elena released my arm. "I'm staying here until dawn. Someone has to keep watch on these patients. You take that sample to BATC. But Mara..." She paused, searching my face. "Don't just deliver it like a good little EMT. Make them listen. Scream if you have to. Because people are dying, and we both know who's responsible."

I thought of Cole walking into the night, the cold rolling off him like judgment itself. A sliver of justice. The phrase echoed in my skull.

I tucked the vial deeper into my pocket, feeling its weight—a small, terrible burden—and headed toward Sub-Station Seven where my car was parked.

---

## CHAPTER 10: THE BURIED VIAL

The fluorescent lights hummed overhead like dying insects as I waited in the observation room behind thick glass. Through it, I could see the lab tech—a skinny Gnome named Piotr who always smelled faintly of burnt coffee—working the controls of the mass spectrometer. His goggles reflected the blue glow from the machine's interface.

My fingers drummed against my thigh inside the pocket of my Aegis jacket. Twenty minutes now since I'd submitted the sample. Twenty minutes while my mind kept circling back to Reyes' smirk, to Martinez's dead eyes, to the way the black water had looked against pale lung tissue under the scope back at County General.

The door hissed open behind me. I turned, expecting another tech, but instead found myself face-to-face with Director Chen from BATC's Environmental Division. Her smile was thin and professional, the kind that doesn't reach your eyes.

"Commander Vance," she said smoothly, extending a manicured hand. "We've been monitoring your case files. Quite the workload you're carrying out there on the South Side."

I shook her hand briefly, noting how her grip was firm but calculated. "Director. I'm waiting for preliminary results from this sample."

Chen's smile widened fractionally. "Actually, we've already reviewed them. The analysis is complete." She gestured toward Piotr's station where he was now printing out readouts. "Perhaps we should discuss the findings in more detail, away from the noise."

Something in my chest tightened. "There shouldn't be any need for privacy. This is standard protocol—a contaminant identification, full documentation."

"Standard protocol also includes executive briefings when potential liability exceeds certain thresholds." Chen's tone remained pleasant, but her eyes had gone cold. "We've classified your findings as Level Three—corporate sensitivity required."

The words hit like a punch to the gut. Level Three meant cover-up. It meant someone powerful didn't want this information public.

Piotr approached cautiously, holding a stack of printouts. He glanced between us nervously before setting them on the observation counter. "Here are the readings, Commander. Full spectral analysis, elemental breakdown, organic compound identification..."

I snatched up the top sheet, my eyes scanning rapidly through columns of data. Carbon. Hydrogen. Oxygen. Nitrogen. Standard enough. Then I saw it—trace elements of something marked with a red flag: *THAL-9, synthetic origin, industrial catalyst.*

"Thallium-based compound," I muttered, flipping through the subsequent pages. "Heavy metal poisoning agent, stabilized with arcano-chemical binding agents to make it psychologically inert. This isn't runoff. This is deliberate contamination."

"It appears so," Chen said softly, stepping beside me and pointing at another section of the report. "Note here—the manufacturing markers match three different BATC subsidiaries operating out of the Newark Bay industrial zone. The water table beneath the South Side housing projects has been systematically poisoned over the past eighteen months."

My hands were shaking now. Eighteen months. That meant Martinez, Reyes, everyone we'd lost in that district... they hadn't died from shoddy infrastructure or bad luck. They'd been murdered by their own company. By our company.

"We need to file immediate reports," I said, my voice strained. "Evacuations, medical interventions for exposed populations, criminal investigation—"

Chen's hand came down on mine, stopping me from reaching my radio. Her grip was surprisingly strong. "Commander, you're upset. Understandable. But you need to consider the broader picture."

"The broader picture?" I yanked my hand free. "People are dying!"

"And more will die if this becomes public knowledge." She gestured at the printouts. "Think about the stock value, Commander. Think about shareholder confidence, regulatory investigations, litigation costs running into the billions. An entire division of BATC could collapse. Thousands of jobs lost across multiple sectors."

"So we just let them keep dying?"

"We manage the situation." Chen's smile had vanished entirely now, replaced by something hard and businesslike. "Here's what's going to happen: You'll seal these findings under Level Three protocol. You'll continue your investigations but focus on prevention measures rather than source identification. We'll redirect contaminated water flows, implement filtration systems, treat affected residents quietly through our medical network."

"You want me to bury this."

"I want you to be strategic." She pulled a document from her briefcase—a formal promotion packet bearing my name. "Commander Mara Vance, promoted to Section Chief of South Side Operations. Authority over all field teams in Districts 7-12. Substantial salary increase, executive benefits package."

My eyes fixed on the paper even as disgust churned in my stomach. A promotion. They were offering me a gold-plated cage.

"In exchange," Chen continued smoothly, "you provide confidential testimony at a closed-door internal hearing. You acknowledge that while contamination exists, its source is indeterminate—possibly industrial accidents, possibly terrorist sabotage targeting infrastructure. You recommend increased security funding for your district instead of external investigation."

I looked back through the glass at Piotr, who was carefully sealing the original sample vials in evidence lockers. He didn't look happy about it either.

"What happens to the people still breathing that water right now?" I asked quietly.

"We deploy portable filtration units within forty-eight hours. We offer voluntary relocation incentives to high-risk populations. It's a comprehensive solution."

A comprehensive lie. A managed truth where BATC could control the narrative and limit their liability without ever admitting culpability.

"My promotion letter requires my signature," Chen said, sliding it across the counter toward me along with a pen. "Sign, and this becomes an opportunity for both you and your career. Refuse..." She let the implication hang in the air. "And I'm sure we can find another commander better suited to execute our new strategic directives. Someone more... flexible."

The pen felt heavy in my hand. Through the glass, I could see Piotr finishing up, boxing away the evidence that would prove corporate murder. My other hand moved unconsciously to my chest pocket where I kept my personal notes, the ones I'd been keeping separate from official channels.

If I signed, I became complicit. But if I refused, they'd just bury someone else—the investigation, the victims, all of it. And I'd be out of position to do anything about it.

The fluorescent lights hummed on, indifferent and cold as justice.

* * *

I pressed my back against the cool glass of the pillar, watching them disappear around the corner. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. The coffee cup trembled in my grip.

They knew. All this time—every contaminated victim I'd dragged from those flooded streets, every burn case from the chemical runoff—they'd known exactly what was happening. And they didn't care.

The white-lilac glow around my fingers flickered, responding to the rage building in my chest. I forced it down, smothering the light until only the faintest shimmer remained. Getting emotional now would be suicide. These people played for keeps.

I waited ten minutes. Fifteen. Long enough for them to clear the building. Then I moved.

My boots clicked softly against the polished floor as I approached the intake counter where Thorne had taken the vial. The Gnome tech looked up at me, his eyes wide with fear.

"Lieutenant Vance," he stammered. "I—I don't know anything."

I placed both palms on the counter, leaning forward just enough to make him uncomfortable. "The hell you don't. You handed that poison to Agent Thorne like she was taking a goddamn prescription. What's your name?"

"K-Kevin. Kevin O'Malley." His Adam's apple bobbed nervously.

"You're going to tell me everything about Sector 7, Kevin. Starting with why you have black-iron water on a County General intake log instead of at some high-security biohazard facility." I kept my voice low but sharp as broken glass. "And you're going to do it right fucking now."

His eyes darted left, then right, searching for an escape route that wasn't there. Sweat beaded on his upper lip despite the lab's climate control.

"It wasn't supposed to come here," he finally whispered. "Sector 7 is—it's one of the waste processing plants near the Kearny Marshes. They've been dumping stabilized chemical runoff into the Newark Bay for years. We thought it was contained. But last month, something changed. The stabilization process started failing."

"How?" My magic pulsed again, unbidden. I clamped down hard, forcing it back into submission.

He shook his head. "I don't know. The engineers from High-Spire Labs came in, did their tests, and then... nothing. The reports stopped coming through official channels. Everything went dark." He wiped his hands on his lab coat, a nervous gesture. "Then yesterday, we got a sample. It showed up in our intake system with no paperwork, no warning. Just... appeared. I called Agent Thorne immediately."

"Did she say anything? Anything at all before she took the vial?"

Kevin's face went pale. "She said it never existed. That if anyone asked, the intake log had been scrubbed clean." His voice dropped to barely a whisper. "But Lieutenant, I made a backup copy. Before they erased the main record. I—I didn't trust them."

My blood went cold. "Where?"

He gestured toward a computer terminal behind him. "Password protected. I'll delete it after you leave. Please. I have kids."

I stared at him for a long moment, measuring his fear against my own desperation. Finally, I nodded. "Show me."

The file opened with a click. A digital photograph of the vial, timestamped and logged. Below it: chemical composition analysis, stability readings, origin coordinates pinpointed to a specific BATC processing plant near the marshes. And beneath that—most damning of all—a memo chain between Sterling and Voss discussing cost-benefit analyses on "stabilization failures" versus "labor disruption mitigation."

They'd weighed human lives against profit margins. And found the bodies cheaper.

"How many people know about this?" I asked.

"I don't know. Maybe a dozen engineers at Sector 7. Some techs here. But everyone who could talk has either gone silent or disappeared."

Disappeared. The word settled in my stomach like lead.

"Send me that file," I said. "Encrypted. Burn your copy afterward."

Kevin hesitated only a second before hitting send. My PalmPilot chimed softly in my pocket. "It's done," he said. "God help us both, Lieutenant."

I was already walking away when he called out: "What are you going to do?"

I glanced back over my shoulder, meeting his terrified gaze. "What I should've done from the start."

The elevator doors closed behind me with a pneumatic hiss. As we descended toward the ground floor, I pulled up the encrypted file on my PalmPilot, scrolling through the damning data. The numbers didn't lie. The coordinates didn't lie. The chemical signatures matched every contaminated victim I'd treated.

High-Spire Labs wasn't just aware of the poison. They were manufacturing it.

And now they'd caught me looking.

* * *

The elevator descended through floors of sterile concrete and fluorescent lighting, each level bringing Mara deeper into the belly of High-Spire Labs. She could feel it pressing against her ribs—the weight of Briggs's words, the slick lie about a "lost sample," the gilded cage of promotion he'd offered like candy to a child who'd just watched her world burn.

Her fists were still clenched inside her pockets, knuckles aching from how hard she'd gripped them during that meeting. The white-lilac light of her magic pulsed faintly there, barely controlled, like a fever she couldn't shake. It wanted out. Wanted to tear through these walls and find the truth buried beneath layers of corporate rot.

*Keep it frosty.*

She repeated Graves's mantra like a prayer, forcing her breathing to slow. The elevator dinged—sub-level three—and the doors hissed open onto a loading dock thick with exhaust fumes and the chemical tang of the Kearny Marshes beyond. Night had fallen while she was in that suffocating office, and now the warehouse district sprawled before her like a tombstone graveyard of container units and rusted shipping containers.

"Commander Vance?"

She turned. A younger tech—couldn't have been more than twenty-two, face still soft around the edges—stood near a row of evidence lockers, his BATC uniform crisp but ill-fitting. He held up an evidence tag on a lanyard.

"I'm Martinez. They said you'd be coming down for the... uh..." He trailed off, glancing nervously at the shadowed corners of the loading dock. "The secured transport."

Mara's jaw tightened. "Show me."

Martinez led her past rows of climate-controlled storage units, their digital readouts blinking green against the concrete. At the far end, sealed behind a reinforced door with dual-key access, sat what looked like an unmarked black van. But Mara recognized the plates—custom government issue, magnetic field dampeners built into the chassis.

"The sample," she said flatly.

"That's the thing." Martinez pulled out a keycard and swiped it through the reader. "It wasn't lost, Commander. Not officially. It was transferred under a Level Five security directive. Classified transfer protocol. We were ordered not to log the destination until confirmation from Sector Command." His voice dropped lower. "But my supervisor—he's old school. Made me write it down anyway. In case things went sideways."

He handed her a small notebook. Inside, scrawled in hurried handwriting:

*Sample 9-ALPHA: Transferred 1800 hrs. Destination: Sterling Manor Research Facility. Contact: Dr. Lysandra Voss. Security Detail: Omega Team. No further access authorized.*

Mara stared at those words. Sterling Manor. The name sent ice crawling up her spine. She knew that place—not by reputation, but by the look in Reyes's eyes when he'd mentioned it back in Sub-Station Seven. A place where people disappeared. Where evidence went to die.

"Did you see who picked it up?" Her voice came out sharp as broken glass.

Martinez shook his head. "Black SUVs. Tinted windows. Armed guards in civilian dress. They didn't say much. Just... took it." He paused, then added quietly, "Commander Vance? I've been doing logistics for six months now. I've seen a lot of classified transfers. This one felt different. Like they were scared of it."

Mara closed the notebook, tucking it into her tactical vest. Outside, beyond the loading dock, thunder rumbled across Newark Bay. Rain had started falling, fat drops hammering against the corrugated metal roof above them.

She thought of the vial burning in her palm back in those marshlands. The way the liquid inside had pulsed with that sickly green luminescence. Whatever was in Sample 9-Alpha, it was important enough to bury under layers of bureaucracy and lies.

Important enough to kill for.

"Martinez," she said, turning back toward him. "How long have you been working this dock?"

"Three years, ma'am. Started right after—" He stopped himself, swallowing hard. "Right after the Breach."

The Millennium Breach. That night in March '99 when reality itself had torn open like rotted fabric, spilling otherworldly horrors into North Jersey's streets while Mara and Cole had been trapped in County General ER, fighting just to survive. Before everything changed. Before the world learned magic was real and monsters walked among men.

Before she'd lost half of herself trying to keep people alive.

"I need you to do something for me," Mara continued, pulling out her phone. She pulled up the photo she'd taken—snapshots from the crime scene log before the system had "corrupted." The sample. The coordinates. Everything. "I'm going to send you some files. Encrypted. I want you to burn them onto a drive and get them somewhere safe. Somewhere off BATC servers."

"Why?" Martinez's eyes went wide with fear. "Commander, if they catch me—"

"If they buried this sample, they're covering up something bigger than one contaminated site in the marshes." Mara met his gaze dead-on. "And if there's one cover-up, there are others. People deserve to know what's really happening out there. Not the sanitized version they feed us on the nightly news."

She hit send on the encrypted file transfer, watching it ping across secure channels to his device. His hands trembled as he caught it, thumb hovering over the download button.

"Martinez," she added softly. "Whatever happens next, you didn't hear any of this from me. You don't know anything. Understand?"

He nodded quickly, then rushed back toward the administrative offices without another word. Smart kid. He knew when to run.

Mara stood alone in the loading dock, rain hammering down outside while thunder rolled like dying gods across the sky. Sterling Manor Research Facility. Lysandra Voss.

The name resonated in some deep, buried part of her memory—not personal knowledge but institutional. Instructor Graves had mentioned it once during advanced tactical training: a black-site research facility specializing in containment protocols for breach entities that couldn't be killed or controlled through conventional means.

A place where the Aegis Sector buried their mistakes.

Her phone buzzed—a text from unknown number:

*STAY OUT OF STERLING MANOR, COMMANDER. SOME WALLS ARE MEANT TO REMAIN STANDING.*

Mara deleted the message without reading further. Then she turned and walked back toward the elevators, her white-lilac magic burning cold and bright inside her chest like a star refusing to die.

They wanted her to play the golden saint.

Fine. She'd play along.

But first, she was going to find out exactly what they were hiding in Sterling Manor—and why Lysandra Voss wanted Sample 9-Alpha badly enough to drag it into the darkest corners of BATC's underworld.

The elevator doors slid shut behind her with a soft hiss, sealing Mara away from the loading dock and its secrets. As she rose upward through High-Spire Labs' tower

---

## CHAPTER 11: THE GOLDEN SAINT OF NEON HOLLOW

The green room smells like chemical rain.

I sit rigid in the makeup chair, shoulders squared despite the weight settling into my spine—part stress, part the unfamiliar heft of Lieutenant bars on my collar. Silver, freshly minted, cold as surgical steel. The Aegis tactical jacket chafes at my neck where the zipper sits too high, too tight. Everything about this uniform screams *authority* when what I feel is a child playing dress-up in her father's coat.

"Tilt your head left. Good. Left some more."

Saelis circles like a shark in Armani, her silver stylus tapping a nervous rhythm against her PalmPilot IIIc. The device chirps softly—a synthesized voice whispering focus-group demographics into her ear while she watches my reflection with eyes that miss nothing and understand less.

"You know what the numbers are saying?" She doesn't wait for an answer. They never do. "Sixty-three percent positive response to 'pure white-lilac.' The Orc communities, they're scared shitless, Vance. Mutations. Conspiracies. We need you to look..." she pauses, gesturing at my face with the stylus, "...reassuring."

The vanity lights buzz overhead, harsh fluorescent halogens that make my skin look paper-thin. I can see every pore, every faint line etching itself deeper around my eyes from nights spent in County General's ER. The makeup artist—human, blessedly silent—dabs concealer under my lower lids. Foundation. Powder. Each layer another mask.

"I'm a trauma paramedic," I say flatly. "Not a sparkler."

"The public needs a saint." Saelis taps her screen. "Golden Saint. That's the new branding. Focus groups ate it up."

My jaw clenches. I taste copper.

The bio-wards hum beneath my sternum—not happy, not angry, but aware. Caged. White-lilac burning with suppressed energy, fresh cedar crackling with potential that wants to *move*, to *heal*, to burn through arterial tears and bone fractures. Instead it sits coiled tight behind my ribs, buzzing like trapped bees. The sterile air conditioning makes it worse, recycling the same dead atmosphere over and over until my magic feels like it's suffocating.

"When you step to that podium—" Saelis is still talking, her voice smooth as corporate spin, fast as a auctioneer, "—I want a soft push of cedar. Not the full thing. Just enough so the cameras catch it. Make them feel safe. Make them feel managed."

*Managed.* The word settles in my gut like spoiled milk.

I meet my own eyes in the mirror. They're dark, tired, reflecting the harsh lights without giving anything back. My hair has been forced into submission with aerosol hairspray—the smell cloying, synthetic lavender mixed with acetone—and pulled back severe. Professional. Contained.

Everything about this moment screams *prop*.

"You submitted those water samples three weeks ago," Saelis continues, softer now, almost sympathetic. Almost. "High-Spire has been running analysis. They'll present findings alongside your 'reassurance speech.' Everything will be fine, Lieutenant. We just need you to smile for the cameras first."

The way she says *Lieutenant* tastes like a bribe.

I think about the Orc on the docks two nights ago. His skin had gone translucent around the edges where the contaminated water touched him, veins showing black against gray flesh like ink bleeding through wet paper. He'd screamed while I worked on him, not from pain but from terror—the certainty that his body was betraying him, cell by cell, mutation creeping inward no matter how many IVs we ran or how bright we made the trauma bay lights.

"Smiling doesn't stop mutations," I say quietly.

"Public relations does." Saelis smiles, and it's beautiful and empty as a doll's face. "You've earned clearance to see the full report after today's briefing. Access to Sub-Station Seven's archives. But first—"

She gestures toward the door. Beyond it, I can hear voices, cameras whirring to life, the controlled chaos of a media briefing room warming up.

"—you sell them safety."

My hands curl into fists in my lap. The white-lilac flares hot for a heartbeat, singeing the air with absolute purity before I crush it down again. Bite it back. Make myself small enough to fit inside their corporate box.

"I want to see those reports," I say. "Before the cameras."

"You will." Another beautiful lie. "After."

The makeup artist finishes, stepping back. I look polished, professional, *perfect*. Like a weapon someone else designed. Someone else loaded. Someone else aims.

Saelis extends her hand. "Ready to save the world, Golden Saint?"

I take her hand because I have to. Because Lieutenant bars mean security clearance means answers. Because three weeks of waiting has hollowed me out until all that's left is hunger for truth.

"The water samples," I press one last time. "Show me proof they're clean."

Her smile never wavers. "Come on, Lieutenant. Let's go show everyone how safe they are."

The green room door swings open.

Beyond it: fluorescent lights brighter than these, harsher. Cameras. Microphones. Hundreds of eyes wanting salvation they don't deserve from a saint they don't need.

And beneath it all, hidden in plain sight, the rot spreading through Newark Bay like poison.

I stand.
