I watched Elena's hands shake as she keyed the power button, tried again. Nothing. The Nextel was a brick now, its secrets locked tighter than a virgin on prom night.

"Cole." Her eyes were huge in her skull, pupils blown wide. She grabbed my wrist—harder than I'd ever felt her touch before. "You need to go. Now."

"What? No, we need to—"

"The backup drive." She was already moving, yanking open drawers at the clinic's ancient filing cabinet, papers scattering like autumn leaves. Her movements were frantic, desperate. "It's not done. The encryption took longer than expected. Go to Danny. Guard him. Don't let anyone near that workshop."

"I'm not leaving you here alone." My jaw set stubborn. South Side pride, stupid and thick as concrete.

"You don't have a choice!" She slammed a canvas tote shut, shoved it into my chest hard enough to knock me back a step. "Danny is alone with the Iron-Lung. If the power dips, he suffocates. *Go!*"

I wanted to argue. Every fiber of my being screamed to stay, to fight, to do something other than run away while my mother faced down assassins in a freezing clinic that smelled like disinfectant and desperation. But I heard the hum of Danny's lung in my head—that constant mechanical wheeze, the rhythm I'd memorized during those long hours welding arcane iron, keeping it stable, alive.

"If anything happens to—"

"It won't." Her smile was terrible, brave, broken. "I'll be right behind you. Just... ten minutes. Finish the backup. Then I'm coming."

She pushed me toward the door. I stumbled backward, caught myself on the frame. Through the dusty window I could see nothing but darkness pressing against the glass, the city holding its breath.

"Elena..."

"Ten minutes, mijo." She turned away from me, bent over her laptop, fingers flying across keys like she was conducting some kind of digital exorcism. "Then we run together."

The fire-door swung shut behind me with a heavy thud that echoed through my bones. The lock clicked home. I pressed my palm against the cold metal, feeling the vibrations of footsteps inside—the frantic rustle of papers, the desperate click-clack of keys—but couldn't make myself turn the handle again.

Couldn't bring myself to look at her face one more time.

The March wind cut through my jacket like knives made of ice and regret as I ran toward Kearny, toward Danny, toward the workshop that suddenly felt miles away instead of blocks. Behind me, somewhere in that darkened clinic, my mother faced down the Shadow Serpent's Four Heads with nothing but a laptop and a lie about backing up files.

I didn't know then that I would never hear her voice again.

I didn't know that when I finally made it back to the South Side with police sirens wailing in the distance behind me, that the clinic would be dark, empty, the smell of copper hanging thick in the air where Elena Reyes had breathed her last.

But the blood-iron magic humming in my veins knew.

It sang its warning in metallic dread even as I ran, faster, desperately, toward a future that had just been rewritten without her in it.

* * *

The February air hits me like a slap across the face when I burst out of the clinic's back door. Cold. Sharp. Real. Unlike whatever the fuck I just saw on that screen.

My boots splash through puddles in the alley—black water reflecting the sodium lights that bleed orange against the brick walls. The '99 Crown Vic sits there like an old friend, dented hood and all. I yank open the driver's side, and the engine coughs to life with a deep V8 rumble that shakes the whole frame.

I don't bother with seatbelts. Just slam it into drive and floor it.

The South Side blurs past my window—a kaleidoscope of flickering neon signs advertising check cashing places, bodegas selling dream books and loose cigarettes, and the occasional flicker of arcane light from some occultist's shop front. Rain starts coming down harder now, streaking the windshield with dirty water. I wipe it manually. No cruise control in this beast, no fancy wipers that actually work right.

My hands grip the steering wheel until my knuckles go white. And beneath that pressure, I can feel it—that humming warmth starting to spike. Blood-iron magic doesn't ask permission. It responds to adrenaline, to fear, to rage. Right now it's all three.

"Fuck," I mutter, loosening my grip slightly. The wheel creaks as I ease off.

The city stretches out before me, a maze of industrial decay and desperate hope. Pulaski Skyway looms in the distance, its concrete arches disappearing into the rain-soaked night. Somewhere under there, Danny's mother is probably still working double shifts at County General ER. Still fighting battles she doesn't know are already lost.

I think about what I saw. Those documents. Sterling Manor on the manifest. The High-Spire Elves' signatures. And underneath it all—that symbol. The one that matches the brand on Danny's back.

Coincidence? Bullshit. There's no such thing in a world where magic bleeds through reality like rust through iron.

Twenty minutes later—I'm not counting anymore—I pull up outside the chop-shop garage. The bay doors are half-open, just enough for my Crown Vic to squeeze through. Inside, the space smells like motor oil and brass shavings, hot metal and ozone. My workshop. My sanctuary.

"Danny?" I call out, killing the engine. The sudden silence feels wrong. "Elena?"

No answer except the rhythmic *hiss-thump, hiss-thump* coming from downstairs. The Iron-Lung never stops. Can't stop. Not while Danny needs it breathing for him.

I take the stairs two at a time down to the sub-basement, flashlight beam cutting through the gloom. Water drips somewhere in the darkness—plumbing issues I haven't had time to fix—and my footsteps echo off concrete walls lined with my tools and spare parts.

The Arcane Iron-Lung dominates the space. Brass tubes gleam dully in my flashlight beam. Glass chambers fogged with condensation. Pressure gauges clicking softly as they cycle through their measurements.

And inside... Danny. Small form curled up in the main chamber, suspended in that artificial womb of arcane engineering. His chest rises and falls with each mechanical breath the machine provides.

"He's stable," I whisper, checking the gauges anyway. Needles hovering right where they should be. For now.

But I can feel it—that spike in my blood-iron magic getting stronger. Like something's calling to me from deep inside this machine, or maybe from deeper inside myself.

My Nokia pager vibrates on my belt. 911 code from Elena.

Then—a sound from above. A muffled *THUMP* that rattles every window in the garage.

The glass chambers of the Iron-Lung sing in response, tiny fractures spiderwebbing across one pane.

"Shit."

I grab my phone before I even process what I'm doing.

---

## CHAPTER 7: THE NECRO-THERMITE PROTOCOL

My boots slammed against concrete as I burst from the machine shop's fire exit, the metallic tang of blood still coating my tongue. Behind me, the steel door clanged shut—locked down tight, the way Elena taught me. No witnesses. No loose ends.

The Crown Vic sat where I'd left it, engine ticking as it cooled in the February chill. I yanked open the driver's side door hard enough that the latch popped, threw myself behind the wheel, and fired the ignition.

The V8 roared to life like an angry god waking from sleep.

I didn't bother with seatbelts. My hands—still shaking slightly from the adrenaline dump back at Sub-Station Seven—gripped the leather-wrapped steering wheel as I floored it out of the alley. Tires screamed against wet asphalt, leaving twin trails of black rubber that stank of burned synthetic compounds. The Crown Vic lurched forward with violent acceleration.

"Come on, come *on*," I muttered through clenched teeth, slamming the shifter into third. A beat-to-shit Honda Civic ran a yellow light ahead of me—I didn't slow down. Horn blaring, I cut hard right around them, hornet-stitching through the intersection as their headlights painted my interior in strobing white flashes.

The South Side streets blurred past, neon signs bleeding into watercolor smears against rain-slick pavement. Budget Motel 6. Check Cashing. All-Night Diner with its flickering "OPEN" sign. Each landmark meant distance covered, seconds shaved off whatever was happening at the clinic.

My Nextel crackled to life on the passenger seat. I snatched it up one-handed while swerving around a pothole the size of a bathtub.

Static. Then screaming—no, not screaming. Something worse. A signal caught between dimensions, raw quantum noise that made my teeth ache and my left eye twitch. Whatever number I'd dialed, it wasn't connecting.

"Fuck." I threw the device back onto the seat, knuckles going white again on the wheel.

Then I saw it: rising above the rooftops like a tombstone made of night itself—a column of smoke unlike anything natural. Blue-black and writhing, pulsing with a rhythm that suggested something breathing inside it. Necro-Thermite. The stuff Elena had whispered about once during a three-day bender, when we were both too drunk on cheap whiskey to care what we said.

"The only fire that burns cold," she'd slurred, tapping ash from her Camel Light. "Burns away flesh without heat. Turns bone to powder, leaves the soul trapped in the residue."

I slammed my palm against the steering wheel hard enough to set off the horn—that ugly mechanical blare cutting through the night. My heart hammered so hard I could feel it in my throat, taste copper blood again.

A Razor-Wire Street-Elf on a crotch-rocket screamed past going the wrong way down a one-way street, his yellow eyes reflecting in my mirror for just a second before he vanished into an alley. Didn't even register whether he was friendly or looking to peal my skin off for sport.

The smoke plume grew thicker as I approached, spreading across the sky like bruised clouds pregnant with storms. My foot stayed pinned to the accelerator. The Crown Vic's engine howled in protest, pushing sixty through neighborhoods where fifty was aggressive.

A semi-truck—one of those industrial haulers pulling double-wides stacked with shipping containers—loomed suddenly around a corner. Its halogen headlights turned night into noon, blinded me with their glare reflecting off rain-slick pavement. I jerked the wheel left, tires losing grip, fishtailing across two lanes before I caught it.

"Shit! *SHIT!*"

The trucker laid on his air horns—a deep, mournful sound that shook my bones—and swerved wide. In my rearview, I saw him brake lights flaring red as he slowed to navigate around the madness in his path.

Another vehicle was coming *toward* me now, cutting through the opposite lane. A trauma-ambulance, all chrome and brutalist angles, its emergency lights painting everything in strobing reds and blues. Behind the wheel sat an Ogre-kin paramedic, his massive frame hunched over the controls, heading straight for the same destination I was racing toward.

We passed each other like bullets, close enough that I could see his face—furrowed brow, tusks glinting, eyes locked forward with grim determination. He didn't slow down either.

Then the smell hit me.

Burning copper. Chemical accelerants. That unique stench of necromantic combustion bleeding through the Crown Vic's ventilation system, turning the recycled cabin air toxic and wrong. I killed the AC with a jab of my finger, but the smell clung to everything—the upholstery, my clothes, the inside of my nose.

I turned the final corner onto the clinic's block and slammed on the brakes.

The wall of heat hit my windshield like a physical blow—dry, suffocating, unnatural in its intensity despite the blue-black smoke promising cold fire. The Crown Vic skidded sideways, nose pointed at the burning building, tires screaming their protest against asphalt.

And there it stood: Dr. Elena Volkov's clandestine medical facility, half-consumed by flames that shouldn't have been possible, surrounded by a perimeter I couldn't yet see but felt pressing against my awareness like static electricity before lightning strikes.

I threw open the door and ran into hell itself.

* * *

I slammed the car door and ran.

The clinic was burning.

Not just burning—the whole three-story brick building was *writhing* under a writhing blanket of flame that shouldn't exist in nature. Blue-black tendrils shot up from shattered windows like frozen lightning, spitting jagged spatters of residue that sizzled when they hit the pavement. The sound wasn't crackling wood or roaring gas—it was a *screaming*, a high-pitched metallic shriek that made my teeth ache.

"MAMA!"

My voice tore raw from my throat. I was already twenty feet past where I'd abandoned the Buick, engine still running, hazard lights blinking uselessly at the destruction ahead.

This wasn't fire.

The flames were wrong—too sharp-edged, too hungry. They clawed across brick and mortar like iron gall etching copper, leaving behind charred tracks that glowed white-hot before crumbling into ash. A parked sedan thirty feet from the building's front entrance had its paint bubbling black in sheets. Another one had collapsed on melted tires.

I could feel it even from here—the cold. My breath came out frost-white. The temperature around me dropped ten degrees as my magic flared in panic, ice crystals forming and dissolving along my fingertips. Something primal had triggered deep in my bloodstream, the first stage of the shift I couldn't control, wouldn't control because all I could think about was her being inside that hellish crucible.

"ELENA!"

Two figures in yellow turnout gear materialized from the smoke-laden night, moving with surprising speed for their size. Dwarven firefighters, Local 405 South Side—I recognized the patches even through my tunnel vision. One grabbed my shoulders while the other moved to block my path forward.

"You're dead if you go in there, kid!" The one holding me grunted, his grip like iron clamps. "It's an arcane burn! You'll be vapor before you hit the—"

"I don't *care*!" I struggled against him, but he had a firefighter's strength and years of experience wrestling panicked civilians. His partner moved closer, ready to help subdue me if needed.

"She's in there!" I screamed at them. "My mother is inside!"

The lead firefighter's helmeted head shook. Through the gaps in his gear, I caught the glint of eyes that had seen too much, knew too much about what necro-thermite could do to flesh and bone.

"The whole structure's compromised," he said, voice muffled by his breathing apparatus. "Second floor just collapsed. We can't get close enough to—"

A tremendous *WHUMPH* cut him off.

The clinic's second story—which I'd known as Elena's office space, where she kept those hard drives with all our secrets—exploded outward in a shower of molten glass and superheated debris. The blue-black flames roared higher, fed by whatever chemical cocktail was making this hellfire possible. The explosion threw chunks of burning brick across the street like shrapnel.

"COLE REYES!" someone else shouted from the growing crowd of emergency responders. A female voice, sharp and commanding. "Stand down or we'll sedate you!"

I stopped fighting then, but only because the dwarf's grip would've broken my collarbone if I'd continued. My knees buckled. He eased me down to the wet asphalt while I stared at what used to be my mother's clinic, her sanctuary, the place where she'd healed people who couldn't afford County General.

Now it was a tomb.

And I hadn't been fast enough to save her.

* * *

The moment my boots hit pavement, I knew something was wrong. The air tasted like copper and ozone, thick enough to choke on. My lungs burned with each breath—part panic, part the metallic tang of blood-magic running hot through my veins.

"Elena!" Her name tore from my throat raw and broken.

The Clinic—a squat concrete box that had seen better days even before tonight—was already screaming. Not people screaming. The *building* screaming as flames licked up its sides, feeding on something far more than wood and plaster. The fire moved wrong. Too hungry. Too deliberate.

I ran hard toward the entrance, my vision tunneling red at the edges. My fingers were starting to numb—the first sign of frost-cobalt kicking in when adrenaline spiked too high. Magic always found a way to fuck me over at the worst possible moment.

Then they hit me.

Two masses of solid muscle slammed into my ribs from either side, driving the air from my lungs in a wet gasp. We went down in a tangle of limbs, my head cracking against asphalt hard enough to see stars. Dwarven firefighters—both of them, easy 250 pounds of dense muscle packed with weave-resistance training.

"Easy! Easy!" one shouted, but I wasn't hearing words anymore. Just the roar of blood in my ears and the sick certainty that Elena was in there dying while I wrestled with—

My knuckles connected with something solid. Cartilage crunched. The dwarf grunted, his grip loosening just enough. That's all I needed.

Pure desperation turned my right fist into a meteor. Blood-iron magic flared hot through my arm—the metal rings under my skin glowing dull blue through my skin—and I caught the second dwarf square across the jaw. He flew sideways, crashing into a parked car with enough force to dent the door.

The other one recovered fast, wrapping both arms around my torso in a bear hug that squeezed the remaining air from my lungs. "Stop it! Stop it now!"

"LET ME GO!" I screamed, bucking like a madman. My elbows found soft spots—solar plexus, throat, temple. The dwarf coughed, stumbled, but didn't release. His helmeted face swam in front of mine, voice muffled by smoke and distance.

"It's too late! The structural—"

*CRACK.*

The sound cut through everything else. Concrete groaning. Steel beams shrieking as they lost integrity. And then—

The roof collapsed inward.

It happened slow-motion and all at once. The center section gave way first, pulling down sections like dominos. The fire roared in response, feeding on oxygen, sending up a column of blue-black smoke that climbed toward heaven like an accusation. Slag dripped from the frame, white-hot and hissing where it hit wet pavement.

"No," I whispered. "No no no no—"

The dwarf was still holding me, but his grip had changed. Less restraint. More support. When he spoke again, his voice carried genuine sorrow. "Nothing left in there, son. The weave-fire ate it all. I'm sorry."

I stopped fighting.

My knees buckled. The dwarf eased me down gently onto asphalt slick with rainwater and worse things. Somewhere nearby, Ford trauma-ambulances pulsed their lightbars—strobe-red painting smoke, turning it into hellish tapestry.

I stared into the inferno.

Blue flames danced along what remained of load-bearing walls—Necro-Thermite doing exactly what it was designed to do: ensuring nothing biological survived. No bodies. No DNA. Nothing but slag and memory.

Elena was gone.

Lysandra was gone.

And I...

"Cole." The dwarf's hand came down on my shoulder, heavy as judgment. "Cole, you need to—"

I looked up at him blankly. My mouth tasted like ash and iron. My eyes reflected the blue flames back at him—I could see them in the black pupils if I squinted just right.

"Danny," I said hoarsely. "There's... there's still Danny."

But even as I said it, the words felt hollow. Because Elena had made her choice. Lysandra too. They'd staged this—they'd *wanted* this—to protect their boys from whatever was coming next.

Now I was alone with one kid while the other burned somewhere in that white-hot furnace.

The Clinic collapsed another foot inward with a sound like God breathing out. Sparks scattered upward like dying stars.

And I knelt in the cold February night, surrounded by firefighters and first responders who couldn't help because there was nothing left to save, watching everything burn until morning.

---

## CHAPTER 8: ASH AND IDENTIFICATION

The cold bites through my jacket like teeth finding skin. I don't feel it anymore—that's how you know you're deep in shock. Your body stops bothering with things that don't matter.

Dawn comes up over Neon Hollow like someone dragging a dirty rag across the sky. Gray light filters through the perpetual smog that hangs over the South Side, painting everything in shades of ash and regret. The Clinic Ruins spread out before me, still smoking in places, though the fire burned itself out hours ago. Necro-Thermite doesn't need anything—no oxygen, no fuel. It just *takes*. Burns so hot and clean that by the time it's done, there's only slag and silence.

I duck under the yellow police tape. A beat cop, this big Uruk named Grask who used to buy coffee at Mom's place every Tuesday morning, shifts his weight and starts toward me. He takes one look at my face—my eyes probably reflecting that dead-winter-ice color they get when the blood-iron retreats—and stops. His hand drops from the radio clipped to his shoulder.

"Reyes," he says, voice flat as week-old beer. "You shouldn't be here."

"It's my mother's clinic." My own voice sounds distant, like I'm hearing it through water. "I should probably see what's left."

Grask looks past me at the ruins, then back at my face. Whatever he sees there makes him flinch. "Ain't nothing left to contaminate anyway," he mutters into his radio. "Yeah. Let the kid walk." Then to me: "Don't touch anything. Don't take anything. Just... look if you gotta look."

I nod. Walk past him. The crunch of pulverized brick and melted glass echoes through the footprint where the building stood. Everything is gray and black and white-hot in patches—the slag from the Necro-Thermite still glowing faintly orange in the pre-dawn gloom. It stinks of iron-gall residue, that acrid chemical burn smell mixed with something worse. Something organic.

The wind cuts through the devastation, carrying ash and debris across the South Side. Police tape snaps in the gusts, a sound like breaking bones.

I navigate by memory. This was Mom's space—forty years she worked here, healing people the system discarded. I know every doorway, every support beam, every window. Even now, with everything collapsed and melted and scattered, I can map it in my head. Second floor, northwest corner—that's where Elena's office was. Where her second bedroom connected to her secret lab.

Now it's just a crater in the earth.

My boots find the right spot. Here, where the foundation gave way. Here, where the second story imploded down into the basement. I stop at the edge, looking into the collapse. Melted steel I-beams jut up at impossible angles, twisted like pretzels. The concrete has turned to dust and fused slag.

And there—buried under three tons of wreckage—I see red.

Not blood. Worse than blood.

Ceramic shards, painted the color of arterial spray. Pieces of the containment vessel Elena used for her research. The one she swore was stable. The one that burned clean and hot enough to melt steel in seconds flat.

"You stupid fucking woman," I whisper to the ruins. "You beautiful, brilliant, dead idiot."

The words taste like copper. Like I'm chewing on old coins.

My hands are shaking—not from cold, not from fear. From the blood-iron magic coiling tight inside me, retreating deeper and deeper as shock sets in. It wants to help. Can't. There's nothing left to heal. Nothing living to pull back from death's edge.

Just ash and slag and the acrid stench of failure.

I drop to my knees at the crater's edge. Dawn light catches the white-hot slag, makes it gleam like diamonds. Beautiful. Deadly. Final.

Somewhere behind me, Grask coughs into his radio. The city wakes around us—the distant sound of traffic on the Pulaski Skyway, the rumble of early-morning trains crossing Newark Bay. Life goes on.

For everyone else.

I dig my fingers into the pulverized brick. Feel it sift through my grasp like sand. Like time. Like all the moments I should have spent here instead of out there, playing vigilante, thinking I could make a difference.

"Cole."

* * *

The dawn comes cold and gray over the ruins. I can't feel it.

My breath clouds white in front of my face as I stand at the edge of what was the Clinic. The fire's gone out—burned itself into exhaustion sometime in the last few hours—but the ashes are still alive with heat. Hundreds of degrees. Hot enough to melt glass, hot enough to fuse steel. I can see the glow of it pulsing beneath the gray surface like the heartbeat of something dying.

I drop to my knees without thinking about it. The impact sends a jolt up through my legs, but I barely register it. My hands hang above the ash, trembling slightly. They're covered in soot already, black streaks running down my wrists, under my shirt sleeves. My knuckles split somewhere during the night—I don't remember when—and there's dried blood caked around the cuts.

Then the change starts.

It always begins the same way. A coldness that has nothing to do with temperature, spreading from deep inside my chest outward. My blood-iron magic responding to something. Fear? Grief? Rage? I don't know anymore which emotion triggers it. Maybe all three at once. The warmth that kept me going through the night—the fever-bright certainty that pushed me through the smoke and flames—dries up like spit on summer pavement.

And then the frost comes.

My skin begins to pale, starting at my fingertips and creeping up toward my elbows. That familiar cobalt hue spreads across my hands like veins of ice beneath the surface. The color deepens until my fingers look carved from frozen moonlight, translucent and deadly cold. But I know better than to trust appearances. This isn't real cold. It's the opposite—a burning chill that protects rather than damages, a magical sheath that lets me touch things that would normally flay the flesh from my bones.

The moment the frost-cobalt coating settles fully over my hands, I plunge them into the ashes.

The heat hits me like a solid wall. Even through the protection, I feel it—a crushing pressure of thermal energy trying to force its way past my defenses. Steam hisses where my skin touches the hottest embers, tiny puffs of white vapor erupting around my fingers as moisture in the ash flashes to gas.

I dig anyway.

My hands move frantically now, scooping and sifting through the debris. Ash cascades between my fingers like black sand, revealing fragments beneath: a twisted lump of aluminum that might have been part of a filing cabinet, now warped into impossible angles; melted plastic fused into glass-like sheets; chunks of insulation turned to sludge.

I find what used to be the IBM ThinkPad first. Or pieces of it. The chassis has collapsed inward on itself, the keyboard melted into an unrecognizable pancake of carbon and silicon. There's still a faint smell coming from it—burnt electronics and scorched polymers—but no glow from any components. Whatever data was on those drives is gone now, reduced to molecular chaos.

Deeper into the wreckage. My breathing gets ragged, each exhale coming harder than the last. The cold inside me spreads further down my arms now, creeping toward my shoulders. My blood-iron magic is pulling inward, retreating from everything except the absolute minimum needed to protect these searching hands.

There. Another piece of tech—the Nextel phone, maybe? It's hard to tell. Just a fused lump of plastic and metal components, all the separate parts welded together by the fire's fury. I pull it out slowly, holding it up to the gray dawn light. Nothing recognizable remains. Just garbage. Worthless slag.

But I keep digging.

The ashes are deeper here, nearer where the main explosion must have occurred. The heat intensifies with every inch I descend into the ruins. More hissing steam. More white puffs erupting around my frozen-blue hands. My knees ache from pressing into the charred earth, but I don't stop. Can't stop.

Another metal fragment. Larger this time—a section of desk support beam, twisted beyond recognition. I toss it aside without looking. Not important. None of it matters unless—

My fingers brush against something different.

Harder than the ash. Smoother. Acrylic, maybe? Some kind of plastic that didn't melt completely in the inferno. Buried deep beneath layers of debris, protected by the collapsed structure above it.

I freeze for just a second, my heart hammering so hard I can feel it in my throat.

Then I dig faster.

Ash flies everywhere as I excavate frantically around the object. More pieces of melted furniture. Chunks of ceiling tile turned to blackened pulp. A shard of what might be window glass, fused into grotesque shapes by the arcane heat.

And there it is.

Barely visible through the haze of settling dust and steam: a dark shape buried in the soot. Scorch-resistant acrylic, definitely. Intact enough that even after everything—the explosion, the fire, the collapse—I can make out its general form.

My hand reaches for it, frost-cobalt skin trembling inches away from the surface.

I pause.

For the first time since I started digging, I actually hesitate. Because part of me—the part that's slowly dying inside like the fire died during the night—that part whispers that some things aren't meant to be recovered. That some ashes are better left undisturbed.

But I've never listened to that voice before.

Not when it mattered anyway.

My fingers close around the object and pull.

The acrylic comes free with a soft tearing sound as old soot clings to it reluctantly. I lift it up toward the dawning light, watching the gray gloom illuminate the surface slowly, revealing—

My breath catches.

Oh god.

I stare at what's in my hand like it's something from another world entirely. Like finding this here makes no sense whatsoever. Like it changes everything or nothing depending on how I look at it.

Which maybe it does.

Or maybe it doesn't.

Hard to say anymore which thoughts are real and which ones are just the shock talking.

I stand up slowly, still holding the scorched acrylic fragment, still coated head-to-toe in ash and soot and blood. The dawn wind cuts across the ruins, bringing with it the smell of burnt wood and worse things underneath.

Behind me, the Clinic is just memory now. Whatever secrets it held—whatever truth about what really happened last night—are buried under tons of debris and confusion.

But I have this.

Whatever it means.

Whether it matters or not.

I turn away from the ashes and start walking back toward where I left the car, frost-cobalt magic fading from my skin as the cold inside me finally reaches critical mass and shatters into numbness.

The acylic piece fits in my palm like a coffin.

Like an answer.

Like another question wearing a different face.

Hard to tell which anymore.

* * *

The fire is dead now. Just ash and steam rising from wet charcoal, the stench of burnt plastic and cooked meat hanging thick in the dawn air. My boots crunch into the soft debris as I move through what used to be The Clinic's eastern wing.

I'm not warm anymore. Haven't been since I watched the roof cave in. The blood-iron magic that keeps my core temperature regulated has pulled back inside, conserving itself, leaving my skin cold despite the residual heat radiating off the ruins. Each breath comes sharp and clear—no fog, no warmth. Just function.

My hands are steady as I sift through the rubble. Methodical. This is what I do when engines seize or transmissions fail. You don't panic. You look for evidence. You diagnose the damage.

Except there aren't any engines here.

Just pieces of chairs. Twisted metal beds. A melted IV stand bent into a pretzel shape. I turn over chunks of drywall with my boot, watching black flakes cascade down like dirty snow. The rain came during the night—I can tell by how the ash clings together, wet and heavy.

That's when I see it.

Half-buried under a collapsed ceiling beam, barely visible beneath a layer of gray sludge, something catches the early light. Not wood, not metal. Plastic. The warped edges of an ID badge, still attached to its lanyard, which has burned away to frayed threads.

My heart stops. Actually fucking stops.

I drop to my knees without thinking, ignoring the heat radiating up from the coals below, and dig it out with bare fingers. Ash gets under my fingernails. Doesn't matter.

It's hers.

The acrylic is clouded white along the edges where the fire touched it, the plastic bubbled and warped. But the photo in the corner is still there. Still *her*. Smiling at some hospital administrator during orientation, her dark hair pulled back, those tired eyes crinkling with professional politeness.

*ELENA REYES - HEAD TRAUMA NURSE*

The name is embossed in raised letters that have survived the heat somehow. Still legible. Still real.

Still *true*.

I hold it between both hands, turning it over slowly. The magnet strip on the back has bubbled and separated from the card. One corner is gone, melted completely away. But it's enough. More than enough.

This isn't conjecture anymore. Isn't assumption or hope or denial. This is proof. Physical. Undeniable.

She was here. She wore this badge. And she died wearing it.

The realization hits me like a hydraulic press—slow, inexorable, crushing every rib inward until I can't breathe. Can't think. Just *know*.

My sister is dead. My mother's already dead. My father's been dead for years except in memory, and even that's fading. Everyone who ever gave a shit about Cole Reyes, everyone who mattered, everyone who made me human instead of just another machine grinding through shifts at Sub-Station Seven—

Gone.

The badge trembles in my grip. I look down at my hands and realize they're shaking. Not from cold. From something deeper. Something fundamental breaking apart inside my chest.

But I don't cry.

Can't. The shock has frozen whatever part of me could produce tears. Instead, there's just this hollow ringing in my skull and a pressure building behind my eyes that feels like it wants to crack bone.

Something snaps.

Not loud. No dramatic sound effect. Just a heavy, metallic *clack* as something essential inside me locks shut. A vault door sealing. A switch being thrown. The difference between before and after so absolute you could measure it with instruments.

I am not Elena's brother right now. That identity burned up with her.

I'm something else.

I clutch the badge to my chest, feeling its heat through my jacket—the last warmth I'll touch today—and close my eyes. The wind picks up, cutting through my clothes like knives. Ash settles on my shoulders, my hair, coating me in gray dust.

When I open my eyes again, everything looks different. Sharper. Colder. The ruins aren't tragedy anymore. They're evidence.

In the distance, beyond the police barricades, a corporate drone in a pressed suit steps out of a black sedan. Elf, by the pointed ears visible beneath his expensive haircut. He's got one of those new PalmPilot devices in his hand, thumb moving across the screen as he takes notes.

Looking at the damage. Assessing liability.

Probably working for whoever paid to burn this place down.

The hatred comes on slow, deliberate, settling into my bones like sediment. Cold and heavy. Permanent.

I stand up, joints popping from staying too long in one position, and carefully fold the badge into my pocket. It presses against my hip—a weight that won't go away.

I walk out of the crater.

Each step is measured. Deliberate. My boots leave prints in the ash, but I don't look back.

I'm not a son anymore. Not a brother.

Just a mechanic who's found a problem that needs fixing.

And I know exactly where to start looking.

---

## CHAPTER 9: THE THREEFOLD CORD

The chop-shop smells different when I return. Not better, just different. Like copper pennies left out in the rain.

I push through the hanging plastic sheeting—some kind of waterproof tarp that used to cover Uncle Sal's delivery truck before he stopped showing up three months ago—and descend the metal stairs to the sub-basement. Each step rings out too loud, echoing off concrete walls covered in rust stains that look like blood splatters under the single flickering bulb overhead.

Danny is awake inside the Iron-Lung.

His eyes find mine through the glass portal immediately. Those same brown eyes Mom had, wide and dark and full of questions I don't want to answer. The machine makes its rhythmic wheeze behind him—the *thump-hiss* of the bellows driving Telluric pressure into his collapsed lungs, keeping him alive when every law of physics says he should be dead.

"Cole," his voice comes through the speaking tube, muffled and small. "Where's Mom?"

I stop halfway down the last flight of stairs. My hand grips the charred ID badge in my jacket pocket so hard it hurts. The metal is still warm against my palm, singed around the edges from the fire at County General. I can smell it—that chemical stench of burning plastic and cooked meat that won't wash off no matter how many times I scrub my hands.

"I told you to stay quiet, kiddo," I say, my voice flat. Empty. I'm surprised how easy it is to sound this way now. "Conserve your strength."

But Danny isn't listening. He never does. That stubbornness he gets from her—from Mom—is already hardening in him even as his body softens inside the brass cage.

"Why are you looking at me like that?" His head tilts slightly to the left, trying to track my movement as I finish descending the stairs.

I walk past the half-dismantled Buick in the corner, its engine block split open like a ribcage. Past the workbench cluttered with socket wrenches and brake lines. Past everything that used to matter before Tuesday night when the accident happened.

Before Mom died.

I set the charred ID badge down on the workbench next to a greasy socket wrench, watching the way the light catches the melted plastic. Dr. Sarah Chen. County General ER. The woman who tried to save him and couldn't.

"She had to go into hiding," I say, sitting down on a milk crate beside the Iron-Lung. The wood creaks under my weight. I rest my elbows on my knees and look directly through the glass at my little brother's face. "The people who did this... they're still looking for witnesses."

Danny's expression shifts from fear to confusion. His eyes dart away from mine, focusing somewhere past my shoulder. "But... she was here yesterday. When you were—"

"The situation changed." Each word tastes like iron. Like blood. I force myself to hold his gaze. To lie straight into those brown eyes that trust me absolutely. "She sent word this morning. Said it's not safe anymore. That we need to lay low for a while."

*Lay low.* As if this massive brass machine keeping Danny alive counts as laying low. As if anything about our lives will ever be normal again.

The Iron-Lung continues its mechanical breathing behind him. *Thump-hiss. Thump-hiss.* The condensation on the glass is starting to fog over, obscuring parts of his face. Making it easier to pretend.

"You have to promise me something, Danny." My voice doesn't crack. Doesn't break. Somewhere deep inside me, something cold and hard has already crystallized around Mom's death—a frost-cobalt shell that won't let the grief out. Won't let anything out except words. "When people ask questions, you tell them Mom went away on business. That she'll be back soon. Can you do that?"

He nods slowly, but there's hesitation in it now. Doubt creeping in where innocence used to live.

"Promise me," I repeat.

"I promise." Barely a whisper through the speaking tube.

I stand up from the milk crate and walk over to the concrete wall above my workbench. There's still space left there—I can see it clearly now with a kind of terrible clarity. Space for another name. Another sacrifice.

My hand reaches into my jacket pocket and pulls out a grease pencil, its tip worn smooth from use over the years. I uncapped it without thinking, turning back toward the wall.

* * *

The sub-basement air tastes like rust and old diesel fuel, but underneath that industrial tang runs something else now—a crystalline cold that wasn't there before. My breath fogs as I kneel beside Danny's bed, the grease pencil thick and waxy between my fingers like a surgeon's scalpel.

I press it to the concrete wall above where his still body lies in the Iron-Lung's embrace. The first word scrapes free:

**PENANCE**

The sound echoes wrong in here—too loud, too final. The pencil's wax freezes solid against the concrete as frost-cobalt bleeds through my palm, through the tool itself. When I lift it, the letters remain sharp and black and slightly raised, rimmed with ice crystals that catch the red emergency lights.

My hand moves again without thought. Muscle memory from years at the machine shop, from blueprints and schematics, from building things that work even when they shouldn't.

**REVENGE**

Two words sit there on the wall, and I can feel them vibrating in my chest cavity like tuning forks struck by some cosmic hammer. The sub-basement grows colder. The Iron-Lung's gauges tick-tick-tick in their eternal rhythm while Danny remains suspended in that horrible twilight state, neither living nor dead, his lungs full of black iron filings from the men who thought a thirteen-year-old boy was expendable collateral damage.

I write the third word slower, savoring the scrape of wax against stone:

**JUSTICE**

There. Three pillars. A trinity of purpose.

But I stare at that last word—*Justice*—and the grease pencil trembles in my grip. The cold intensifies until my breath comes out in sharp white plumes. Because I see what's coming now. I *understand* what this path actually means.

I cross out "Justice" with a violent slashing motion, shattering the frozen wax into glittering fragments that scatter across the floor like broken stained glass.

Below where I've crossed it out, I write smaller, more precise, the frost-cobalt magic flowing through my fingers until the pencil becomes an extension of bone and will:

*A SLIVER OF JUSTICE*

That's all I'm ever going to get. That's all anyone gets.

The truth hits me like a hydraulic press—a physical blow to the sternum that knocks the air from my lungs. This sliver isn't enough. It won't reverse the damage done to Danny. Won't unburn my mother from the ash pile they called a home. Won't bring back any of the nameless ghosts haunting these North Jersey streets, ground down between the High-Spires' gears and thrown away like machine parts that wore out too soon.

A sliver doesn't fill the void. It can't heal. Can't resurrect. Can't undo.

But it exists.

And zero is less than one, no matter how small.

My reflection stares back at me from the Iron-Lung's chrome casing—gaunt, eyes hollowed by grief that's calcifying into something harder, colder. Something that won't break because it's already shattered completely and reassembled itself around razor wire.

I look at Danny, suspended in time, and I know exactly what this means.

I'll have to become something monstrous to carve even a sliver of justice from men who measure human lives in profit margins and inconvenience. The acts required will be abyssal. I'll cross lines that don't have return tickets. Some of the things I'll do won't just bend the law—they'll snap it clean through and piss on the broken pieces.

The thought should horrify me. Should send me running back to the shop floor, to normalcy, to pretending the world wasn't built on bones and broken dreams.

Instead, I feel nothing but clarity.

No guilt. No doubt. No hesitation.

The last remnants of civilian Cole Reyes evaporate like morning frost under the sun—or rather, like frost that got hammered flat by something too heavy to name. What remains is this: the mechanic who understands leverage and pressure, who knows you sometimes need to apply force beyond what seems reasonable to make anything change.

I stand up slowly, my joints protesting from kneeling so long. The words remain on the wall:

**PENANCE. REVENGE. A SLIVER OF JUSTICE.**

My doctrine. My operating system for whatever comes next.

Behind me, the Iron-Lung keeps ticking its eternal countdown.

* * *

The sub-basement feels colder than it should be. February air filtering through cracks in the foundation, maybe, but I know better. This cold comes from inside.

I'm standing at my workbench, and for the first time since moving into this chop-shop space beneath Sub-Station Seven, I see it clearly—every personal object, every reminder of who Cole Reyes used to be. The Sony MiniDisc player sits on the corner of my desk, its green power light still blinking, some indie rock band's album frozen mid-track. There are three photos thumbtacked to the corkboard above it. Me, Elena, and Danny at Great Adventure last summer. Smiling. Alive.

Dead men don't need memories.

My fingers find the power button on the disc player. Click. The green light dies. Silence crashes over everything like water filling an empty well. I reach up and pull the first photograph down—the one where Danny's losing a tooth and Elena's laughing about something stupid I said. The cardboard backing bends as I fold it in half, then quarters, then shove it hard into the metal drawer beneath my feet.

Danny's watching from behind the reinforced glass partition. His face is pressed against it, breath fogging the surface. Through the distortion, I can make out his expression. Fear. Good. He needs to understand what's happening here.

"Cole?" His voice comes through the speaker system, tinny and distant despite being only thirty feet away. "You're scaring me."

I don't turn around. Can't. If I look at him now, if I really see those eyes—the same eyes as mine—I might hesitate. And hesitation gets you killed in this world. Gets people you love killed.

"Good," I say, my voice flat, mechanical. "If I scare you, imagine what I'll do to them."

The second photo comes down next—Elena teaching Danny how to change a tire on her Beetle, both of them covered in grease and grins. Fold. Quarter. Drawer. The third follows immediately after. Our whole life, compressed into confetti, buried beneath spare parts and ammunition.

My workbench is still cluttered with evidence of my former self. A coffee mug with "World's Best Brother" written in fading marker. A half-finished model car kit. Loose change. A deck of cards. All the detritus of a normal guy living a normal life.

None of that exists anymore.

I sweep everything off with one motion of my arm. The crash of porcelain and plastic and metal echoes through the sub-basement like breaking bones. Danny flinches behind the glass, and I feel something twist inside my chest—but it's not pain exactly. It's more like watching someone else's emotions through thick ice.

I pull open all three drawers of my tool chest and begin sorting. Screwdrivers go in the first. Wrenches in the second. Third drawer is already full of weapons maintenance kits—cleaning rods, bore brushes, oils, solvents. My hands move with practiced efficiency, each item finding its proper place.

From the corner of my eye, I see the rune-etched MP5 submachine gun leaning against the wall where I left it last night after coming back from the Kearny Marshes. Blood on the barrel. Not mine. I lift it now, feeling its weight settle into familiar grooves in my hands. This is what matters. Tools for survival. Instruments of vengeance.

The weapon finds its new home on my workbench, centered, ready to be disassembled and cleaned. Beside it, I place the blueprints for the Iron-Lung—my masterwork, the armor that will let me breathe in places others suffocate. The paper crackles as I smooth it flat.

There. That's better. Everything unnecessary has been removed. Only purpose remains.

"Cole, please," Danny says again, his voice higher now, cracking. "What are you doing? Why won't you look at me?"

Still I don't turn. Because if I do, I'll see his face, and Elena's face, and Mom's face, all overlapping, and I'll remember why any of this matters. Love. Family. Human connection.

Weakness.

"I'm doing what needs to be done," I tell him, pulling out a rag and weapon oil, beginning the methodical process of breaking down the MP5. Click-click-whirr—the bolt release. Slide the charging handle. Field strip. Each piece laid out in order: upper receiver, lower receiver, trigger mechanism, barrel assembly.

The cold in the room deepens. My breath comes out in visible puffs now, though I know the temperature hasn't actually changed. This cold is magical, alchemical, born from blood-iron resonance crystallizing in my veins. Where once there was warmth—passion, rage, grief, love—I feel nothing but stillness. Dead-silent frost-cobalt.

I should be terrified. Some part of me understands this transformation is wrong, dangerous, a violation of whatever human essence makes us more than animals or machines. But terror requires emotion, and emotions are what I'm excavating from myself like cancerous tumors.

Danny's crying behind the glass now. I can hear it in the wet catching of his breath, see it in the way his shoulders shake. Good. He needs to understand that the brother he knew died with Elena. What's left is something else entirely.

Something necessary.

"Cole Reyes is gone," I say aloud, not to Danny, but to myself—to whoever or whatever I'm becoming. "He died on February 14th, 2000."

I look down at my hands as they work, assembling and disassembling the submachine gun with mechanical precision. The veins beneath my skin have lost their warmth. No more pulsing red-gold warmth flowing toward my heart, no more heat radiating from my palms when I grip tools or weapons.

Just stillness.

Terrifying, perfect stillness.

And underneath it all, deeper than thought, runs one truth like a river through frozen ground:

*They took everything from me.*

*Now I'll take everything from them.*

---

## CHAPTER 10: FROST-COBALT

I climbed the concrete steps from the sub-basement, my boots echoing in the hollow stairwell. The smell hit me first—motor oil, transmission fluid, the metallic tang of rust sleeping in scrap metal. The chop-shop was quiet this morning. Too quiet. Like it was holding its breath.

The main garage sprawled before me, a cathedral of broken machinery and stolen parts. Fluorescent tubes flickered overhead, casting everything in that sickly yellow-green light that made the oil stains look like pools of infected blood. I'd spent enough nights down here to know every creak and groan of the building's skeleton.

My eyes found the V8 engine block immediately. It hung suspended from a chain hoist near the center of the space, swaying slightly from residual air movement. Cast iron, rusted through, probably pulled from some flooded sedan out in the marshes. Good weight to it. Solid.

I walked over, my reflection fragmenting across puddles of old coolant. The rust on that engine block was thick—years of neglect crystallized into orange-red flakes. My bare hand hovered over the rough surface, feeling the temperature differential even without touching. Cold metal, warmer air, the whole dance of thermodynamics waiting for a catalyst.

Time to test what's changed inside me.

I pressed my palm against the rusted cast-iron.

The resonance came instantly, but wrong. Not the warm rush I remembered, that flush of heat that preceded the spark-bloom of welding torch flame. Instead, something else entirely. A coldness spread through my fingers, up my wrist, settling in my chest like a slab of dry ice. The magic didn't pulse or crackle. It hummed—a dead-silent vibration that felt less like fire and more like the moment before a blade breaks skin.

Frost-cobalt.

The name just came to me, clear as steel forged in shadow. I watched as an eerie blue glow emanated from where my hand met metal. The rust around my palm began to crystallize, forming delicate frost patterns that spread across the engine block's surface with geometric precision. Each crystal formation was perfect, mathematical, merciless.

Then the rust simply flaked away. Not melted by heat, not scraped off by force, but frozen brittle and falling like snow. The metal beneath was exposed, clean, unblemished. The cast iron itself had taken on a faint metallic sheen, as if newly machined.

And the temperature.

Jesus Christ, the temperature dropped exactly ten degrees in the entire garage. I could feel it on my skin, see it in the sudden condensation forming on every metal surface. My breath plumed into white vapor before my face, small clouds dissipating in air that had gone from mild to bitterly cold in seconds.

Ten degrees. Not nine. Not eleven. Exactly ten.

I lifted my hand slowly, staring at my palm. No burns, no blisters, no marks whatsoever. Just clean skin, though it should have been reddened from what I'd channeled through it. But there was nothing. Cold to the touch now, almost clammy.

I felt... nothing.

No rush of adrenaline. No heat in my blood. No passion or rage fueling the magic. Just cold. Mechanical precision. My heart beat steady and slow. My breathing remained even. It was like watching someone else perform the magic, observing it with clinical detachment while I stood here wearing my own skin.

This is the state, I thought. The abyssal doctrine made real. Zero doubt means zero heat. Zero guilt means zero passion. What's left when you strip all that away?

An executioner's tool.

The realization didn't frighten me. Should've. Probably would've, six months ago. But standing here in this cold garage with frost-cobalt magic crystallizing in the air around me, I understood something fundamental about what I'd become. Doubt was friction. Guilt was resistance. Remorse was dead weight.

I'd shed them all.

The rolling metal door rattled violently from the alleyway—three heavy knocks that echoed through the garage like hammer strikes on a coffin lid.

* * *

The button clicks under my thumb. Metal groans against metal as the bay door rises, flooding the garage with February sunlight that cuts through the grease-stained air like a knife.

Bram Kovacs steps inside, carrying a wooden crate that rattles with brass fittings. He's got that dwarven solidness about him—broad shoulders, calloused hands the size of hams, his leather apron dark with decades of machine shop stains. Local 405 South Side union written across the chest pocket in faded white paint.

He stops three steps in.

"Christ," he mutters, exhaling clouds into air that shouldn't be this cold. His eyes narrow at me, then dart around the garage. "What the hell happened to your heating? It dropped ten degrees just walking through that door."

I don't answer. Can't answer without saying something that would make it real. Elena is dead. Elena burned. Elena screaming.

My right hand finds the workbench edge. The frost-cobalt sits heavy in my bones now, locked permanent. No doubt left to bargain with. No guilt to compromise its purity. Just the humming silence underneath my skin where warmth used to live.

Bram sets down the crate. The brass fittings clink inside. He pulls off thick work gloves, shoving them into his apron pocket while studying my face like he's reading blueprints.

"You look like shit, kid." His gravel-voice softer now. "And you're standing there like a corpse at a wake. What happened?"

"The clinic burned." The words come out flat. Wrong. Like I'm reading someone else's dialogue. "Elena didn't make it."

The temperature drops another degree. Bram notices, shifting his weight, rubbing his forearms.

"That's... Jesus, Cole, I'm sorry. I know she meant something to you."

"I don't want sympathy."

His jaw tightens. Good. He understands. "Right. Fair enough." He gestures at the crate. "These are the custom fittings for the pressure regulator. Should fit Danny's lung assembly perfect. But if you need anything more than standard medical grade—"

"I do." My fingers drum against the bench. "I need Telluric pressure-valves. Illegal ones. High-capacity."

Bram goes still. Really still. The kind of stillness that means he's calculating odds and consequences and probably praying to whatever dwarven forge-gods he believes in.

"Cole." Slow, measured. "You saying what I think you're saying? That you want me to point you toward Black-Circuit Syndicate suppliers?"

"Yes."

"No." Flat as mine was. He shakes his head hard enough to make his beard bristle. "Absolutely not. Those Gnome frequency runners will gut you, kid. They'll have you running packages through the Undercity before the week's out. You become Syndicate property the second you take their money."

"Nobody owns me anymore."

The way I say it—what's underneath those six syllables—I can see Bram hearing all the things I'm not saying. All the doors I've already burned behind me. The clinic ash still coating my lungs even though I scrubbed three times last night.

He pulls a Nextel from his apron pocket, grease-stained and cracked. His thumb hovers over the screen while he stares at me like I'm already dead.

"You're serious about this," he says. Not a question.

"The lung comes first. Then I need contracts. Targets. Someone who pays cash and doesn't ask where I learned to work machinery."

Bram exhales hard through his nose. Swipes a hand across his face. Finally looks away from me, down at his phone.

"Fucking hell." His thumb moves across the screen. "Listen close then. There's an Undercity drop on the Newark Bay side, near the old industrial terminals. Second shipping container from the north pier. You go there tonight—after midnight, when the fog rolls in—and you ask for Rix. He's a Gnome broker runs the lower circuit frequencies."

I memorize every word. The location. The timing. The name.

Rix.

"Thanks, Bram."

He pockets the phone, waves me off with that same motion my old man used when he didn't want to argue. "Yeah, well, don't thank me yet. And Cole?" His eyes lock onto mine again, hard as rivets. "If you're going into the Undercity, you bring backup. Someone who knows how to watch your six. Because if you're carrying Telluric gear, you're painted a target the second you cross those thresholds. Syndicate, Freelancers, the whole fucking food chain."

I nod because it's what he expects. But we both know I'll be alone.

The sun shifts behind clouds, dimming the garage light. Bram grabs his crate of fittings and heads back toward the door.

"One more thing," he says without turning around. "You feel different, kid. Wrong different. Like standing next to something that shouldn't exist but does anyway." He pauses at the threshold, one boot already out into the alley daylight. "Whatever happened at that clinic, whatever you've got running through your veins now... it changed you. Be careful what you ask the dark to give you."

The door comes down with a clang that echoes through the empty space.

I'm alone again.

Outside, the city breathes its morning routine—I-95 traffic building, machinery starting up in the yards across the street, the perpetual hum of Newark industry. But inside, where the frost-cobalt has made its home, everything is silent.

Dead quiet.

Perfect.

I pull Danny's lung assembly from the workbench drawer where I left it last night. The brass components gleam under the fluorescent lights while I begin fitting Bram's new pieces into place. Each connection clicks with finality. Each seal holds perfect.

By midnight, I'll have the illegal valves.

By tomorrow, I'll have my first contract.

And by next week?

Nobody in this city will remember the name Cole Reyes was born with.

* * *

The garage falls silent after Bram's boots fade down the driveway. I twist the deadbolt—*clunk*—then throw the heavy industrial lock. Triple-check the side door. Same. Everything locked tight except the sub-basement access.

"Danny," I call into the intercom, my thumb resting on the button. "I'm locking the blast door. Don't open it for anyone."

The speakers crackle with static before Danny's voice comes through, small and metallic: "Okay, Cole."

I release the button without another word. The blast door—a reinforced steel monster I'd welded shut myself last month—hums downward into its seal. Hydraulics hiss. Bolts *thunk-thunk-thunk* into place around the perimeter. The garage is sealed now. A tomb.

I head to the locker in the back corner where I keep the gear. Civilian clothes come off first—the grease-stained mechanic's shirt I've been wearing since yesterday morning. It hits the concrete floor with a soft thud. Underneath I'm just skin and muscle, scars from old jobs crisscrossing my torso like a roadmap of bad decisions.

The jacket goes on next. Heavy canvas, reinforced at the shoulders and elbows with ballistic plating I salvaged from an abandoned police cruiser out in the marshes. It's stiff when cold, smells like gun oil and iron dust. I work my arms into it, feeling the familiar weight settle across my shoulders. Good weight. Protective weight.

My hands move to the MP5 sitting on the workbench. The weapon feels right as soon as my fingers wrap around the polymer grip—familiar, balanced. Rune-etched stock glows faintly with residual magic I carved into it three weeks ago during one of those sleepless nights. Blue-green light pulses along the grooves.

I slap the magazine home—*clack*—then rack the charging handle. The bolt cycles forward with a sharp metallic *snap-snap*. Chambered round. Safety off. Thirty rounds of silver-tipped hollow points loaded with salt and blessed iron filings. Not that bullets mean much against what lives down there, but they'll hurt enough.

The cold starts then.

It always starts with my knuckles. Frost spreads across them like veins of ice beneath my skin, creeping up my fingers. I hold my hand out, watching the blue flame dance silently over my palm. No heat. Never any heat anymore—not after that night at Sub-Station Seven. Just cold. Dead silent cold that drops the temperature exactly ten degrees wherever I am.

The frost-cobalt magic responds to thought now, locked in permanent state because of whatever the hell happened inside me when I stopped caring about consequences. 4th Law of the Weave or some shit Bram muttered about before he left. Doesn't matter what it's called. Matters that it works.

I flex my fingers. The flame jumps from knuckle to knuckle without burning me, without casting shadows, without making any sound except the whisper of wind through frozen air that shouldn't exist indoors.

Above my workbench, pinned to the wall with rusty nails, are three blank index cards. Nothing written on them yet. Bram suggested I might need to remember things eventually, that this vigilante shit tends to blur lines between justice and revenge if you don't keep notes. I'm not convinced I'll use them, but I haven't taken them down either.

My eyes linger on those empty cards for a second longer than necessary, then drop back to the weapon in my hands.

"Alright," I mutter to nobody in particular. My voice sounds flat even to myself.

I check my pockets one last time: lockpicks, bolt cutters, flashlight with fresh batteries, duct tape wrapped around my forearm. Standard gear. Everything else I might need is already stashed at safe houses scattered across the South Side—places the Gnome frequency brokers won't find unless they're looking real hard.

A gust rattles the side door as I approach it. The lock releases with a heavy *clunk* and the door swings open into afternoon light that makes me squint after hours under fluorescent bulbs.

The Neon Hollow stretches out beyond the garage—a sprawl of warehouses and industrial lots bleeding into each other beneath a gray February sky. Wind whips past carrying the smell of exhaust fumes from the Pulaski Skyway and something else underneath it. Something like rot from the Kearny Marshes.

I step out into it all and let the cold bite through my jacket. The frost-cobalt magic pulses steadily in my veins, keeping me warmer than I should be while making everything around me colder than it has any right to be.

Down toward the sewer grates now. Where Grimjaw's pack lives in the pipes and tunnels beneath Newark Bay. Where the Gnome frequency brokers conduct their business in exchange for favors that'll probably cost me more than I'm willing to pay when this whole thing blows up later.

But that's tomorrow's problem.

Today I just need to find them. Make contact. Take the contract.

First step down into the dark.

My boots hit pavement, then dirt, then concrete again as I descend toward where the storm drains disappear beneath iron plates rusted half through by decades of pollution. The wind follows me like an angry ghost, whipping my jacket against my sides.

This is it.

No turning back now.

The first grate comes into view about fifty yards ahead—steel bars set into cracked concrete, dripping with moisture and god-knows-what-else. Somewhere below that is everything Bram warned me about: rogue metahumans, frequency dealers pushing synthetic weave highs, sewer rats big enough to eat your face off if you're stupid enough to get close.

Somewhere down there is also my target.

I stop at the edge of the grate and kneel down. One hand rests on the cold metal bars.

"Here goes nothing," I whisper.

Then I start prying it open.

---

## CHAPTER 11: THE BLACK-CIRCUIT CONTRACT

The garage reeked of ozone and burnt copper. I had my left arm buried up to the elbow in Danny's Iron-Lung, fingers working around the brass casing while my right hand held the Panasonic Toughbook at an angle where I could see the pressure gauge without moving my head.

Hiss-thump. Hiss-thump.

The rhythm was all wrong. The Mk. I Arcane Iron-Lung shouldn't sound like that—shouldn't feel like it was fighting itself with every breath. Through the transparent section of the casing, I watched Danny's chest rise and fall, slow and mechanical. The black iron crystals inside were starting to form again, tiny sparks of dark matter coalescing against the crystal matrix that kept him alive.

"Pressure's spiking," I said, voice flat. Dead-silent. The words came out wrong somehow, detached. Like they belonged to someone else.

Bram Kovacs moved around behind me, his boots heavy on the concrete floor. Dwarf. Local 405 union card. Beard full of grease stains and old solder flux. He leaned over my shoulder, squinting at the readouts.

"Casing seals are cracked," he said, his North Jersey drawl making it sound less urgent than it was. "You push another twenty PSI through this rig, the whole thing blows. We're talking shrapnel radius of about ten feet." He wiped his hands on a rag that had been clean once, maybe. "Standard parts won't cut it."

I pulled my arm free, leaving trails of blue-black residue across the brass fittings. The temperature in the garage dropped ten degrees when I moved. Frost-cobalt. Zero-remorse state. I didn't even feel it anymore—that cold that should've made my teeth chatter but just numbed everything down to a dull ache behind my eyes.

"What do you need?" I asked.

"Military-grade Telluric pressure-valves." Bram pointed at the cracked seal flange with a thick finger. "These babies can handle the arcane pressure we're talking about. Problem is, nobody sells them retail. You want ones that'll actually work? Gotta go deep Undercity. Frequency brokers got 'em."

My Nextel i1000plus buzzed on the workbench. Grease-stained. Screen lit up: 917 number. Unknown caller. But I knew who it was. Always did.

I ignored it for now.

"How much?" I asked instead.

Bram shrugged, wiping more grease from his beard into his palm. "Couple hundred. Maybe more if you're buying black market. Plus whatever they tack on for delivery and not shooting you in the head."

The Iron-Lung wheezed again. Hiss-thump.

Danny's life measured in PSI and cracked seals and frequency broker prices I couldn't afford.

"I'm going," I said.

"Figured." Bram straightened up, cracking his back. "You gonna take the piece?"

I looked at my MP5 where it sat on the bench, rune-etched metal catching the sodium-vapor light bleeding through the window. Loaded with depleted-bismuth rounds. Good against anything non-corporeal. Against most things corporeal too.

Yeah. I was taking the piece.

Loaded a fresh magazine—eight shots, each one costing me half an hour of sleep to stabilize the runes properly. Tucked it under my leather jacket. Grabbed my keys. The Nextel buzzed again.

Same number.

I picked it up this time. Held it to my ear without saying anything.

"You know what you need," the voice said. Male. Accent I couldn't place. Might've been anywhere between Newark and Newark Airport. "And you know where to find it. Sterling Manor. Sub-Station Seven. Midnight. Don't be late."

Click.

Dead line.

I put the phone down. Looked at Danny through the casing. Watched him breathe that mechanical breath.

Sterling Manor meant crossing the Kearny Marshes after dark. Sub-Station Seven meant dealing with frequency brokers who played by rules that weren't exactly compatible with staying alive long-term. And midnight meant three hours to get there from the South Side.

I pulled my jacket tighter around the MP5.

The garage smelled like dying machinery and ozone.

I locked the door behind me when I left.

* * *

The Circuit Board reeked of burnt flux and desperation.

I descended the rust-streaked stairs into the underbelly of Neon Hollow, where the South Side's tech underground had taken root like some electronic fungus. The temperature dropped with each step—my own doing, I knew that now. The frost-cobalt was always there, waiting just beneath my skin, turning my breath into white plumes in rooms that should have been warm.

At the bottom, the arcade sprawled before me like a cathedral of forgotten gods. Pac-Man ghosts still blinked their yellow eyes at empty corridors. Street Fighter II cabinets hummed with synthesized bass lines that nobody came down here to play anymore. The place existed for one reason: hardware brokering outside any legal framework the city could enforce.

Digits sat hunched over his workstation—a dining table littered with circuit boards, soldering irons, and what looked like a disassembled cell phone network. His oversized aviators reflected the blue-white glow of his work lights. He didn't look up when I entered, just kept working on whatever contraption occupied his attention.

"Got your message," I said.

"Yeah? Well, I got your money?" His voice carried that particular Gnome inflection—not quite mockery, but close. He finally glanced up, those too-large eyes taking my measure behind tinted lenses. "Because the merchandise ain't cheap."

I crossed the space between us, boots crunching on scattered components. Behind him, three other Gnomes worked at various stations, all of them looking up at the sound of my approach. They knew what I was. Everyone did after last month's incident at County General.

"The Telluric valves." My voice came out flat, mechanical. Good. When I felt nothing, I sounded like nothing. "Class-4 pressure regulation units. You have them or not?"

Digits set down his soldering iron with exaggerated care. He reached into his windbreaker—baggy 90s style, probably stolen—and produced a silver cylinder no bigger than my palm. Even from here, I could see the telluric etchings spiraling around its surface, catching the light like oil on water.

"This one of 'em," he said, holding it up. The metal gleamed, pristine despite being corporate-grade hardware. "Transponder frequency locked tighter than a virgin's legs. These babies are fresh off a Union Pacific shipping manifest that disappeared two days ago. Some engineer in Secaucus must be shitting bricks right now."

"How much?"

His grin showed too many teeth. "Fifty grand. Cash. I don't do layaway, I don't do trades, and I sure as hell don't do favors for vigilantes who turn people inside-out with their fucked-up magic."

My knuckles began to tingle. That familiar sizzling sensation spread across my fingertips as frost-cobalt energy pooled there, seeking an outlet. The temperature in the immediate vicinity dropped ten degrees. I saw my breath plume white in front of my face.

"Twenty-five," I said quietly.

The smile vanished from Digits' face. His eyes darted to my hands, then back to my face. Smart Gnome. Around us, the other brokers had gone still, watching this negotiation with the intensity of predators identifying prey.

"I said fifty." His hand drifted toward something beneath the work table. Probably a weapon. Probably stupid.

I took another step forward. The arcade cabinets behind me began to ice over, condensation forming on their plastic facades, running down in crystalline rivulets. My vision had taken on that edge—the world sharper somehow, every detail hyper-real while simultaneously distant, like I was observing it through glass.

"You have the valves or not?" My voice never rose above conversational level. That was worse than shouting. Everyone knew that.

Digits opened his mouth to respond—probably something foolish—but a new voice cut through the tension like a scalpel through skin.

"Gentlemen."

We both turned. A figure had emerged from between two pinball machines in the back corner—a man I hadn't seen come down the stairs. Well-dressed. Human, by the look of him, maybe mid-forties, slicked hair and a suit that probably cost more than everything in this basement combined.

"Fifty thousand is... ambitious pricing for Mr. Reyes' needs," the stranger continued smoothly, stepping into the pool of light from one of the work stations. "Though I can certainly appreciate the market forces at play here."

Digits' expression cycled through confusion and annoyance before settling on suspicion. "Who the fuck are you?"

The man's smile didn't reach his eyes. "Someone who appreciates efficiency. Vargas." He extended a hand, which neither Digits nor I took. "And I'm authorized to cover the mechanic's tab. Assuming he's looking for work."

My jaw tightened. Every instinct screamed danger, but Danny was dying in my garage, locked inside iron lungs that were running out of air faster than I could manufacture replacement parts. The Telluric valves were non-negotiable. They regulated pressure in the Mk. II system—I'd need them if I wanted to keep him alive past another week.

"What kind of work?" I asked.

Vargas' smile widened fractionally. He reached inside his jacket—not for a weapon, but for a manila folder, which he slid across the nearest arcade cabinet with practiced ease. "The kind where someone of your particular skill set might find employment. Plumbing, as it were. Though in this case, we're dealing with something more esoteric than water pipes."

I opened the folder without touching it—just flipped back the cover enough to read the header page. Black-Circuit Contract. Below that, a series of technical specifications written in language that made my engineering brain ache even as frost-cobalt magic crackled along my nerve endings.

"You want me to break into Union Pacific's telluric network," I said flatly.

"Perceptive. And discreet about it." Vargas nodded. "There's been... leakage. Information flowing where it shouldn't. My employers would like that stopped. Permanently."

"The valves," I said. Not a question.

He gestured at Digits, who looked like he'd bitten into something sour. The Gnome reluctantly placed both silver cylinders on top of a nearby crate—they landed with heavy, machined weight, each one worth more than most people made in a month working legitimate jobs.

"They're yours once the job is complete. I'll even throw in transport—we've got a truck waiting topside that can get you anywhere in tri-state within an hour."

My breath came out as white fog. The cold was spreading now, frost creeping up the sides of the arcade machines, ice crystals forming on Digits' soldering station. Around us, the other Gnomes had started backing toward the exit, recognizing the signs.

"What's the catch?" I asked.

Vargas' expression finally shifted, showing something beneath the polished exterior. Hunger maybe. Or desperation. "The usual ones, Mr. Reyes. You don't talk about what you see. You don't deviate from the objective. And if anyone asks..." He paused, letting the implication hang. "...you were never here."

* * *

The Circuit Board stank of stale beer and ozone. I stood in the back corner where the neon signs bled through greasy windows, casting everything in sickly pink and electric blue. Vargas leaned against the pinball machine, arms crossed over a shirt that probably cost more than my monthly rent. The kind of money the Syndicate didn't mind spending on disposable muscle like him.

He slid a manila folder across the scarred Formica table.

"Got a problem down in Junction Seven," he said, not bothering to look up from his Motorola StarTAC. "Sewer line beneath the old textile mills. Couple weeks ago, some kind of... contamination started turning the local population. Feral cases. They're chewing through our shipments."

I didn't touch the folder. Just stared at it, watching the condensation on the outside leaves dark patterns across the glossy surface. My knuckles were already starting to frost over, even without touching any metal. The temperature in the arcade had dropped maybe five degrees since I'd walked in.

"Feral ghouls," Vargas clarified, finally meeting my eyes. "Whatever the hell they are now. They killed three of ours last night. Messy business." He gestured at the folder. "Blueprints are in there. Gas main access points, ventilation shafts. Should be simple extermination work for someone with your particular skill set."

*Simple.* Right.

"The job pays twenty grand," he continued. "Half upfront. We've got some Telluric valves you might find useful—scrapped from a decommissioned hospital plant up in Newark. Might keep that brother of yours breathing a little longer."

My jaw tightened. The cold was spreading up my forearms now, leaving that blue-black iron-gall residue along my veins. I could feel it sizzling against my skin, smell the acrid burn of oxidized metal.

"You know what I am?" I asked quietly. My voice came out flat, dead-silent.

Vargas smirked. "Heard stories. Machine-shop mystic. Works with metals and blood-iron magic. Rings true enough—I saw what you did to those Deeper traders last month."

"I'm not a fucking exterminator." I reached for the folder, my fingers leaving frost patterns on the table. "And I don't do the Syndicate's dirty work."

"No?" He flipped his phone shut. "Your brother's been in that iron-lung what, six months? The Mk. I model runs on Telluric current. Those valves are custom-fitted. Can't buy replacements off the shelf."

I pulled the folder open. Blueprints spilled across the table—a network of tunnels and junctions beneath the South Side, marked with red X's where the ghouls had been spotted. Junction Seven sat right at the heart of it all, surrounded by warning symbols.

"Fifteen grand now," Vargas said. "Another ten when you confirm the junction is clear. Plus the valves."

"What happens if I say no?"

"You can watch your brother suffocate over the next few weeks while he waits for parts that aren't available anywhere except through us."

The cold intensified. Ten degrees now. I could see my breath misting in front of me as I stared down at those blueprints, imagining Danny hooked up to machines that would fail without intervention.

*But a sliver of justice for Danny is better than no justice at all.*

I reached into my duffel bag and pulled out a metal toolbox. Set it on the table between us. "I'll need my equipment."

Vargas nodded to someone behind me—one of his muscle types, who'd appeared silently from the shadows. The man set down a heavy case, then stepped back without a word.
