Need intel first. Need to know what they're protecting down here besides their pathetic lives.

The telluric tap is there, visible past the firing line—a cluster of crystalline nodes pulsing with captured lightning, feeding power up to High-Spire through conduits that disappear into the ceiling. Illegal as hell. This whole operation is a violation of every treaty signed after the Breach.

And they're willing to kill their own people to protect it.

A rocket-propelled grenade screams through the smog.

I see the trail of fire arcing toward a cluster of Goblins, all chained together, too terrified to run. The warhead will vaporize them.

Mara Vance doesn't hesitate.

I vault the catwalk railing.

* * *

The coordinates led us down through layers of concrete and despair until the air itself turned thick with the taste of sulfur and old blood. Sub-Level 4 of the Foundry Sector was where Neon Hollow kept its dirty secrets—the kind that didn't appear on any city planning documents or official maps.

My boots hit wet concrete as I dropped through the maintenance hatch, Aegis Squad following behind in controlled chaos. The first thing that registered wasn't the workers or the weapons, but the *sound*—a wet, rhythmic thudding like meat being pounded against stone.

"Commander!" Reyes' voice crackled through my comm. "We've got hostiles at three o'clock—"

I saw them before he finished. High-Spire Elves, their armor gleaming even in the sickly yellow light filtering through decades of accumulated grime. They weren't here for salvage or territory. Their rifles were trained on a group of laborers chained to the wall—Ogres, Trolls, a few desperate humans—and one of those rifles had an RPG round already locked and loaded.

The world went sharp and clear.

My hands erupted in white-lilac fire so bright it burned away the smog around me like a surgical incision through diseased tissue. The flames sang up my arms, spiraling into a bio-ward that expanded outward in a perfect hemisphere. Pure. Clean. Everything about it screamed *official BATC intervention*.

"You want to start this dance?" I called out, my voice cutting across the underground chamber. "Because I guarantee you won't like how it ends."

The Elf commander—a tall bastard with silver hair and enough ritual scars to make him expensive—froze. His eyes tracked the glow of my wards, then widened as he recognized what he was looking at. Not some street mage. Not even regular BATC enforcement.

Aegis Commander.

His rifle lowered fractionally. Behind him, two more elves moved, optical-camo cloaks beginning to shimmer around their forms. Smart. They knew exactly what those cloaks meant—they could vanish into the shadows and make this whole thing disappear, no witnesses, no incident reports, just another night in the Undercity where people who didn't matter got disappeared.

But they hadn't counted on my squad dropping through every maintenance hatch within a hundred meters. Non-lethal suppression rounds began pinging off concrete around them, not quite hitting but making it crystal fucking clear that we had them surrounded.

"Stand down!" The Elf's command was sharp, precise. To his men: "Cloak. Fall back. We abort."

And just like that, they were gone. Optical-camo hummed and faded, leaving nothing but empty air and the acrid smell of cordite mixing with something sweeter, cleaner—that fresh cedar scent that always accompanied major magical expenditure.

I dropped to my knees beside the nearest laborer without thinking, my hands already shifting from combat weaves to medical triage. White-lilac light traced over an Ogre-Kin with a gut wound so bad I could see bone through the tear in his hide. Blood slicked my medical gloves hot and wet.

"Triage! Now!" I barked to my squad. "Reyes, you've got three more casualties over there—start compression. Martinez, get me the field trauma kit!"

The Ogre grabbed my arm with surprising strength for someone bleeding out. His eyes were wide, pupils blown wide with shock and pain. "They... they just pushed us in front..." he gasped, each word a struggle. "Said we were cheaper than Kevlar..."

My jaw tightened so hard my teeth hurt. Rage wanted to burn through my veins, wanted to pour itself into a retaliatory strike, but I forced it down into something useful. Controlled. Focused.

"I've got you," I said, my voice tight as I applied a glowing white-lilac cauterizing weave across the worst of the damage. The smell changed again—cedar and ozone overwhelming even the blood and sulfur. "Stay with me. You're going to make it."

Behind him, chained to the same wall, another worker—a Troll with half his face missing—wasn't so lucky. Reyes was already shaking his head at me. Can't save them all. Never can.

But you try anyway.

That's what separates us from the monsters who'd chain people up as meat shields.

As I worked on stabilizing the Ogre, my peripheral vision caught something that made my stomach drop. Stamped on the heavy chains binding these workers: a Sterling-Voss corporate insignia, clear as day.

Not Morvain.

The Board of Directors.

*Shit.*

This wasn't some rogue operation. This was sanctioned. Official. Someone high up had decided that Undercity laborers were disposable resources, and Sterling-Voss had provided the chains to make it legal.

I looked down at the dying Ogre-Kin, at his eyes finding mine with desperate hope as my weaves knit his flesh back together. Whatever came next—I'd deal with it. But first, this man survived. All of them who could be saved would survive.

Because that's what Aegis does in the dark places where no one else wants to look.

We bring the light.

---

## CHAPTER 8: CHAPTER 8

The coffee tasted like regret and burnt filters, but I'd drunk worse. Much worse. The mug sat cold between my palms while I stared at the rusted iron chain links sprawled across my desk—evidence from the Undercity raid, evidence that Sterling-Voss had been moving blood-iron through the sewer systems for months now. Maybe years.

My office smelled like cedar and old paper, the lingering scent of my own magic clinging to everything I touched. The warmth was familiar, comforting even, after three days of processing what we'd found down there. Bodies. So many fucking bodies.

The Motorola Nextel on my desk started buzzing.

I didn't recognize the number, but I recognized the code that flashed across the tiny screen: **187-Arcane**. Homicide with metaphysical components. My jaw tightened as I reached for my medical kit—the leather bag felt heavy with its contents, bandages and antiseptic and more arcane materials than any field commander should have to carry.

"Vance." The dispatcher's voice crackled through the speakerphone. "Foundry District. Behind the old textile mills on Penn."

"I know where it is."

"You need to see this one yourself. Cops are spooked. Says the crime scene's... freezing over." She paused. "And Vance? Forensics won't touch it. They're calling it active magic."

Active. That meant the working wasn't finished. The spell was still running.

I grabbed my coat—a heavy wool thing that had seen better decades—and headed out into the October rain.

---

The Crown Vic's tires sang against wet asphalt, rhythmic and hypnotic. Rain hammered the windshield in sheets, the wipers barely keeping pace. I merged onto Route 1 & 9, lights cutting through the darkness, and thought about Sterling-Voss. About chains and blood and whatever fresh hell was waiting for me behind those textile mills.

Forty minutes later, I pulled up to a cluster of patrol cars, their emergency lights painting everything in strobing yellow and red. Cops huddled under awnings, shoulders hunched, breath visible in clouds despite the temperature gauge on my dash reading fifty-two degrees.

I killed the engine and stepped out into the downpour.

"Commander Vance?" A young cop—couldn't be more than twenty-five, face pale beneath his cap—approached with a flashlight extended like an offering. His hands were shaking. "Forensics won't go near it, ma'am. Says the magic on the vic is still active. It's..." He swallowed hard. "...it's quiet. Too quiet."

I took the flashlight without responding and ducked under the yellow police tape.

The moment I crossed that line, something changed.

The rain stopped hitting me.

I looked up, watching droplets freeze mid-air a few feet ahead, suspended like crystalline beads before transforming into sleet and continuing their fall. The temperature plummeted—I could feel it in my lungs, each breath suddenly sharp and cold. Ten degrees. Maybe fifteen. The air itself felt wrong, dense and heavy and somehow *listening*.

My cedar-scent magic pushed back automatically, warmth radiating from my chest as I activated my wards reflexively. But this wasn't normal arcane work. This was something else.

I clicked on the flashlight and walked forward.

The alley was narrow, walls of crumbling brick pressing inward like a throat. Garbage cans overflowed with refuse, and somewhere water dripped with that particular emptiness of abandoned places. My boots splashed through puddles that shouldn't have been frozen at fifty degrees, ice forming in fractal patterns where they touched the ground.

Then I saw him.

A man—middle-aged, business suit torn and soaked, face twisted in an expression that was neither surprise nor pain but something beyond both. He lay sprawled against the wall, one arm outstretched toward the mouth of the alley like he'd been reaching for help or escape or just air when whatever happened, happened.

But it wasn't the body that made my stomach clench.

It was the frost spreading across the pavement around him, creeping outward in intricate geometric patterns. And the silence. God, the silence. No birds, no traffic noise filtering from the street beyond—just the soft hiss of sleet hitting the ground and my own breathing.

"Fuck," I whispered.

This was Cole Reyes's work. Had to be.

I'd read the reports from Sub-Station Seven, seen the aftermath of his confrontation with the Undercity gangsters. The way metal had frozen solid mid-air. The way blood turned to iron filings before anyone's eyes. But reading about it and seeing it were two different things entirely.

I knelt beside the body, cedar magic flaring bright as I established a perimeter ward. The cold hit me immediately—not the ambient temperature drop, which my wards could handle, but something deeper. A wrongness that sank into bone marrow and made my teeth ache.

The victim's skin was blue-tinged, frost forming on his eyelashes. But there was no blood. None. His chest had been opened—cleanly, surgically—and whatever had been taken was gone. Only the cavity remained, perfectly smooth edges that shouldn't have existed without massive hemorrhage but somehow didn't bleed at all.

"Christ," I breathed, leaning closer.

There, in the center of the wound, where a heart should have been: a single chain link, no bigger than my thumb. Frost-cobalt. The same material Sterling-Voss had been moving through the Undercity.

And it was still pulsing with active magic.

My pager buzzed again. Same number as before.

*You wanted proof, Commander.*

*Look closer.*

* * *

The rain hammers against my back as I step into the alley's mouth, boots squelching in the oil-stained puddles. October in North Jersey should smell like wet pavement and dying leaves. Instead, my nose fills with something else—a metallic tang that makes my teeth ache.

"Commander Vance." The uniform who flagged me down looks green around the gills. Smart kid. He stays at the alley entrance while I push deeper into the shadows.

My Maglite cuts through the darkness like a lighthouse beam. The warmth from its handle seeps into my palm—solid, electric, real. I need that reality right now because what the light illuminates is anything but normal.

An Elven male, tall even in death, pinned to the brick wall by his own hand. Literally. A jagged spike of something dark and crystalline erupts through his right palm, driving straight through his chest cavity. The point of impact is a perfect circle of frozen tissue, black ice radiating outward in spider-web patterns across his lab coat. Sterling-Voss corporate logo barely visible under all the frost.

I pull out my micro-cassette recorder, voice steady despite the cold knifing through my wool coat.

"Victim is a High-Spire Elf. Estimated age two-hundred-sixty, maybe older. Cause of death appears to be massive arcane trauma. The hex... it's blood-iron metallurgy. But I've never felt a weave this cold."

I move closer, beam tracking over the details. No pooled blood. None. What should have been gallons of lifeblood has flash-frozen into this grotesque sculpture of ice and iron. The surface shimmers with an oily blue-black sheen—cobalt mixed with something else. Something wrong.

"There's no residual anger in the magic. It's just... absolute zero."

The words feel inadequate. My cedar-scented wards always run warm, protective, alive with purpose. This thing that killed him? It's the opposite. Dead-cold precision without malice or passion or any human emotion whatsoever.

And the ledger.

A thick black leather journal sits wedged against his sternum, perfectly parallel to his ribs. The cobalt spike drives clean through its center pages before penetrating flesh. The pages aren't just stuck—they're welded to the wound, fused by some impossibly hot-and-cold process simultaneously.

Frost coats my eyelashes as I lean in. Each breath clouds white in air that shouldn't be this frigid. My thermal vision would normally show heat signatures, but around this body there's just... absence. A void where warmth should be.

"The execution was performed at close range," I continue recording. "No defensive wounds. Victim likely didn't see it coming or couldn't react. Point-of-origin suggests the attacker stood approximately three feet distance, right-hand dominant."

* * *

The rain falls wrong tonight.

I kneel beside the corpse in the alley behind the Foundry District, watching droplets hit the ground ten inches away where they should fall on me instead. The temperature plummets—ten degrees in three steps, like crossing an invisible wall. My breath clouds white while the world beyond stays November-wet and autumn-cool.

The victim's name was Marcus Webb. Forty-seven years old, former vice president of waste management at Sterling-Chem. His body lies pinned to a brick wall by what looks like an icicle made from liquid mercury that forgot how to flow. Frost spreads from the wound points, crystalline patterns that eat into his suit jacket, his flesh, the mortar between bricks.

No blood. That's the first thing you notice—should be arterial spray, pooling, dripping down the wall. Instead there's just... absence. A cold so deep it sucks heat from everything around it.

Cole Reyes did this.

I've seen his work before—every Aegis Commander has—but never up close. Never when the air still tastes like frozen void. I extend my right hand slowly, summoning the white-lilac flame that marks my magic. Cedar scent blooms warm around me, fighting against the sterile nothingness radiating from those cobalt spikes.

The smell helps. Always does. Fresh cedar means life, growth, the way things should be. Whatever Cole is, he's the opposite of that.

My fingers stop six inches from the nearest spike. Even through the flames, I feel the wrongness—the psychological residue baked into the weave. This isn't malice exactly. It's colder than that. More disciplined.

*Justice*, whispers something in my bones. *Penance. Necessity.*

I don't let myself dwell on it. Analysis can come later. First priority: evidence preservation.

Using my free hand, I trace bio-wards in the air—a complex pattern of protective sigils that cost me half my remaining stamina for the night. The frost recedes fractionally where they intersect with Cole's work. Just enough.

"Someone is hunting the people who poisoned the South Side," I mutter to the corpse, carefully working my magic to thaw the frozen blood without damaging whatever's underneath. "And they aren't asking questions."

Steam hisses as my white-lilac flames touch the cobalt frost. Ice cracks with sounds like breaking glass. The leather ledger pinned under Webb's left shoulder begins to emerge—stiff, waterlogged, but intact.

I slide it free. Open it.

Shipping manifests. Dates from 2000. Sterling-Chem Experimental Sludge Unit, Batch 734-B through 812-G, all dumped into the Undercity sewer network between March and June. The same sludge that caused the Black-Iron Lung epidemic. The same poison that killed two hundred families down south while the company filed paperwork claiming 'controlled agricultural runoff.'

My stomach turns. Not from the death—I've seen worse—but from what this means.

Footsteps echo at the alley entrance. I look up fast, hand already moving to my sidearm before I register the BATC Internal Affairs badges.

Two men in suits, faces I recognize from headquarters briefings but whose names I can't place right now. They're here for the body. Here for *me*.

"Commander Vance," says the taller one, not smiling. "We need you to come in. Now."

---

## CHAPTER 9: CHAPTER 9

The elevator ride up was silent except for the pneumatic hiss of hydraulics and the soft chime of each passing floor. I watched my reflection in the polished chrome walls—blood crusting on my cheekbone, the BATC insignia on my soaked uniform stained crimson instead of regulation black. Someone had tried to clean the elevator since my last visit. They'd failed.

The doors opened onto the 80th floor.

IA.

Internal Affairs didn't have offices. They had sanctuaries. Glass walls separated the briefing room from the rest of the Spire's sterile expanse, but I could see the elves moving like ghosts through the cubicles beyond—high-society metas in pressed suits, their pointed ears catching the fluorescent light. The air smelled wrong. Too clean. Ozone-purified. Expensive cologne mixed with the electric tang of equipment that cost more than a Kearny tenement building.

Vane Thorne stood by the panoramic window overlooking Neon Hollow. Sunrise painted the city in shades of bruised plum and sickly orange, the chemical plants belching smoke over the marshlands. He turned as I entered, his smile razor-thin and utterly cold.

"Commander Vance," he said, voice smooth as silk pulled across broken glass. "You look like you've been wrestling hogs in the slaughterhouse."

I didn't move closer. Let him come to me if he wanted something.

"The chemist is still warm enough to smell," I replied. "Your people should hurry if they want first dibs at the autopsy."

Thorne poured himself water from a crystal decanter, ice cubes clinking like tiny bells against the glass. His suit was immaculate—a charcoal grey that probably cost more than my monthly salary. Not a wrinkle. Not a stain. Perfectly groomed hair, perfectly manicured nails. Everything about him screamed High-Spire superiority.

"You recovered a ledger." Not a question. He took a measured sip, those elven eyes never leaving mine. "The one the deceased was so carelessly clutching when you arrived."

My hand instinctively went to my belt pouch. The leather felt wet and heavy.

"That's evidence."

"We are all evidence, Commander." Thorne set down his glass on a tray beside an IBM ThinkPad that looked fresh from the factory floor. "The chemist—Marcus Thorne, Sterling-Voss division—was killed with blood-iron hexwork during what appears to be a corporate dispute. This makes it *our* matter."

"Bullshit."

His smile widened, showing too-white teeth. "Excuse me?"

"He died in my sector. In my city. With a hex signature that matches three separate attacks on BATC infrastructure over the past month." I took two steps forward, boots squelching on the imported Persian rug. "Someone's testing our defenses. Someone's good enough to walk through wards that should've stopped a goddamn nuke. That makes it my problem."

"And yet," Thorne gestured lazily toward the door behind me, where two IA enforcement officers stood with their arms crossed, "you're here. Speaking to me. Which suggests someone above your pay grade disagrees with your assessment."

I hated this. Hated every inch of polished marble and climate-controlled air. Hated how clean everything was while the city below rotted in its own filth. Hated that he was right—I'd been summoned like a dog on a leash.

"Give me the ledger, Commander. You can consider yourself... temporarily reassigned."

"What's that mean?"

"It means," he turned back to his laptop, fingers dancing across keys with unnatural speed, "that you're going to find whoever killed Mr. Thorne. But you'll do it under our supervision. Our rules." The projector hummed to life behind him, bathing the room in cold white light. A file folder appeared on screen: *OPERATION MECHANIC - EYES ONLY*.

"We have a name for your suspect."

The image changed. A grainy surveillance photo from one of Newark Bay's cargo terminals—too dark to make out features clearly. Male. Tall. Moving with the precise economy of motion I recognized from combat training.

"The Mechanic," Thorne said softly, dimming the lights until we were both bathed in the monitor's glow. "Cole Reyes. Former Sterling-Voss security contractor. Discharged for 'excessive zeal' after an incident in 2001. Since then, he's been a ghost. Three years of silence. Then suddenly..." He clicked again. More images. Security footage showing impossible feats of strength, hexwork that violated fundamental laws of arcane physics.

"He didn't just kill the chemist," Thorne continued, voice dropping lower. "He broke into Sterling-Voss's primary research server. Stole proprietary data on blood-iron weaponry. Data that could level this entire city if deployed improperly."

"Why?"

That smile again—that predatory, corporate smirk.

"That, Commander, is what you're going to discover."

* * *

The briefing room sits thirty stories above Newark Bay, all chrome and smoked glass that reflects nothing. I feel like I'm breathing through a straw.

Vane Thorne stands at the control panel, his perfectly pressed suit the color of charcoal smoke. Behind him, the projector hums—an old-school Epson that smells like burning dust and ozone. Click-clack. Click-clack. The carousel advances.

"Commander Vance." His voice is smooth as river stones. "Thank you for coming."

I don't respond. My fingers find the armrest of my chair, dig in slightly. The leather creaks.

"The Mechanic," Thorne begins, and already I hate the nickname. Criminals get nicknames when they escape us, when they become myths instead of men. "Real name Cole Reyes. Thirty-two years old. Former BATC contractor, dismissed 2001 for insubordination during the Kearny Marshes cleanup."

Click-clack.

The first image slams onto the wall—a photograph so grainy it looks like an x-ray. A man slumped over a steering wheel in some Lincoln Town Car, frost spreading across the windshield in crystalline fractals. Ice crawls down the driver's face, turning his expression into something frozen between rage and surprise.

"Victim number one. Anthony Scavo. Union boss, 43rd Street Waterfront Coalition. Found November 3rd, 2001. Body temperature was minus-17 degrees Celsius."

Thorne gestures with his pen, laser-pointer dot dancing across the ice-crystal patterns on the glass. "Notice anything?"

I notice everything. That's my job.

"The frost," I say quietly. "It didn't melt. Even after we found him, even when he'd been dead for hours. Forensic team said it was like... like the cold was still there. Still clinging to him."

"Precisely." Thorne clicks again. Click-clack.

Another photo: a Black-Circuit smuggler impaled against a warehouse wall, iron rebar punched clean through his chest. Blood has frozen in rivers down his torso, black as tar in the flashbulb glare.

"This is Viktor Kozlov. September 8th, 2002. Same signature—body temp at discovery, minus-23. And here..." He pauses, lets the silence stretch. "...here's where it gets interesting."

The carousel slides to the next shot. My stomach drops.

The chemist from the alley. The one I watched Cole walk away from, back in August. He's sprawled in what looks like a meat locker, flesh blue-white, lips pulled back in a silent scream. But this time I can see more—the context. A laboratory freezer, equipment scattered, chemical formulas scrawled in his own blood before it froze solid.

"He killed the chemist," Thorne says unnecessarily. "Three weeks ago. August 24th. Burned the lab, but not before our analysts recovered enough data to trace his supply chain all the way back to the Pylon Project."

My knuckles whiten around the armrest.

Thorne turns, and for the first time, something flickers across his face—not quite concern, not quite fear. Ambition, maybe. Or calculation.

"You know about the Pylon Project, Commander?"

"The deep-level infrastructure contract." My voice stays flat. "Undercity renovation, wastewater management, slag reclamation. Twenty-billion-dollar federal grant."

"And who won that contract?"

"Sterling Manor Consolidated."

He smiles—that practiced, corporate smile that belongs on magazine covers and never near real violence.

"Yes. Sterling Manor. Which means..." He pulls up another image: a schematic of some massive underground structure, all cylinders and conduits and glowing nodes. "This is Phase Two. Not just cleaning up the Undercity. This is weaponizing it. Turning the entire Northeast Corridor's waste disposal system into an arcane power grid. The Mechanic understands what he's interrupting."

Click-clack. Another photo: closer now, zoomed in on the chemist's frozen hand. His fingers are curled around something—a vial, half-crushed.

"What was in the vial?" I ask.

"Stabilized Null-Glyph Matrix. Experimental compound designed to neutralize chaotic magic signatures. In layman's terms? It makes ghosts invisible to our sensors. Makes them untrackable." Thorne walks toward me, and I catch the scent of his cologne—expensive, sharp as broken glass. "Cole Reyes used it to wipe himself from our grid for six months. He reappeared two weeks ago in Hoboken. Killed another target. A BATC subcontractor."

The air tastes like copper and ozone.

"Why am I here, Vane?"

His eyes narrow slightly at my use of his first name. Good.

"Because Internal Affairs has designated Cole Reyes a Category-One threat to BATC operations. Because he's eliminated seventeen individuals connected to the 2000 Sludge Trials and the subsequent cover-up. And because," he steps closer, voice dropping to something almost confidential, "he's not stopping at low-level enforcers anymore. He went after one of Sterling Manor's senior chemists. He's coming for the executives next."

I stand. The chair rolls backward with a soft squeak.

"The mechanic doctrine," Thorne continues, watching me carefully. "Our profilers have developed a complete psychological profile. He doesn't kill for money, Vance. He operates on a twisted doctrine. Penance for his own sins, revenge for his family, and what our profilers call 'a sliver of justice.' He knows he can't fix the city, but he'll butcher our executives just to get that sliver."

"And you want me to stop him."

"I want you to understand him first. Then stop him." Thorne moves back to the projector, clicks through more photos—a gallery of frozen corpses, each one precise, surgical, terrible. "He's escalating. And he's getting too close to the Pylon Project."

The carousel stops on the chemist's face, blue-white and beautiful in its horror.

"We need you inside this investigation, Commander. Full authority. Unlimited resources." He turns, and there's something hungry in his expression now. "Find Cole Reyes. Bring him in alive if possible. Dead if necessary."

I look at the photographs—all those frozen bodies, all that precision.

"What happened to his family?" I ask quietly.

Thorne blinks. "Excuse me?"

"Cole Reyes. Your profilers mentioned revenge. What did we do to his family?"

For the first time since I walked into this room, Vane Thorne looks uncomfortable.

"That information is classified pending—"

"Vane."

He exhales sharply through his nose.

"A wife and daughter. Both died during the Kearny Marshes cleanup operation, 2001. Industrial accident. Our contractors were using unshielded arcane equipment near residential zones. The official report cleared everyone involved." He pauses. "But Reyes was working site security that day. Saw everything. Blamed BATC directly for their deaths."

Click-clack. The projector wind-down sound echoes in the sterile silence.

I turn toward the

* * *

The air inside High-Spire's briefing room tastes like money—expensive cologne mixed with ozone-purified atmosphere and the faint metallic tang of the holographic projector humming at the center of the obsidian table. I can feel it pressing down on my lungs, this manufactured sterility, making my skin crawl beneath the stiff fabric of my commander's jacket.

Vane Thorne sits across from me, his silhouette sharp and perfect in the indirect lighting. He hasn't offered me coffee. Hasn't even acknowledged my entrance beyond a slight tightening around his eyes when I walked through the door.

"Commander Vance," he begins, his voice smooth as chrome, "thank you for joining us."

Us. There's no one else here but me and him, but I don't correct him. IA types love their passive aggressive bullshit.

He gestures toward the projector. A file folder materializes in mid-air between us, glowing faintly blue. "We have a situation requiring your particular... expertise."

I lean back in the chair, feeling its cold glass surface against my spine. My fingers find the edge of the table, gripping hard enough that my knuckles whiten. The cedar-scented flare of my magic rises instinctively, pushing back against the oppressive weight of Thorne's corporate aura trying to pin me in place.

"Cut to it, Vane. I've got three bodies cooling in the morgue and a squad of detectives who need actual work orders, not your bureaucratic runaround."

His smile doesn't reach his eyes. Those eyes are cold. Calculating. "Three murders in three weeks, all targeting Sterling-Voss executives. All displaying the same signature—impossible precision, untraceable methods." He pauses, letting the words settle like poison. "The media is calling the perpetrator 'The Mechanic.'"

"So you're telling me what I already know because you read it in my morning report."

"I'm *assigning* you the investigation, Commander. Aegis Division has been tasked with apprehending this individual before they compromise the stability of our entire region."

I laugh, sharp and bitter. "You mean before they expose how Sterling-Voss dumped Black-Iron Lung sludge into the Newark Bay and killed thousands of people?"

Thorne's expression doesn't change, but the temperature in the room drops several degrees. "This isn't about Sterling-Voss, Mara. This is about protecting the peace of Neon Hollow. About preventing vigilante justice from destabilizing everything we've built here."

"My squad saw what that sludge did to the Kearny Marshes. We pulled bodies out of toxic water while your Board members signed bonus checks at their country clubs."

"Watch yourself." His voice carries an edge now, something dangerous beneath the corporate polish. "Your funding comes through my department. Your squad's equipment, your personnel files—all of it traces back to decisions made in rooms exactly like this one."

My magic flares hotter, the cedar scent intensifying until it burns in my nostrils. I can feel the weight of his threat pressing against my sternum, trying to crush the breath from my lungs.

"You want The Mechanic caught," I say slowly, carefully. "Fine. But if I find evidence that Sterling-Voss ordered those dumps—if I uncover even a whisper of corporate responsibility for Black-Iron Lung—I'm bringing them in too. That's non-negotiable."

We stare at each other across the obsidian table. Outside the floor-to-ceiling windows, Neon Hollow spreads below us, its neon glow already flickering to life despite the early hour. Somewhere down there, Cole Reyes—the man Thorne has labeled 'The Mechanic'—is preparing his next move.

"And if you disobey a direct order from Internal Affairs?" Thorne asks quietly.

"I'll deal with that when I get there."

Another long silence. Then Thorne exhales, and the pressure on my chest eases slightly.

"Find him, Commander. Find him and stop him. Leave the corporate governance to the Board." He waves his hand dismissively. "You're dismissed."

I stand without another word, my boots clicking sharply against the polished floor. As I reach the door, his voice stops me:

"Mara?"

I turn, not trusting myself to speak.

"If you go after Sterling-Voss without authorization, I will personally see to it that Aegis Division is dissolved. You and your detectives will be reassigned to traffic duty in Bayonne." His smile returns, thin as a razor blade. "Have a productive investigation."

The door hisses shut behind me as I leave, cutting off whatever response might have escaped my lips. My hands are shaking—not from fear, but from the effort of keeping my magic contained, stopping myself from doing something stupid like cracking that fucking obsidian table in half.

The elevator ride down feels endless. I pull out my PalmPilot, fingers working automatically through muscle memory as I navigate to the floppy disk data Torin Kaelen gave me last week. The Pylons. If I'm going to hunt Cole Reyes, understand what he's killing for, I need to know what those things really are.

*Need to understand before I find him,* I think as the elevator doors open onto ground level. *Before he finds me first.*

Outside, the morning air hits me like a slap—polluted, thick with exhaust fumes and the smell of fried food from the 24-hour diner across the street. Real world smells. Alive smells.

My phone buzzes. Text from Detective Kowalski: **Found something on the third victim. Need to talk.**

I text back one-handed while flagging a cab: **Sub-Station Seven. Thirty minutes.**

As the yellow checkered vehicle pulls up, I glance back at High-Spire's gleaming facade reflecting the dawn light. Somewhere inside, Vane Thorne is probably already filing reports about our conversation, building his case to bury me if I step out of line.

Let him try.

I slide into the cab, giving the driver directions to Sub-Seven. In my palm, my phone buzzes again—this time it's an alert from the system. New file dropped into my secure folder. I tap it open:

**CONFIDENTIAL: STERLING-VOSS PROJECT PYLON – INTERNAL MEMORANDUM**

The cab accelerates into traffic as I begin reading, my heart hammering against my ribs. This is it. This is what Cole Reyes died for—or killed for. Either way, nothing in Neon Hollow will be the same after this investigation ends.

If it ends at all.
