## CHAPTER 10: CHAPTER 10

The descent into Telluric Engineering felt like diving into the earth's own guts. I took the service elevator down past Sub-Level Three, past the maintenance corridors where pipefitters still worked their shifts, and into the subterranean heart of BATC's power infrastructure.

The noise hit me first—a deep, resonant thrumming that vibrated through my bones. Then came the smell: hot copper, burning ozone, and the acrid tang of machine oil. My magic responded immediately, grounding itself against the raw industrial energy saturating every steel beam and concrete pillar.

I found Chief Engineer Torin Kaelen exactly where the shift foreman said he'd be—screaming his lungs out in Bay Seven.

"WHAT PART OF 'TIGHTEN THE GODDAMN CONNECTIONS' DON'T YOU UNDERSTAND?" Torque's voice carried across the bay like thunder. The Dwarf was built like a brick shithouse, all shoulders and muscle packed under stained canvas overalls. Burn scars crisscrossed his forearms—the telltale marks of telluric burns. "THIS ISN'T ROCKET SCIENCE! CHECK YOUR TORQUE SPECS!"

He had three machinists backed against a massive busbar assembly, their faces pale with fear. The blue-white arc of electricity still sparked between two connection points, making the air crackle with dangerous energy.

Torque spotted me approaching and cut off mid-rant. His expression shifted from fury to wariness. He wiped grease-stained hands on a rag already black with accumulated grime.

"Vance." He kept his voice lower now, but it still carried weight. "You got no business down here unless Morvain cleared you through security."

"I need to talk to you. Privately." I pulled the printed schematics from my jacket pocket—the ones from that dead drop in Newark Bay. The paper was warm to the touch, thrumming with residual magical energy.

His eyes narrowed. Then widened. Recognition flashed across his face before he schooled it back to neutral. He grabbed my arm—not roughly, just firmly—and steered me away from the crew.

"Where the hell did you get this?" His voice dropped to something barely audible over the generator noise. "If Morvain knows you're looking at the Pylon collars, he'll have both our badges, and maybe our heads."

"My people are dying in the Undercity over these taps, Torque. What are you building down there?"

He glanced around, checking if anyone was within earshot. The machinists had returned to work, but I could feel their nervous glances in our direction.

"Not here." He headed toward a reinforced door marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The lock clicked open under his palm—skin contact authentication, military-grade security. "Come on."

The sound-proofed blueprint room was an oasis of silence after the deafening roar outside. Climate control hummed quietly. Halogen lights illuminated a massive table covered in overlapping schematic sheets, seismic charts, and geological surveys. And sitting at the far end, hunched over a chart showing fault lines like spider webs, was a human man who looked like he hadn't slept in a week.

Dr. Arthur Halcyon didn't look up when we entered. His fingers traced patterns across the paper, muttering numbers and calculations under his breath. He wore a white lab coat that had seen better days—stained with coffee rings and what might have been food. Or maybe blood. Hard to tell.

"Halcyon," Torque said sharply. "We got company."

The geophysicist's head snapped up. Dark circles shadowed his eyes. His hair stuck out at odd angles, and when he focused on me, there was something desperate in that gaze.

"Commander Vance. They told me someone would come eventually." He stood abruptly, nearly knocking over his chair. "But I need more time. We're not ready—"

"Ready for what?" I stepped closer, my hand instinctively moving toward the schematics. "Torque gave you a warning shot about these Pylon collars. What aren't you telling Morvain?"

Halcyon snatched the papers from my hand before I could react, his movements quick despite his disheveled state. His eyes scanned the diagrams with frantic intensity.

"They didn't give you the full picture." His voice rose slightly, edging into hysteria. "Look at the metallurgical stress points."

I leaned over his shoulder as he spread the schematics across the table. Red markings I hadn't noticed before highlighted specific sections of the collar designs—places where gold and bismuth alloys met under extreme pressure.

"What am I looking at?"

"The Gold-Bismuth Collars are designed to compress seismic fault lines, yes." Halcyon tapped a finger against one of the red-marked zones. "But the compression isn't stable. The alloy degrades under sustained stress. These marks—these are failure points."

My stomach dropped. "How long do we have?"

He met my eyes, and I saw the answer before he spoke it.

"Not long enough."

* * *

The engineering bay smells like my father's garage used to smell back in Sterling Manor—hot copper, machine oil, and that particular ozone tang that means magic's been working overtime. Except this isn't some suburban tinkering space. We're three levels below the BATC Telluric Engineering complex, where the real machinery hums through walls thick enough to stop tank rounds.

Torin Kaelen stands beside me, arms crossed over his barrel chest, looking about as comfortable as a dwarf can look in any place that isn't a proper stonework cellar. His beard bristles with irritation.

"Show her," he growls at Halcyon.

Dr. Marcus Halcyon—officially suspended from duty, unofficially still digging through data like his life depends on it—is hunched over a modified ThinkPad connected to what looks like a salvaged Sony MiniDisc drive. The thing whirs to life with an asthmatic wheeze, and suddenly the screen illuminates with a schematic overlay I recognize immediately: Watching Party architecture for the five Pylons anchoring Neon Hollow.

But there's more here. Red lines pulse beneath the official blueprints.

"The Gold-Bismuth Collars," Halcyon says without looking up. His hands are shaking. I notice because they're projecting holographic controls, ghostly fingers dancing in the air above the keyboard. "BATC narrative says they stabilize the fault lines. Prevent tectonic buildup."

"You know better than that." Torin's voice is flat.

The disc drive clicks. A new layer appears on screen—a seismographic readout, but not one I've seen in any official briefing. The red lines aren't random; they're converging around each Pylon location.

"It's a battery," Halcyon finally turns to face me, and Christ, he looks like he hasn't slept since we found those bodies in the Kearny Marshes. There's something raw in his eyes, the kind of terror you only see when someone's had their entire worldview dismantled piece by piece. "A massive, geological battery. They're compressing the fault to store the kinetic energy of the earth itself."

I stare at him. Then at Torin. Then back at the screen where those red lines pulse like angry veins.

"Explain. Slowly."

Halcyon gestures at the display. "Gold-Bismuth alloy—you feel it, right? That resonance?" He doesn't wait for confirmation. Of course I do. It's why the Pylons hum against my bones whenever I get within three blocks of them. "It's semi-permeable to telluric forces. When they wrapped those collars around the fault zones beneath Neon Hollow, they created a pressure system. The earth keeps trying to shift, build up stress—but the collars trap it. Contain it."

"The energy keeps building," Torin adds, stepping closer to the screen. His shadow falls across the glowing lines. "Years of compression. Every seismic tremor, every micro-earthquake, all that kinetic force gets bottled up inside those collars instead of releasing naturally."

"And if that pressure isn't vented?" I ask quietly, already knowing I won't like the answer.

"Or if the collars crack?" Torin continues with the same flat affect, like he's reading from a technical manual rather than describing an apocalypse. "The whole damn Undercity collapses. Millions of tons of rock, straight down. Everything built on top of those fault lines—Neon Hollow, the Sub-Stations, the entire grid infrastructure beneath the Jersey flats—"

"—turns into a rockslide that would make the Newark Bay quake look like a hiccup." Halcyon finishes, then laughs bitterly. "That's why they needed the Gold-Bismuth. That's why the Watching Party has been mining for it since 1987. Not for protection. For storage."

The heat in the room suddenly feels oppressive. I can feel sweat beading along my spine, and it's not just from the machinery.

"How much pressure are we talking about?"

Halcyon brings up another window. Numbers scroll past too quickly to read, but the summary at bottom makes my stomach drop: *Estimated telluric potential: 4.7 million megajoules. Current containment integrity: 62%. Critical threshold: 50%.*

"Why would anyone—" The question dies on my lips because I already know. You don't build something this dangerous unless you're planning to use it as a weapon. "When were these numbers run?"

"Six months ago," Torin says. "We found Halcyon's research logs buried in the County General server farm. He'd been collecting data off the Pylon monitoring systems for three years before someone caught him."

"And killed three other researchers who noticed the same thing." Halcyon's voice cracks. "I was next. Probably still am."

The MiniDisc drive whirs again, cycling through images now—a time-lapse sequence showing microscopic hairline fractures spreading across a cross-section of Gold-Bismuth alloy under stress. Beautiful patterns, almost artistic, except each one represents catastrophic failure waiting to happen.

"The collars weren't designed to last forever," Halcyon continues. "Or even this long. They knew when they installed them that containment integrity would degrade over time. That's built into the calculations."

I close my eyes, trying to process this. Trying to fit this horror into what I thought I knew about BATC operations, about the Watching Party's mission parameters. But nothing fits anymore.

"Show me the personnel files." My voice comes out sharper than intended. "Who authorized this project? Who signed off on the Gold-Bismuth allocation?"

Halcyon taps another command. Faces appear on screen—I recognize some from briefings, others are unfamiliar. But there's one name at the top of every document, every budget approval, every installation authorization:

**Controller Voss.**

Of course. The architect of everything terrible I've encountered since taking this Aegis Commander position. The puppeteer pulling strings from whatever shadowed office he occupies in Sterling Manor.

"Why?" The word escapes before I can stop it. "Why risk the entire city for... what? What's the payoff worth millions of lives?"

Torin and Halcyon exchange glances—an old argument clearly reheated between them.

"Because it works." Torin's expression hardens. "That much stored telluric energy? Vented properly, it could power the entire Eastern Seaboard for a year. Or it could tear open a rift straight to the Outer Dark and summon something that makes the Hollow Gang look like street thugs."

"Or both," Halcyon mutters. "Voss isn't stupid enough to just blow it all at once. He'd leak it gradually—enough to destabilize everything while keeping the lights on. Create chaos. Make himself indispensable during the recovery."

The engineering bay suddenly feels smaller, the walls closing in as reality itself narrows to this single, horrifying truth: I'm standing on top of a bomb built into the bedrock of North Jersey, and the clock started ticking before I ever became Aeg

* * *

The telluric generator bay hums beneath my fingertips, that familiar copper-tinged thrum of raw earth-magic pulsing through the ancient machinery. My white-lilac aura flares involuntarily as Halcyon spreads the soil core samples across the metal workbench, each cylinder wrapped in preservation film that catches the fluorescent light like trapped lightning.

"Pre-dynastic," he says, voice tight. "Fifteen meters down, Mara. Fifteen *meters* beneath Pylon 3's foundation."

My magic responds to his anxiety—a sharp cedar scent cuts through the industrial ozone and machine oil that permeates these sub-levels. I lean closer, watching dust motes dance between us in the flickering light.

"Explain it to me like I'm still a patrolman, Arthur." My hand finds his shoulder, grounding both of us. "Because whatever you're about to say feels like we're standing on the edge of something very fucking bad."

Torin Kaelen shifts against the far wall, his dwarven senses making him uncomfortable in this cramped blueprint room. The heavy steel door clicks shut behind us—automatic seal on the soundproof chamber. Good. Whatever comes next doesn't need ears outside this room.

Halcyon's fingers trace the soil samples with the reverence of a priest handling relics. "The Gold-Bismuth Collars aren't just compressing the fault lines, Mara. They're doing something worse. Something the board knows and is hiding." He pulls out his worn leather briefcase, extracting a tablet of notes covered in radiometric data that makes my head swim. "See here—the mineral composition isn't stable. It's... transforming. Under pressure from the telluric generators, bismuth begins acting like a catalytic agent at depth. The geological strata are essentially cooking."

"The earth is cooking?" The words taste wrong on my tongue.

"Not cooking. Compressing. Warping." Halcyon taps the soil cores. "These samples contain mineral formations that shouldn't exist for another three million years. The arcane pressure is accelerating geological time itself beneath our facilities. And Morvain knows. Thorne definitely knows."

My magic flares harder now, panic bleeding through—I can smell cedar so thick it's choking. "How certain?"

"Ninety-seven percent confidence margin. I've cross-referenced against pre-industrial baseline cores from the New Jersey Geological Survey archives." He meets my eyes, and I see the fear there. "Someone has to stop this, Mara. Before one of these compression zones reaches critical mass and we're talking about an earthquake that could swallow half the state."

The fluorescent lights flicker again. In the corner, Torin's voice rumbles low: "Commander, we got bigger problems than science. If Morvain catches wind you two are planning mutiny—"

"It's not mutiny," I snap, then soften at Halcyon's pained expression. "Arthur, listen. You cannot go to your lab alone tomorrow. Let me send an Aegis detail—"

"No." The word comes out hard as granite. "Corporate security monitors all Aegis deployments. They'll know instantly. I have to do this quietly. Finalize the radiometric data, lock down the complete findings in triplicate." His hand clamps over mine on his shoulder—a gesture of comfort that terrifies me more than anything. "Tomorrow, Mara. We blow this wide open tomorrow. Get the samples to the press directly. Bypass Morvain and Thorne entirely."

I want to argue. My training screams at me to secure him, protect him, keep him within command structure where he belongs. But looking at those soil cores, at the impossible mineral formations that shouldn't exist...

"What time?" My voice cracks slightly.

"Nine AM. My office hours end at eight-thirty. Give me thirty minutes to prep everything." He slides three smaller sample cylinders into a padded case inside his briefcase. "These are for you. Proof. Your insurance policy if things get ugly."

Torin pushes off from the wall, moving toward the door. "You two need to clear out. Engineering shift change starts in ten. Too many eyes down here after dark." He pauses, hand on the steel door. "And for fuck's sake, Commander, burn whatever phones you use to coordinate this. Don't trust the network."

The door swings open with a pneumatic hiss, and suddenly we're back in the larger generator bay—the massive telluric engines making the floor vibrate beneath our boots. Technicians are already filtering in for the night shift, their coveralls stained with copper dust that glows faintly under the work lights.

I watch Halcyon leave through a different exit, his worn leather briefcase clutched tight against his chest like it contains the fate of worlds. The cedar scent has faded, leaving only the sharp tang of ozone and my own sweat.

Tomorrow cannot come fast enough.

---

## CHAPTER 11: CHAPTER 11

The sodium-vapor lamps cast everything in that sickly orange wash, turning the BATC Research Wing parking lot into something out of a David Lynch fever dream. I killed the Crown Vic's engine and sat there for a moment, watching my breath fog against the windshield. Late autumn 2003, and already it felt like the world was holding its breath.

My Nextel chirped—not the usual digital warble but an old-school pagershake that made my teeth ache. CODE 9 - COME ALONE. No context. Just those three words bleeding across the LCD screen in green phosphorescent dread.

I pocketed the pager and stepped out into the cold. The Crown Vic's door clunked heavy, final. My bio-wards flamed to life automatically—pure white-lilac threading through fresh cedar, clean and sharp and ready. They didn't need to be; this was supposed to be secure BATC property, but habit is a bitch that dies hard when your habit keeps you breathing.

The research wing lobby reeked of sterile floor wax and something else underneath it. Ozone. Sizzling, angry ozone like someone had been running unshielded telluric currents through copper wiring. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, casting everything in that clinical blue-white glare that makes everyone look dead except for their eyes, which always look too alive under fluorescents.

"Commander Vance." Dr. Arthur Halcyon materialized from the hallway leading to the core lab, moving with the kind of frantic energy that means someone just watched the numbers come back wrong on every equation they thought they understood. His lab coat was half-buttoned, tie askew. "Thank Christ."

"Dr. Halcyon." I kept my voice level, even though my wards were already tasting the air, parsing the chemical signatures. White-lilac and cedar overlaid against… fuck. Blue-black iron-gall residue. That wasn't right. That wasn't even *possible* in a sealed lab facility.

He grabbed my forearm with fingers that trembled. "You need to see this. Now. Before they—" He stopped himself, glanced over his shoulder at the empty desk where security should have been. "Before anything."

I let him pull me down the corridor. His IBM ThinkPad sat on a workbench, cooling fan whining like a dying mosquito, screen displaying geological survey data that hurt my head just looking at it. Those Gold-Bismuth collar readings weren't stabilizing. They were *compressing*.

"The Pylon Collars," he said, words tumbling out faster than sense could catch up. "The whole project briefing, the official report, it's all lies wrapped around truth like candy coating around shit, Commander. They're not stabilizing the Undercity faults. They're building a pressure cooker and calling it engineering."

My wards spiked bright white-lilac, alarm bells ringing silent in my skull. The floor tiles beneath us felt wrong. Not temperature wrong or structural wrong but something deeper, telluric wrong. Like standing on ground that had forgotten how to be solid.

Downstairs, through the open stairwell door, an Orc security guard was speaking into his radio, South Side accent thick as molasses. "Doc, you got unauthorized movement on sublevel two. Need Aegis down here. It's bad, man. Real bad."

Halcyon fumbled in his coat pocket and pressed something into my hand—a Sony MiniDisc case, warm from being against his body. "Everything. All the soil core analysis, the pre-dynastic Egyptian samples, the compression vectors. It's all there. When this hits, Vance, when they activate those collars—"

The floor tile directly beneath the ThinkPad cracked.

Not hairline. Full-thickness fracture, spider-webbing outward with that wet, organic sound of ceramic breaking under sudden stress. Blue-black iron-gall residue began oozing up through the cracks, smoking where it touched the air, smelling like burning metal and old blood.

"GET BACK!" I shoved Halcyon away from the workbench, my wards flaring so bright they threw violet shadows across every surface. My Nextel exploded with chatter—I didn't listen, already moving, already calculating angles and escape routes and what fresh hell was brewing beneath our feet.

More tiles cracked. Then began to melt.

Blue-black slag, glowing hot enough to light the corridor in hellish shadow, spreading like water across the floor. The cooling fan on Halcyon's ThinkPad hit a higher pitch before dying completely, circuit boards probably just vaporized by ambient heat.

"They're activating early," he whispered, face gone pale as hospital sheets. "Oh God, they're activating early and it's not ready and it's never going to be ready because this whole fucking thing is a death trap designed by men who wanted a weapon instead of a shield."

My bio-wards screamed pure white-lilac alarm. Whatever was coming up from sublevel two wasn't just unstable arc-alchemy. It was *awake*.

* * *

The lab smelled wrong before it burned.

I noticed it three seconds before Halcyon opened his mouth—the faint metallic tang underlying the sterile antiseptic, like blood on fresh paint. My wards were already climbing, that instinctive fourth-law response that kept me alive when my training couldn't.

"Commander Vance, you need to see this." Halcyon's voice was tight, wound too many turns past breaking. His hands trembled as he gestured at the soil core samples arranged on the examination table, each one glowing with that sickly green-gold luminescence that meant ancient telluric binding. Pre-dynastic Egyptian, he'd said. Older than the Pyramids by a factor that made my teeth ache.

Then the air *screamed*.

Not sound—not yet—but pressure, a violent vacuum that pulled at my lungs and inverted every bio-ward I had standing. White-lilac erupted from my skin, pure and coruscating, cedar-scented light burning away the half-second of darkness before the flash.

The explosion hit like God's fist through a plate glass window.

Shrapnel stitched across my left shoulder, deflected by the wards at the last microsecond. The force slammed me backward into Halcyon's server rack, copper-and-fiber cables snapping like guitar strings, showering sparks across my faceplate. Alarms shrieked. The IBM ThinkPad on the desk behind us—our only backup system for Halcyon's data—exploded in a spray of molten plastic and vaporized silicon.

*Crash.* My spine hit metal. My Razr clattered out of my pouch, skittering across the suddenly buckled floor tiles. Through the static in my ears, I heard it ringing, ringing, ringing.

The smoke came next—thick black oil that tasted like burnt iron-gall residue and boiling ozone. Heat washed over everything in waves, making my tactical vest feel like it was melting onto my ribs. I could smell synthetic carpet fibers combusting, the acrid sweetness of overheated electronics, the copper-tang of vaporized copper wiring.

"VANCE!" Someone shouting through the chaos. My voice. My own fucking voice, hoarse and desperate.

I dragged myself upright, wards still blazing white-lilac around my frame like a halo gone wrong. The lab had become a warzone—overturned tables, shattered beakers, and there, twenty feet from where I'd been standing, Halcyon lay sprawled across his workstation, half-covered in debris.

"No no no NO."

I ran through the smoke, each breath scorching my lungs. The Dwarven tech—what was her name, Bronson?—was pinned under a fallen equipment cart, one leg twisted at an angle that made me gag even through the adrenaline. Blood soaked her white lab coat, dark and spreading.

"Commander." Her voice was gravel and broken glass. "That wasn't... gas line..."

My hands found her shoulders, hauling her free with strength borrowed from places I didn't want to think about right now. Her beard was singed, face blackened with soot except for two clean tracks where tears had cut through the grime.

"That was a wire-runner's breach-charge," she gasped, coughing blood onto my gloves. "I felt the hex-signature. They wanted you dead. Wanted all of us dead."

Behind her, barely visible through the dissipating smoke, I saw him.

Halcyon hadn't just been caught by shrapnel. The blast pattern radiated outward from his position—this wasn't random. This was targeted. Precision. Professional.

He was trying to say something, lips moving soundlessly, blood bubbling between them. His hands clutched at his chest, then extended toward me, fingers reaching.

I dropped beside him, ignoring the heat still radiating from the floor, the acrid smoke burning my eyes. My medical kit was gone—lost in the explosion or scattered somewhere in this nightmare—but I pressed both hands against his chest anyway, feeling the wet warmth seeping through his shirt, hot and wrong and final.

"Easy, easy, you're gonna be fine—"

The lie tasted like ash.

His hand grabbed my vest, pulling me closer with strength he shouldn't have possessed. His eyes focused on mine, blue and clear despite everything else failing.

"The MiniDisc," he whispered. "Your pocket. Get it out. Before they—"

The Razr stopped ringing. In the sudden silence—not real silence, never that, but a relative absence of electronic screaming—I heard footsteps. Heavy boots. Coordinated. Military-precise.

Through the smoke, shapes emerged. Tall. Too tall. Corporate Elites wearing High-Spire tactical gear, pulse rifles already tracking targets through thermal scopes.

They'd breached the outer door while we were distracted by trying not to die.

My wards flared brighter, white-lilac turning violet, cedar-scent giving way to the metallic tang of defensive hex-work. Halcyon's grip tightened, nails digging through Kevlar into flesh beneath.

"Get... it..." Another bubble of blood. "Out..."

The lead Elf raised his weapon, aiming center-mass. Behind him, two more spread out, flanking positions, textbook room clearing. They weren't here for questions. They were here for cleanup.

I reached into my tactical pouch, fingers closing around the Sony MiniDisc case. Warm. Still intact somehow, miraculously unmolested by heat or shrapnel.

Halcyon smiled then—a small, bloody thing—and released me.

His body went slack as the last breath left him, leaving a perfect bloody handprint across my chest, bright red against black carbon scoring where the explosion had come closest to taking me too.

The Corporates advanced, weapons still trained on center mass.

"BATC jurisdiction!" My voice cut through the smoke like a blade. "This is an active crime scene. Stand down."

They didn't even slow their pace.

* * *

The ozone sting hit my lungs first—sharp, chemical, wrong. Then came the heat, radiating from where Halcyon's workstation had been, now a crater of blackened composite and fused circuitry that stank of burned plastic and something deeper, metallurgical and ancient.

"Commander Vance."

I didn't turn at the voice. Didn't need to. That measured cadence, smooth as polished obsidian, belonged to only one man in the BATC hierarchy. Vane Thorne. Internal Affairs. High-Spire Corporate Elf. The kind of metahuman who wore his heritage like armor under bespoke Italian wool.

My bio-wards were white-lilac and fresh cedar, already flaring hot around my knuckles before I even consciously called them. The air between us shimmered, protective and hostile in equal measure.

"You're standing in a crime scene, Inquisitor," I said, my North Jersey accent cutting through the sterile lab atmosphere. "Unless you've got clearance I haven't seen filed."

Thorne stepped forward anyway, his midnight-blue suit immaculate despite the chaos surrounding us. Rain-dampened wool, expensive cologne masking something more clinical underneath. Behind him, I heard the soft shuffle of boots on waxed tile—his team, already moving into position.

"Clearance arrived seven minutes ago." He produced a datapad, its screen glowing pale blue against his dark skin. "Direct from Director Kincaid. We're taking jurisdiction."

That made my wards flare brighter, white-lilac light painting shadows across the ruined lab walls. "Kincaid didn't authorize *shit* until after I radioed the breach. You want to explain how your people got here faster than Forensics?"

The sizzle started then—not from Halcyon's melted equipment, but from scattered points across the floor. Small, deliberate burns. Blue-black iron-gall residue catching air, smoking with that distinctive acrid bite. My stomach dropped. I knew that smell. Street-level hex work. Razor-Wire craftsmanship.

"I don't have to explain anything to Aegis field commanders, Vance." Thorne's voice stayed flat, bureaucratic. "My team is securing evidence. You need to step back and let professionals handle this."

One of his technicians knelt beside what looked like optical-camouflage scraps, carefully placing them near the crater's edge. Another was tagging the melted wires with Black-Circuit Syndicate markers—the cheap kind used by street-level elven gangs operating out of the South Side projects.

"You're planting evidence," I said, the words coming out harder than I intended.

Thorne's expression didn't change. "We're preserving context. The Iron-Gall Brigade hits Research Wing labs all the time now. They use street-hex tags to mark their kills. It's in the briefings you apparently aren't reading."

My hands were fists at my sides, wards still blazing. Fresh cedar over ozone. The lab reeked of it now—sterile crime-scene chemicals mixing with planted gang signatures and the ghost-trace of whatever had actually killed Halcyon.

"Don't play me, Thorne." I took a step forward, close enough to see the microfibers in his suit lapel, close enough that he'd feel the heat from my wards if he wasn't blocking. "I smelled the iron-gall when I got here. This whole setup reeks of inside job. Someone wanted those soil cores destroyed, and they didn't want anyone asking questions about *why*."

His jaw tightened—not much, but enough. Thorne was good at hiding reactions, but not perfect. "Commander, your emotional state is compromised. You've been exposed to telluric backlash, possible residual hex compounds—"

"I'm not compromised!" The shout came out raw, angry. My wards spiked brighter, throwing violet light across the white tile floor. Behind Thorne, his team paused, hands hovering near sidearms. I didn't care. "Halcyon was my officer. He was *my responsibility*. And someone just sanitized the entire scene while I was two floors down getting debriefed!"

Thorne's hand moved to his own weapon—a sleek corporate-issue pistol that probably cost more than most South Side apartments. Not drawn yet, but the threat was clear.

"You will stand down," he said, voice dropping into official register. "Or I'll have you restrained for obstruction."

The sterile flashbulbs started popping then—crime scene photographers, all wearing the same midnight-blue suits as Thorne's team. Recording everything. Creating a permanent digital record of a crime scene being systematically altered before Forensics even arrived.

"Fuck you, Thorne." I meant it to sound defiant. Instead, exhaustion crept into my voice like acid. "You can't erase this. Whatever Halcyon found—whatever was in those Egyptian cores—it's still out there. Still real."

He smiled then, cold and bureaucratic. "There were no Egyptian soil cores, Commander. That project was decommissioned last month. Dr. Halcyon was working on routine structural integrity assessments until his lab suffered a terrorist attack by Razor-Wire Street-Elf operatives. The evidence supports this conclusion completely."

"And if I say different?"

Thorne's smile widened fractionally. "Then you're making accusations against a High-Spire Corporate Elf without proof. Against Director Kincaid's explicit authorization. Against BATC Internal Affairs protocol." He paused, letting the weight settle. "That would be insubordination at minimum. Conspiracy at worst."

The melted IBM ThinkPad sat in a containment field near what had been Halcyon's desk. One of Thorne's techs was already bagging it, sealing the evidence with official red tape.

"I want that device," I said.

"No, you don't." Thorne held up a hand. "Evidence is now IA property pending investigation. You'll file your report, Commander. Keep it professional. Mention nothing about soil cores or pre-dynastic artifacts or whatever fantasies the telluric exposure gave you."

My pocket felt suddenly heavy. The MiniDisc—Halcyon's backup copy, transferred during our debriefing just minutes before the blast. I'd forgotten about it in the heat of confronting Thorne. Or maybe part of me had consciously buried it, knowing what this moment would come to.

"Did you have anything else?" Thorne asked, tone dripping with condescension. "Any external media we should know about? Data storage devices not accounted for?"

Every instinct screamed to lie. To protect what little truth remained.

"The data was destroyed in the blast," I said. The words tasted like ash. "Halcyon didn't have time to back anything up."

Thorne studied me for a long moment, those corporate-elf eyes missing nothing. Then he nodded slowly. "Good. Very good. Professional response." He turned to his team. "Bag everything. Let's move."

As they filed out, photographers still clicking, evidence still being planted and repackaged, I stood alone in the sanitized ruins of Halcyon's lab. The white-lilac wards around my hands

---

## CHAPTER 12: CHAPTER 12

The morgue air tastes like copper and formaldehyde, but underneath it all—that fresh cedar scent that follows me everywhere now. My weave is tight as piano wire tonight, pure white-lilac threading through my bones, sharp enough to cut glass. I need it to be. Can't afford anything less when I'm standing over what's left of Halcyon.

He's laid out on slab three under the harsh whites of the surgical lamps, and even death can't erase that stupid smirk he used to wear. The one that said he knew something you didn't. Used to drive me insane when we were partners. Now it just makes my chest feel hollow.

"Gonna stand there all night, Commander?" The Goblin medical examiner doesn't look up from his notes, his clawed fingers already making preliminary incisions. His safety goggles catch the light—thick things, rated for chemical burns. Smart in this line of work.

I step closer to the body table, ignoring the cold that tries to seep up through my boots from the tile floor. "Just give me a minute, Doc."

"You got five. Then I need access to the thoracic cavity." He clicks his pen, a sharp sound that echoes off the refrigeration units humming in the background. "Word's already bouncing around the precinct. Some kind of explosive device. Military grade shrapnel embedded in the ribs. You want to tell me how someone gets that kind of hardware pointed at them in Newark Bay?"

The shrapnel is laid out in a neat row on a stainless steel tray beside the body. Each piece no bigger than a fingernail, but twisted, burned. I reach for my case kit, pulling out the spectral analyzer—a sleek black thing that looks like it belongs in a star-ship cockpit rather than a North Jersey morgue. 

Halcyon deserved better than this. Deserved to die hunting monsters instead of being turned into collateral damage by Syndicate cleanup crews.

I run the analyzer over the first piece of metal. The display flickers green, then blue, then settles on that distinctive frost-cobalt signature. My breath catches.

"The fuck," I whisper.

"That's what I said." The Goblin adjusts his goggles, peering closer at Halcyon's torso. "See those ice crystals forming along the incision lines? That's not normal. That's hex-work. Industrial-grade frost-cobalt residue. This ain't street-level work, Vance."

My fingers tighten around the analyzer. Frost-cobalt. I know that signature. Everyone in Aegis does after the Pulaski Skyway bombing. It's cold. Precise. Clean as winter wind and twice as deadly. The Mechanic's calling card—Cole Reyes, the Syndicate's ghost enforcer. The one who disappears into fog and comes back with targets dead and evidence planted perfect.

But why would Cole kill Halcyon?

"Ambient temperature's dropping." The Doc's voice cuts through my thoughts. He's right. I can see my breath now, thin clouds in the sterile air. The frost-cobalt is active, still working its magic even hours after the hit.

I pull out my Panasonic Toughbook, boots squeaking against the tile as I move to the evidence locker. My weave flares bright, protecting me from whatever residual magic might be clinging to these materials. The laptop screen glows warm in the cold room—a small comfort.

Cross-referencing the frost-cobalt signature against active investigations takes thirty seconds. Forty. Then the hits start rolling in.

Unsolved Syndicate executions over the past eighteen months. Each one tagged with this same frost-cobalt residue. Clean kills. Professional. Targeted.

And Halcyon's death matches the pattern perfectly.

"No way." The words escape before I can stop them. "He wasn't Syndicate. Wasn't even close to their level."

"He was poking around the Kearny Marshes last week," the Goblin offers, still working on his autopsy notes. "Word on the wire says he found something. Something that got him killed."

The Marshes. Where the Pylon fragments went down. Where Marcus Voss has been running operations so deep even Aegis Command doesn't know the full scope.

My fingers fly across the keyboard. If Halcyon found something about the Pylons... if he got too close to what Voss is hiding...

But the evidence doesn't lie. Frost-cobalt is Syndicate. Cole Reyes is Syndicate. This was a Syndicate hit, clean and simple.

Or maybe not so simple.

I pull up the crime scene photos from Newark Bay—Halcyon's apartment building, third floor, east-facing window blown out like a wound. Shrapnel patterns consistent with explosive devices. No witnesses. No survivors. Just Halcyon's body falling five stories into the alley below.

Except...

There. In the background of photo seven. My eyes catch movement in the shadows between buildings. Dark figure. Tall. Broad-shouldered. Moving away from the blast radius at exactly the right moment.

I zoom in. Enhance. The image sharpens just enough to show silhouette details. Not enough for facial recognition, but enough to confirm human. Not a Goblin or Troll. Someone who knew where to stand to avoid the blast radius.

Someone with training.

Someone like an enforcer.

Frost-cobalt blood-iron residue crystallizes along the edges of my evidence bags as I seal them. The cold follows me out of the morgue, clinging to my coat, my skin, my bones. The scent of cedar does nothing to mask it now.

"Commander?" The Goblin calls after me as I head for the door. "You gonna bring him in? The Mechanic?"

I pause with my hand on the push bar. Through the small window in the morgue door, I can see the fluorescent lights of the precinct beyond—Sub-Station Seven, where Aegis runs its North Jersey operations. Forty-seven officers working cases that lead nowhere. Evidence that disappears. Witnesses who get forgotten.

"Yeah," I say finally. "I'm going to bring him in."

Because if Cole Reyes killed Halcyon over whatever he found in those Marshes... then Marcus Voss isn't the only target worth pursuing anymore.

The Syndicate just made itself enemy number one.

My weave burns white-hot as I step into the hallway, ready to hunt.

* * *

The summons came through my Nokia at 0437 hours—a terse message from Director Morvain's secretary that made my jaw tighten. I was still running forensic analysis on Halcyon's body when it arrived, the white-lilac weave humming through my neural pathways like a focused blade.

The elevator ride up to the High-Spire offices took forever. Each floor meant another level away from the real work—the morgue where Halcyon lay under cold sheets, the evidence lockup where I'd secured those telltale fiber samples from the crime scene. Up here, everything smelled like expensive cigar smoke and bureaucratic compromise.

Morvain's office occupied the entire eastern wing. Rain hammered against the reinforced windows, each drop catching the city lights below like dying stars. He sat behind his massive oak desk, looking comfortable in the way predators look comfortable. And there, standing by the window with hands clasped behind his back, stood Vane Thorne.

My commander. The man who should have been briefing me personally if this was Aegis business.

"You're late, Commander," Morvain said without looking up from a document. His voice carried that particular timbre of authority that comes from never having to explain yourself. "Thorne has been updating me on your... enthusiasm."

I didn't apologize. "Director. Commander." The acknowledgment was curt. My eyes stayed on Thorne. There was something off about him today—not in his posture, which remained rigidly military, but in the way he watched me. Like I was a problem he needed to solve.

"Sit down, Vance." Morvain finally looked up, and I caught the flicker of calculation in his gaze. "We need to discuss priorities."

I remained standing. "My priority is finding the enforcer who killed one of our own. I've got forensic evidence linking—"

"The Razor-Wire Elves," Thorne interrupted, turning from the window. His scarred face looked even more brutal in the storm light. "That's what you should be focusing on. Pulaski Skyway incident three days ago. Four bodies, all tagged with that elf sigil."

"I'm aware of the Pulaski incident." My fingers found the Nokia in my pocket, feeling its weight. "But Halcyon wasn't killed by elves. The angle, the execution, the cold precision—the MO matches the Syndicate's top enforcer. The Mechanic."

Morvain steepled his fingers. "A ghost story, Vance. Thorne tells me your informants are feeding you fairy tales."

"They're feeding me facts." I pulled out the evidence file—three inches thick now, filled with witness statements, fiber analysis, ballistics reports that matched nothing in our database because Cole Voss used weapons he fabricated himself. "He left frost-cobalt weld burns in a chemist's hand last week when she tried to short the Syndicate. My sources say he operates on some twisted code—a 'sliver of justice' where he takes out corporate corruption for the Syndicate's benefit."

Thorne's lip curled. "You're chasing shadows while the slums burn. Those Razor-Wire Elves are getting organized. They hit another transport convoy this morning. County General ER is overflowing with casualties."

"Then assign someone else." The words came out sharper than intended, but I didn't take them back. "This isn't about turf wars between street gangs. This is personal. Someone went after one of ours, and I'm going to put him down."

The silence stretched. Outside, thunder rolled across Newark Bay like a warning.

Finally, Morvain sighed. He picked up his pen, clicked it twice. "Commander Thorne has a point about resource allocation. We can't have Aegis personnel chasing urban legends while the city fragments around us."

My hands clenched at my sides. "Sir, with all due respect—"

"However," Morvain continued, his eyes finding mine with something that might have been genuine interest, "you've made a compelling case. The forensic evidence is... intriguing." He glanced at Thorne, who looked like he'd bitten into something sour. "I'm authorizing a limited investigation into this 'Mechanic.' But you'll maintain operational readiness for Pulaski sector. If your lead goes cold within seventy-two hours, you revert to anti-gang protocols."

I felt the trap close even as relief flooded through me. "Yes, sir. Thank you, sir."

"I expect daily briefings." Morvain returned to his documents. "Dismissed, Commander."

I left before either man could change their minds, the Nokia already vibrating in my pocket with new data from my informants. Behind me, I heard Thorne's voice: "She's wasting resources on a myth."

"And if she's not?" Morvain's reply was quiet, almost curious. "Better a myth than what we're actually protecting, Vane. Better a monster she can see."

The doors closed behind me, cutting off whatever else they said. My white-lilac weave pulsed hot and bright through my skull—a focused fury that would have terrified anyone sensitive enough to feel it.

Cole Voss thought he was a ghost.

He had no idea what was coming.

* * *

The armory reeks of gun oil and fresh cedar—the latter from the cleansing runes Torque keeps scorched into the concrete floor. Midnight makes everything sharper somehow, the fluorescent lights overhead casting hard shadows across the weapons racks.

I stand before my locker, methodically checking each piece of equipment. The MP5 feels solid in my hands, familiar weight distributed just right. Bismuth slugs—depleted uranium cores wrapped in silver-trace alloy—click into the magazine one by one. Each round carries a white-lilac weave already embedded in its molecular structure, pure energy waiting to be released.

*Clack.* The magazine seats home with that satisfying finality.

"Going to war over this, Mara."

Torque's gravelly voice cuts through my focus. The Dwarf engineer is leaning against the evidence cage, his stocky frame silhouetted against the barred lighting. He's got a matchstick between his teeth, unlit, rolling it back and forth like some old detective from the noir vids.

I don't look up from my prep work. My fingers move to the next magazine, counting rounds. "Halcyon didn't die for a shadow, Torque." My voice comes out flat, measured. "I'm bringing this Mechanic in. Dead or alive."

"That so?" He spits the matchstick onto the floor. It bounces once. "And you've seen the body? Talked to the witness yourself?"

Now I do look at him. His beard catches the light oddly, making the gray strands seem to shimmer. There's something in his expression—not quite skepticism, more like concern. Dangerous concern.

"I've seen the evidence file," I say. "Sony MiniDisc data from the scene, thermal signature matches, ballistics consistent with Syndicate weapons. The enforcer was there. Halcyon's theory about the Pylons—about Voss pulling strings from somewhere deeper than we thought—that's what got him killed."

My PalmPilot glows green monochrome beside me on the metal workbench, displaying the case files I've been cross-referencing for the last three hours. Photos of shell casings. Thermal overlays showing heat signatures that match the enforcer's known biometrics. A final image—Halcyon's badge, dropped in the Kearny Marshes where the shootout went down.

Torque pushes off from the cage, his boots scuffing against concrete. "Just make sure you're shooting at the right shadows, girl. This whole thing smells wrong."

"The only thing that smells is your breath." I close my palm around the MP5's grip, feeling the capacitors hum with stored energy. White-lilac magic flows through them, clean and untainted—nothing like the corrupt energies the Syndicate uses.

The precinct alarms suddenly blare through the building. Red lights strobe across the armory ceiling.

*ALL UNITS—DISTRICT 4 TRANSIT HUB—MASSIVE RIOT IN PROGRESS—IMMEDIATE RESPONSE REQUIRED*

I holster the MP5, strap on my tactical vest—the Kevlar plates heavy against my ribs—and grab my radio. Torque is already moving toward the door, shaking his head.

"This never stops," he mutters.

But I'm not listening anymore. My mind has already shifted gears, calculating response times, asset deployment, containment protocols. The vengeance for Halcyon will have to wait another few hours.

Sometimes being Commander means setting aside personal vendettas when the city itself needs saving.

I sprint toward the exit, boots pounding rhythmically against concrete, as behind me the armory door slams shut with a metallic *crash*.

---

## CHAPTER 13: CHAPTER 13

The air in the briefing room tastes like old coffee and ozone. Rain drums against the high windows of BATC Headquarters, each drop a tiny percussion against the glass. Director Morvain stands before me, his posture rigid, his eyes somewhere past my shoulder—not looking at me but through me, as if he's already mentally checked out of this moment.

"You're the tip of the spear now, Commander Vance."

The word sits heavy between us. Commander. After three years of being a field officer who could out-shoot half the division, after the blood work and the body counts that followed the Millennium Breach, they finally hand me the rank. Morvain reaches into his suit jacket and produces a silver badge—eagle wings spread around a crystalline shield. The Aegis mark. His fingers brush mine as he pins it to my Kevlar vest, and I feel the cold metal bite through the fabric.

"I don't do politics, Director," I say flatly. "I do containment."

"Containment is politics now." He steps back, adjusting his tie with practiced precision. "The Undercity is boiling. Orc unions are striking. Street-Elves are rioting over Pylon placement. We need stability, Vance. That's what you'll provide."

Behind him, through the one-way mirror, I can see the bullpen—a sea of tired faces hunched over desks, coffee cups cold and forgotten. Somewhere out there, beyond the rain-slicked streets, the city is holding its breath.

Morvain slides a sleek black device across the table toward me. It's smaller than I expected—the neural-link headset. State-of-the-art tech, supposedly. Direct interface between operator and BATC network infrastructure. Real-time threat assessment, tactical overlays, coordinated response protocols.

"Put this on," he says. "Let's integrate you into the system properly."

I pick up the headset. It's surprisingly light, the matte black surface cool against my palm. The smell of burnt coffee intensifies as I lift it to my head, positioning the bands around my temples. For a moment, nothing happens. Then—

*Static.*

A sharp crackle inside my skull, like lightning trapped in a jar. My white-lilac weave responds immediately, disciplined pulses of power surging through my nervous system to meet the intrusion. But the neural-link isn't hostile. It's hungry. Analyzing. Syncing.

**INTEGRATION COMPLETE.**

**WELCOME, COMMANDER VANCE.**

**AEGIS PROTOCOLS ONLINE.**

Information floods my vision—not through my eyes but directly into my consciousness. Transit routes highlight themselves in my mind's eye. Personnel assignments flicker like stars on a map. Threat levels pulse with red urgency.

And then: a spike. A screaming alarm that cuts through everything else.

**PRIORITY ONE.**
**DISTRICT 4 MONORAIL HUB.**
**BLACK-CIRCUIT SABOTAGE ATTEMPT IN PROGRESS.**
**MULTIPLE CASUALTIES REPORTED.**

Morvain's face goes pale. "What is it?"

I'm already moving toward the door, the neural-link feeding me real-time data streams as I go. Coordinates lock into place. Tactical options scroll across my peripheral awareness. "Sabotage at District 4 Hub. Black-Circuit signature confirmed."

"Wait—I need to—"

The door slams open before he can finish, and I'm running.

The rain hits me like a wall of ice as I burst from the building's entrance. The streets are slick, neon reflections dancing on wet asphalt. Behind me, I hear Morvain shouting something about protocols and authorization, but his voice fades beneath the pounding water and the thunder of my boots on concrete.

My car is parked two blocks away. Too far.

I don't hesitate. My weave flares—white-lilac energy cascading down my arms—and I slam my palm against the side of a passing sedan. Metal groans. The engine sputters. I wrench open the driver's door, shove the stunned occupant out without ceremony, and slide behind the wheel.

The ignition turns over. My hand finds the neural-link controls built into the steering column interface—a new feature I hadn't noticed before. Traffic patterns illuminate my path. Green lights sync with my approach. Civilian vehicles automatically brake and pull aside.

*This thing is dangerous,* I think, accelerating hard through the intersection.

District 4 looms ahead, the monorail hub rising like a steel cathedral against the storm-black sky. Even from distance, I see it—the wrongness. Smoke pouring from ventilation shafts. Emergency lights strobing red across the platform level.

Black-Circuit sabotage. Coordinated attack.

My jaw tightens. My fingers grip the wheel until my knuckles ache.

*First day as Commander.*

*Let's not fuck this up.*

* * *

The rain hammers down harder now, turning the District 4 Transit Hub into a slaughterhouse of light and shadow. My breath comes steady and controlled even as adrenaline sharpens every sense. Through the cracked windshield of the trauma-ambulance—I still can't get used to calling them SWAT vehicles—the strobing emergency lights paint everything in violent shades of crimson and electric blue.

"Deploy," I say into the neural-link, my voice cutting through the chaos like a scalpel through tissue.

Behind me, twelve Aegis operatives pour out into the deluge. My first command as Commander. The weight of it settles on my shoulders along with the soaked tactical vest. The white-lilac weave responds instantly, spiraling up from my core with that cold surgical precision I've spent years refining. Each strand pulses in perfect rhythm—no waste, no emotion, pure function.

The transit hub is pandemonium incarnate. Telluric busbars spark and hiss where they've been torn from their moorings, sending arcs of captured lightning dancing across puddles. The air reeks of ozone and wet fur and something darker underneath—blood and fear and the musky stench of Ogre-Kin aggression.

Two of them are tearing apart a ticket vending machine, their massive frames hunched over the twisted metal like gargoyles made flesh. One looks up, yellow eyes catching mine for one terrible second before I raise my MP5.

Rubber-bismuth rounds punch into its shoulder. Not lethal—never lethal unless absolutely necessary—but enough to send the three-hundred-pound brute sprawling. Its partner roars, charging straight at our position with fists the size of cinder blocks swinging wild.

"Kinetic barrier, Sector Two!" I command.

My second-in-command, an Aegis mage named Chen, doesn't hesitate. A shimmering wall of compressed air materializes just as the Ogre-Kin slams into it with enough force to crack the concrete beneath his feet. He rebounds backward, dazed.

I'm already moving forward, boots splashing through water that runs black in the emergency lighting. The neural-link feeds me tactical data: squad positions marked as blue dots on my peripheral vision, thermal signatures showing eighteen hostiles still active within the perimeter, structural integrity of the terminal building at sixty-three percent.

"Commander, we got three heavies barricaded in the ticketing booth!" An Orc breacher's voice cuts through the comm chatter, guttural but urgent. "They're using civilians as shields."

I pivot, rain streaming down my face as I assess the situation. The booth is reinforced glass and bulletproof plating—designed to withstand riots, not Ogre-Kin muscle. Through the smoky interior, I can make out the shapes of something big moving inside. The crackle of weapons fire echoes from somewhere deeper in the terminal.

"Stack up," I order. "Chen, prepare a kinetic pulse on my mark. Everyone else, non-lethal only. We take them breathing if possible."

* * *

The transit hub reeks of ozone and copper. I can taste it on my tongue—that metallic bite that follows when reality gets bent too hard, too fast. My breath fogs in front of me, each exhale a ghost in the fluorescent lighting that flickers overhead like dying neurons.

Three bodies lie scattered across the concourse like discarded dolls. Two are Ogre-Kin security contractors, their massive frames locked in permanent death throes mid-stride. The third—an Elf woman who worked the ticket booth—is face-down in a spreading pool of her own blood. Steam rises from the crimson puddle where it meets the frost creeping across the linoleum floor.

Frost. In July. In a building with working climate control.

I crouch beside the nearest Ogre, studying the crystalline pattern spreading from his wound. This isn't ice. It's something worse—frost-cobalt signature, the kind that leaves necrotic residue deep in tissue. My white-lilac weave flares automatically, pushing back against the cold radiating from the corpse. Ten degrees below ambient temperature, maybe more. The air shimmers between us, magic meeting anti-magic in a silent war.

"Commander Vance?" 

A Gnome in a transit authority vest appears at the edge of my vision, wringing his hands. His whiskers twitch nervously. "Commander, the cameras... they just looped. Forty-seven minutes of footage, same exact thing. Whoever did this, they own the grid."

"No," I say without looking up, pulling out my Panasonic Toughbook. The machine boots with its familiar industrial hum, screen glowing pale blue in the hub's dim light. "He doesn't own the grid. He just knows how to hide in the static." I snap photos of the scene—the body positions, the frost patterns, the way the blood has crystallized instead of pooling naturally.

The Mechanic didn't just kill these people. He made a statement. A demonstration.

My fingers fly across the keyboard as I log the data: *Obsidian casing fragments recovered at previous scenes consistent with frost-cobalt discharge. Current scene shows advanced atmospheric manipulation. Suspect possesses BTC clearance or equivalent knowledge of municipal infrastructure.*

The cedar scent of my magic grows stronger as I work, cleansing the immediate area. Where my wards touch the frost, it sublimates into mist. But there's so much of it—like walking through a freezer that someone decided to fill with corpses.

"Clear the area," I tell the Gnome, not bothering with gentleness. "Evidence team won't be here for another hour. Get your people out."

He scurries away like the rat he resembles, grateful for the escape.

I move methodically through the scene, documenting everything. The Ogres went down first—I can tell by the blood spatter patterns on the walls. The Elf tried to run, made it maybe fifteen feet before the Mechanic caught her. Professional. Efficient. No wasted movement.

Then I see it.

On the ticket counter, half-hidden under scattered paperwork, lies a single spent casing. Depleted bismuth, oxidized green along one edge. Obsidian coating along the other. Fresh enough that heat still radiates from the metal when I pick it up with gloved fingers.

A message.

I turn it over in my palm, feeling its weight. Heavy. Custom ammunition. Expensive. Not something you leave behind accidentally.

"Looking for this?" 

I don't jump. Don't flinch. Because even without turning around, I know he's gone—slipped back into whatever shadows he emerged from. This is just his calling card.

But I hold the casing anyway, studying the manufacturing marks, memorizing every imperfection. My Toughbook records the serial numbers—they'll trace to nothing, I'm sure. But you never skip steps.

My jaw clenches. One week. It's been one fucking week since I saw him at County General, and already he's escalated from surgical strikes to public massacres.

The frost spreads another inch across the floor.

## CHAPTER 14: CHAPTER 14

The rain hammers down in sheets, each droplet a tiny fist against my skin. I don't feel it—not really. Not when my white-lilac magic hums beneath my collarbone, casting that subtle warmth across my shoulders like a shawl I've worn for years.

Below me, on the parade ground, Director Morvain's voice cuts through the storm:

"—exemplary service to the Bureau of Arcane Threat Containment—"

I stand at attention, dress uniform pristine despite the weather, one hand resting on the leather strap of my service piece. Around me, two hundred BATC personnel snap to attention. The flag snaps in the wind. Somewhere behind me, I know there are cameras. News crews. The mayor was supposed to attend, but he sent his deputy instead. Politics.

"Commander Vance has demonstrated unparalleled dedication—"

My jaw tightens. Unparalleled dedication. That's how they package it. How they make sense of the fact that I've spent three years hunting ghosts in Neon Hollow while my own sister disappears. While my own brother-in-law supposedly dies in an industrial accident that smells wrong from every angle.

Dedication.

The word tastes like copper.

"—the rank of Aegis Commander, effective immediately—"

A round of applause, muffled by the rain. I raise my right fist to my chest in salute as Morvain approaches with the insignia pin. Gold and crimson, catching the harsh fluorescent lights strung along the temporary stage. Behind him, the Newark skyline glows sickly orange against the black clouds.

I'm twenty-nine years old. Too young for this kind of command, according to protocol. But we're short-staffed. We're always short-staffed.

Morvain's eyes meet mine as he fastens the pin. His smile doesn't reach his eyes. "Proud of you, Commander."

"Yes, sir."

He moves on to the next portion of the ceremony, introducing my second-in-command. I don't hear the name. My attention snags on something else—a flicker of movement on one of the rooftops surrounding the parade ground.

Fourth-floor. Southeast corner. North Jersey County General, Emergency Wing.

Someone's watching.

The binoculars catch the light for just a second before disappearing into shadow. I track the position without turning my head, keeping my focus forward. Training. Discipline.

Could be nothing. Could be press. Could be someone who knows that underneath this ceremony, underneath all these medals and commendations, I'm still investigating Danny Reyes. Still digging through the wreckage of that supposed factory explosion. Still finding traces of arcane residue that shouldn't exist if it was just a simple industrial accident.

Still hearing whispers about the Arcane Iron-Lung.

"Commander Vance?"

I snap back to attention. "Sir."

"Present your new badge to the assembly."

I take three precise steps forward, draw the Aegis Commander badge from its velvet case, hold it up so every camera can capture the moment. The rain pelts down harder now, drumming against the metal stage like fingernails on a coffin lid.

Behind me, in the crowd, someone coughs.

On that rooftop—if there even is anyone on that rooftop—I imagine whoever they are, they're watching carefully. Waiting to see what I'll do with this rank. What lines I'll cross when I realize that everything we've been told about the Reyes family might be a lie.

My fingers close around the badge.

"I accept this responsibility," I say, voice clear across the parade ground, "in service to the Bureau and the people of Newark."

* * *

The rain hammered down like nails driven by an angry god, each droplet finding some new place to sting my neck where my collar didn't quite meet skin. I stood at attention on the parade ground, my dress uniform already soaking through at the shoulders despite the shimmering barrier of white-lilac magic I'd woven without thinking about it. Pure kinetic work—not the messy crimson chaos of combat, but something cleaner. More controlled.

More hollow.

Morvain's voice droned on through the PA speakers, words about order and justice bleeding together into meaningless static. "…stands as testament to what dedicated officers can achieve when they commit themselves fully to the mission..." The spotlight glared down like a hostile sun, turning the falling water into a thousand dancing blades of light that made my eyes hurt.

I wasn't listening. Couldn't listen. My tactical mind was running scenarios, cataloging exits, counting heads in the crowd of BATC personnel who'd turned out for this charade. Seventy-three attendees. Four perimeter guards—no, five, there was one behind the supply shed trying to stay dry under a tarp. The medical tent had its generator running. Standard protocol.

My neural-link buzzed softly against the base of my skull—a phantom itch from years of interface use even when it was offline now. Stress response. Hallucination.

"Commander Vance," Morvain continued, drawing out my name like he was savoring the weight of it. "For exemplary service in maintaining the public trust during the Neon Hollow purges..."

The applause erupted like a thunderclap. I kept my face forward, expression neutral, though every muscle in my body wanted to twitch with discomfort. They were clapping for a version of me that didn't exist anymore—the officer who'd believed in the system, in the mission, in something beyond just surviving another day.

Vane Thorne materialized at my side, his own dress uniform somehow pristine despite the weather. He clapped slowly, deliberately, those dead gray eyes fixed on me instead of the podium.

"Enjoy the applause, Commander," he muttered low enough that the microphones wouldn't catch it. "The higher you rise, the harder the fall."

My jaw tightened but my gaze remained locked straight ahead, watching nothing. "Just point me at the next target, Thorne."

His smile flickered like lightning before vanishing completely. He leaned closer, and I caught the scent of expensive cologne mixed with wet wool. "Oh, I intend to."

The phantom sensation in my neural-link pulsed again, stronger this time. Not random static. Pattern recognition: an encrypted ping on an old frequency I hadn't used since—

No. Couldn't be.

I scanned the perimeter involuntarily, my tactical mind finally finding purchase on something concrete. The rooftops across the street were slick with rain, half-hidden by the sodium-vapor glare. Movement there? Impossible to tell. My magic flared slightly brighter, responding to the surge of adrenaline.

Then it hit me—that familiar pull in my weave. Like someone was plucking the same harmonic string my consciousness vibrated at. Lysandra's signature had felt like this once, back when she'd still been part of the team. Before everything went sideways.

Before I'd ordered her execution.

"Commander Vance?" Morvain's voice cut through my thoughts, sharp now. Expectant.

Shit. How long had I zoned out?

I forced my attention back to the ceremony, accepting the commendation plaque with hands that didn't quite feel like mine. The crowd applauded again. Someone threw a salute. The rain continued its relentless assault, and somewhere across the parade ground, hidden among the shadows of the adjacent buildings, I could swear I felt eyes watching me.

My neural-link pinged one final time—a brief, unauthorized signal from somewhere across the street. Definitely not a hallucination.

Someone was here. Someone who knew my codes.

* * *

The moment the last applause died away, I was already moving. The medal hung cold against my throat—a weight I didn't earn and didn't want. Below me, the parade ground emptied in orderly rows while I descended the commander's platform, my dress uniform sticking to skin slicked with rain.

My hand found the Panasonic Toughbook strapped to my thigh beneath the formal jacket. The device warmed under my fingers, its screen glowing blue-white in the dim light. While everyone else filed toward the mess hall for the mandatory celebration, I was already hacking into the perimeter security net.

"Authorization Vance-Alpha-Seven-Six." My voice cut sharp across the encrypted channel. "I need eyes on the east wing rooftops. Sector Seven-B. Now."

The response came instant: "Affirmative, Commander."

A spotlight erupted from one of the drones—its beam cutting through sheets of rain like a knife through darkness. I tracked the movement, watching as it swept across wet asphalt, over ventilation units, along the edge of the adjacent building. There. A flicker of motion near the fire escape access.

My boots slapped against pavement already turning to ice. Behind me, someone called out—probably Johnson, probably reminding me about protocol—but I was already at full sprint, white-lilac magic bleeding through my aura in subtle pulses that pushed my legs faster than humanly possible.

The rain hit harder here, wind-driven off Newark Bay. Each droplet felt like a pinprick against bare skin where my uniform had gone half-unbuttoned in the run. I reached the access door to the adjacent building, yanked it open without breaking stride, and took the fire stairs two at a time.

*Metallic clang. Metallic clang.*

My breath came hard now, hot mist in cold air. The Toughbook's display showed the drone tracking overhead, keeping pace with my ascent. Third floor. Fourth. Fifth.

The roof door hung ajar when I reached it—wind pushing it back and forth with a hollow groan. I shouldered through, MP5 coming up instinctively. The rooftop spread before me, empty except for the rhythmic sweep of the drone's spotlight and the steady drumming of rain.

But not quite empty.

Near the ventilation unit on the far side, a cigarette butt smoked itself into extinction. Fresh. Very fresh. Someone who'd been here moments ago, waiting to see if I'd take the bait.

"Dispatch, this is Aegis Actual." My radio crackled with static. "I need a thermal sweep of the south block grid. Two bogeys, on foot."

"Negative, Commander." The Gnome dispatcher's voice held an edge of frustration. "Thermal grid in that sector is blind. New Telluric busbars are throwing off too much ambient interference. Can't get a clean read."

Of course they were. Everything about this case screamed sabotage. Not just the Reyes operation, but the investigation itself. Someone with deep access, someone who knew exactly which systems to corrupt and when.

I holstered the MP5 and knelt beside the ventilation unit, running my hand across its surface. The metal was cold, but beneath the chill, something else—a faint resonance that made my pure weave tingle in recognition.

Not frost-cobalt. That would've been straightforward, professional. This was different. Chaotic. Wild. Magic that tasted of copper and ozone and something darker, older than any training program could teach.

My stomach dropped.

*No. No way.*

I pressed my palm flat against the roof's wet concrete, letting my white-lilac senses extend outward. The magic trail wasn't strong enough to track directly, but it was *familiar*. The same chaotic signature I'd felt before, back in the Kearny Marshes when—

My pager went off, sharp and insistent. A summons from Morvain.

The old bastard never contacted me directly unless it was urgent. Unless he had information that couldn't wait for proper channels.

I stood slowly, rain streaming down my face, and stared at the empty rooftop one last time. Whoever had left that cigarette knew I'd come alone. Knew I'd follow. They'd watched the ceremony—the whole thing—and they wanted me to know they could reach me anywhere, even during what should have been my moment of greatest public visibility.

The wind howled across the gap between buildings. Somewhere below, thunder rolled across Newark Bay.

And somewhere out there in the rain-soaked darkness, two people were running.

But not just anyone.

My hand closed around the pager's message. Whatever Morvain had to tell me, I had a terrible feeling it would confirm what my gut was already screaming: Lysandra and Elena Reyes weren't hiding anymore.

They were hunting.

---
