## CHAPTER 15: CHAPTER 15

The fluorescent lights of the Aegis Command Center cast their cold, antiseptic glow across the tactical display table. I stood at parade rest, the stiff fabric of my dress uniform pressing against my ribs where my white-lilac magic coiled like a sleeping serpent—always ready, always watching.

Director Morvain paced behind the holographic map, his polished shoes clicking against the tile floor. The blue light washed over his angular features, throwing shadows into the hollows beneath his cheekbones. Newark Bay sprawled across the three-dimensional projection before us, the Kearny Marshes rendered in sickly green, the Pulaski Skyway cutting through like a rusted scar.

"Commander Vance," he began, his voice carrying that particular edge of official gravity, "your deployment orders are final."

I straightened further, if such a thing were possible. The crisp manila folder sat on the edge of the table, waiting. Stale coffee and ozone hung in the recycled air—the eternal smell of command centers everywhere. Somewhere in the building's bowels, generators hummed their constant vigilance.

Morvain gestured toward the map, and the projection shifted, zooming deep into the city's underbelly. Neon Hollow's infrastructure materialized in cross-section view: train tunnels, commuter passages, the thick conduits of Telluric energy feeding through the concrete arteries of our civilization.

"There." His finger stabbed at a cluster of red indicators. "Sub-Station Seven."

Chief Telluric Engineer Torque stepped forward from the shadows near the wall, his grease-stained overalls dark with the grime of weeks spent in the deep maintenance tunnels. He was Dwarven—a stocky, powerful figure whose beard had been braided with copper wire for so many years it had become part of him. His eyes, sharp and gray as flint, fixed on the hologram with professional concern.

"You're sitting on a powder keg down there, Mara," Torque said, using my first name in that way subordinates do when they've earned the right through shared dangers. His calloused thumb pointed at the map. "Sub-Station Seven is the central artery. If the pressure from the busbars cracks the bedrock, the whole station floods with raw Telluric energy. We're talking catastrophic overload—everything from the marsh gates to the county line goes dark, and not just dark. *Violent*."

The holographic image expanded to show Sub-Station Seven in detail. It was massive—a sprawling nexus where three major transit lines converged, where millions of commuters passed every day, blissfully unaware of the mountain of engineering holding their world together. The Pylon Collars gleamed like brass rings wrapped around the main conduits, their purpose to contain and regulate the immense flow of Telluric current that powered everything from the streetlights to the hospital systems.

Morvain cut him off with an impatient wave. "Which is exactly why we need our best Commander securing it."

I studied the projection, watching the data streams scroll across the bottom: passenger counts, structural stress analyses, energy throughput measurements. Sub-Station Seven processed more traffic than any other point in North Jersey's underground network. The numbers were staggering—millions of souls passing through every twenty-four hours, all of them dependent on those tunnels staying solid, those conductors staying contained.

"What's the operational mandate?" I asked, keeping my voice level despite the knot forming in my stomach. White-lilac magic pulsed once beneath my sternum—a warning? Intuition? My gift had saved my life too many times to ignore its whispers.

Torque pulled a thick sheaf of technical documents from his satchel, spreading them across the table beside my deployment orders. "Structural integrity is degrading faster than projections. The new Pylon Collar installation has put additional strain on already-compromised bedrock. We're talking micro-fractures throughout the sector. My team can't work down there twenty-four seven without causing more problems than they solve."

"The Aegis Division will establish permanent tactical overwatch," Morvain continued, picking up the manila folder and sliding it across the polished surface toward me. "Full complement. You'll have authority over security protocols, access control, anomaly response—the works. This isn't just about preventing industrial accidents anymore, Mara. Intelligence suggests targeted sabotage efforts originating from Sterling Manor."

My fingers closed around the folder. Inside would be everything—personnel assignments, equipment manifests, strategic objectives, and the official seal that made this real. December 2003. The winter before everything changed.

"Sterling Manor?" The name tasted like copper on my tongue. That decaying mansion on the county line had been a source of arcane corruption since long before I joined Aegis.

Morvain nodded grimly. "We've intercepted communications. Someone down there wants Sub-Station Seven compromised. Whether for simple destruction or something worse..." He let the sentence hang in the air between us.

I opened the folder, scanning the first page. *Commander Mara Vance, Temporary Assignment: Sub-Station Seven Tactical Overwatch, Effective Date: January 1st, 2004.* Temporary assignment. Even they didn't fully understand what we were walking into.

The holographic map still glowed before me, that red dot labeled *Sub-Station Seven* pulsing with its own malevolent rhythm. Somewhere deep beneath North Jersey's concrete skin, millions of people rushed through tunnels every day, their lives balanced on the edge of engineering miracles and arcane dangers neither could see nor comprehend.

And I was about to descend into that darkness, to make myself a guardian for all those unsuspecting souls.

Torque met my eyes, his expression grave. "Once you're down there full-time, Commander, you'll feel it—the whole structure breathing. Groaning. You'll know before any of my sensors if things start to give."

I closed the folder, feeling its weight in both hands—literal and metaphorical. Behind us, the hum of the command center continued its eternal vigilance. Outside, December snow would be falling across Newark Bay, covering the industrial landscape in temporary purity.

"When do I report?" My voice came out steady, professional.

"January first," Morvain confirmed. "Give yourself time to prepare your team, secure your equipment. This is priority one, Mara. Everything else takes a back seat."

I nodded, staring at the glowing red dot. Unaware, then, that this moment marked not just an assignment but a prophecy. That within two years, that station would become the site of such horror that even now, years later, I cannot speak its name without tasting ash and blood.

But that future hadn't happened yet. In December 2003, I was simply Commander Mara Vance accepting orders from Director Morvain, my white-lilac magic bright and pure as fresh cedar, ready to protect the innocent masses flowing through Sub-Station Seven.

The greatest tragedy of my life began with a simple deployment order.

And I accepted it without hesitation.

* * *

The trunk of my Crown Vic slams shut with a metallic *thunk* that echoes through the underground garage of Precinct Three. The sound reverberates off concrete pillars stained with decades of oil and rust, creating phantom echoes in the cavernous space.

I wipe my palms on my tactical pants—still damp from the cleansing ward I cast before loading the gear. Fresh cedar clings to my fingers, sharp and medicinal against the garage's usual stench of motor oil and exhaust fumes. The scent does its job: keeps my head clear, wards off the worse things lurking in shadows like these.

Three kinetic barrier generators go in first, their weight satisfying. Then the trauma kits—four of them, fully stocked with cauterizing agents and enough coagulant to stop arterial spray from a halfling. The sodium flares get wrapped in foam padding; those babies are delicate until you need them, and when you need them, they're the only thing piercing through the Undercity's perpetual murk.

My PalmPilot glows green in my palm as I climb into the driver's seat. The Crown Vic's engine rumbles to life, a familiar V8 purr that vibrates through the steering wheel and up my forearms. I appreciate this car. She's solid. Reliable. No nonsense.

The screen illuminates my face with cold blue light. Pylon schematics scroll past—Halcyon's notation is precise, almost obsessive in its detail. Station Seven's architecture is a nightmare of redundant corridors and dead ends. A choke point designed by someone who either didn't care about evacuations or wanted to make damn sure people couldn't escape whatever went wrong down there.

I cross-reference his notes against the station plans. The math doesn't lie. Three primary commuter routes converge at Platform B. During rush hour, that's five thousand souls funneling through a space barely wide enough for two trains to pass. In an emergency, it becomes a deathtrap.

*Not on my watch.*

A knock rattles my window. I jump—just slightly—and find myself staring at an Orc quartermaster, his tusks gleaming under the fluorescent lights. He's holding something heavy, something that catches the light weirdly.

"Requisition approved, Commander." His voice is gravel and smoke. "You're gonna need this down in the deep dark. The rats down there got teeth."

He passes me a riot shield through the window. It's heavy—unusually so. Rune-work spirals across the surface, etched deep into what looks like reinforced titanium. The metal smells like old blood and older magic.

"I know," I say simply, taking the shield. The weight settles in my arms like a promise. Like a warning.

The Orc nods once, gravely, and retreats into the shadows between the support pillars. Smart. Most of his kind avoid prolonged contact with Aegis Commanders unless absolutely necessary.

I secure the shield in the back seat, then pull out Halcyon's final report. The margins are covered in his cramped handwriting, equations and probability matrices that would make a mathematician weep. But he'd circled one passage in red ink:

*"Commander Vance: The Undercity does not forgive mistakes. It does not release what it claims. Your white-lilac signature will be a beacon in that darkness—but beacons can also attract predators. Trust nothing. Verify everything. And when you feel doubt, remember: you carry more than your own life down there."*

I fold the report carefully and tuck it inside my leather jacket, right over my heart.

The Crown Vic lurches forward as I shift into drive. My headlights cut through the garage's gloom, illuminating dust motes suspended in air thick enough to taste. Somewhere ahead, massive industrial freight elevators yawn open—their entrances like the maws of sleeping beasts.

The descent begins here.

My wards flare bright around the car, cedar-scented protection against whatever waits below. Whatever's been waiting since before the BATC established this precinct. Since before the first commuters stepped onto Platform B.

*Five years,* I think, gripping the wheel tighter. *Just get them through five more years.*

The elevator doors loom larger. Closer.

My magic pulses steady around me—white-lilac pure, defiant against the creeping industrial dark.

But even light has limits when it ventures too deep into places meant to stay buried.

* * *

The Crown Vic's tires scream against the rust-streaked concrete as I guide it onto the freight elevator. My knuckles are white around the steering wheel, but my face remains stone. Behind me, Newark Bay disappears upward into a rectangle of dying winter sunlight that grows smaller by the second.

Ten minutes down.

I've read the briefings—twenty-seven levels deep, older than most of the surface structures above, built during the war when the government needed to hide things from satellites and bombers alike. Now it hides things from itself. Fifty thousand metahumans passing through these tunnels daily, a river of desperate commuters flowing between the ghettos and the corporate spires, all of them pressed together in the dark like cattle.

My magic doesn't like it down here. The white-lilac aura that normally flows around me like fresh cedar smoke feels constricted, compressed by the weight of all this concrete and steel. But it burns brighter for it, fierce and unblemished in this industrial hellscape.

The elevator groans—a sound like the earth splitting open. Metal shrieks against metal. The temperature drops ten degrees in the first minute alone. By the third, I can see my breath fogging inside the car while humidity condenses on the windows outside, running in dirty rivulets down glass already stained with decades of grime.

Five minutes down now. The air tastes like copper and ozone, the constant hum of massive turbines vibrating through the floor panels and up through the frame. Somewhere far below, water drips steadily, echoing through chambers so vast you could never find their edges.

Seven minutes. Eight. Nine.

When the elevator finally lurches to a stop at the tenth minute mark, the hydraulic hiss sounds almost like relief. The doors grind open with a metallic shriek that makes my teeth ache.

Sub-Station Seven explodes into view.

Platforms stretch out in three directions, packed with bodies—humans, dwarves, elves, trolls, orks, goblins, everything in between. Steam vents hissing from grate-covered shafts. Neon signs flicker in broken languages above kiosks selling synthetic food and bootleg datachips. Train lines arc overhead, sparking where they cross, casting strobing shadows across faces lit by the sickly orange glow of emergency lights.

And everywhere—the copper. Telluric copper wiring wrapped around concrete pillars thick as ancient trees, pulsing with captured lightning, the very lifeblood of the Undercity's crumbling infrastructure.

A scuffle breaks out near Platform C. Three goblin scavengers trying to lift purses from a group of human commuters. Transit security moves in slow, uncertain, waiting for someone else to make the first move because nobody wants to be the one to start trouble here, not in this pressure cooker.

I step out of the Crown Vic.

My magic responds instantly.

The white-lilac aura erupts from me like a supernova, pure and absolute, washing across the platform in waves of clean light that cut through the smog and steam like a blade. Every head turns. Every conversation stops dead.

The goblin leaders freeze mid-swipe, their yellow eyes going wide. The human victims stare, mouths agape. Even the transit cops look up from their stances, hands still on their batons but no longer advancing.

"Stand down," I say quietly, my voice carrying anyway, amplified by something more than mere volume.

Nobody argues. They never do.

The scavengers release their would-be victims and melt back into the crowd, which parts before them like water before a stone. My aura follows, pushing outward until it touches every corner of the station, leaving behind that clean cedar scent that means *this space is mine*.

A dwarven transit cop approaches, his weathered face showing relief mixed with exhaustion. He's got scars across both cheeks and a left arm that looks cybernetic beneath his uniform sleeve. "Commander Vance." His voice carries the gravel of years underground. "Welcome to the bottom of the world."

He gestures around at the chaos—at the crowds surging past, at the sparking overhead lines, at the pillars groaning under the weight of everything above. "We got fifty thousand souls moving through here every hour. The walls are humming. You'll hear them if you listen close enough. Never stops."

Above our heads, dominating the entire ceiling space directly over Platform A, the Pylon Collar rises from its mounting brackets. Gold-bismuth alloy, twenty feet thick, bolted into concrete designed to support the weight of the city itself. It pulses with captured energy, that telluric power flowing through copper veins like blood through arteries.

Except right now, it's pulsing wrong.

The light emanating from it has a sickly quality, unstable, flickering between brilliant white and something darker, like shadow given luminescence. I can feel it even from ground level—a wrongness, a corruption seeping through the structure.

I key my neural-link with a thought. "Aegis Actual is on site. Lock it down. Nothing happens in Sub-Station Seven without my say-so."

The confirmation chime sounds almost cheerful compared to the industrial hell surrounding me.

I look up at that Pylon Collar again, watching it pulse and throb with unstable power. Somewhere deep inside my gut, something cold coils tight. Instinct screaming at me that this place—the Pylon, the station, all of it—is going to matter someday.

That it's already too late to turn back.

But I stand there anyway, pure white-lilac magic blazing around me like a defiant flame against the encroaching dark, and I think: *Let them come.*

# BOOK #10: THE SYNDICATE'S BUTCHER
### Prequels Cycle 2 (PB-2)

---

## CHAPTER 1: THE CREEPING FROST

The wrench slipped in my greasy fingers just as the temperature hit forty-three degrees.

I caught it against my shin—a dull thud that barely registered over the rattle of Danny's breathing from the back office. That sound. That fucking *sound*. Like someone trying to inhale through a rusted pipe filled with marbles and blood.

"Shit," I muttered, straightening up from the engine bay. My breath came out in a cloud that shouldn't have been there—not yet. Forty-three degrees inside, and the frost was already creeping across the Crown Vic's windshield in crystalline fractals. Each one of them looked like a spider's web made of broken glass.

The shop smelled wrong tonight. Usually it was all 10W-40 and transmission fluid, maybe a hint of burnt clutch plate when we were running hot jobs. Now there was something else undercutting everything—that metallic tang that meant my blood-iron hexes were running too cold, too tight. The oil in the Vic's pan had started to thicken, going viscous and slow.

Another wet cough from the back office.

I wiped my hands on a rag already black with grease, then immediately regretted it because now my palms were slick and useless. The sodium-vapor lamps outside buzzed their constant electrical hum—the city never slept, even at three in the morning, especially not in Neon Hollow where the streetlights fought shadows that didn't want to lose.

"Danny?" My voice came out rougher than I intended.

Tap-tap-TAP. Tap-tap-TAP.

That was his response. His rhythm. Always three beats, always that emphasis on the third. Danny's way of saying he was still here, still breathing, still alive in whatever hellscape his lungs had become since the Telluric Compressor blew six months ago.

I walked toward the back office, each step crunching on frost that had no business being there. The concrete floor should've been bone-dry—we kept the shop climate-controlled for exactly this reason, kept the humidity low so the brass mechanisms wouldn't seize up. But my hexes didn't give a fuck about climate control when the anxiety hit.

The door hung open. Inside, bathed in the sickly green glow of the monitoring equipment, stood the Iron-Lung.

It looked like something Salvador Dalí would've designed if he'd been drunk on mercury and hallucinating machinery. All brass pipes and glass chambers, copper coils wrapped around pulmonary capacitors, tubes snaking through impossible geometries. We'd built it together over two years—me doing the mechanical work while Danny studied the arcane theory, cross-referencing texts he'd stolen from the Sterling Manor archives. Back when we thought we could out-engineer biology itself.

Now it was all we had left.

Danny's face appeared in one of the larger glass panels, distorted by the curves but unmistakably him. Fifteen years old going on forty, dark circles under his eyes that matched the shadows underneath mine.

"Bro," he said, voice muffled and filtered through the machine, "you know your taste in music is objectively terrible."

The Sony MiniDisc player sat on the workbench behind me, still skipping on the same track it had been stuck on for an hour. Some shitty nu-metal song with too many breakdowns and not enough melody. I'd put it on just to have *something* fill the silence between his breaths.

"Says the kid who tried to make me listen to twenty-minute long black metal songs." I stepped inside, letting the heat from the Compressor wash over me. It felt good against the frost that had settled into my bones. "At least this has a chorus."

"A bad one."

"A *chorus*, Danny."

He tapped again. Tap-tap-TAP. Then he coughed—that horrible wet rattling sound—and I saw the way the brass pistons stuttered in response, how the pressure gauges spiked and dropped like they were having a seizure.

"How's she running?" I asked, though I already knew the answer. Could see it in the way condensation had started beading on the glass, in the faint whine coming from the compressor unit. The thing was deteriorating faster every week.

"The Cough in the Cold," Danny said, and then he laughed, which turned into another cough, which made everything rattle and groan. "Sounds like a bad poetry slam title."

"That's what you're calling it now?"

"Why not? You're the one who keeps freezing the whole fucking shop every time you get nervous." He gestured at the windows, where frost had started creeping down from the top frames. Outside, Neon Hollow looked like something from a noir film—all streaking headlights and neon signs reflecting off puddles of oil-slick water.

I moved closer to the Iron-Lung, studying the readings on the analog dials we'd salvaged from God-knows-where. Pressure dropping. Oxygen saturation falling. The copper coils showing green corrosion that shouldn't have been there yet.

"We need to work on the Telluric Core Compressor," I said quietly. "The upgrade. Sooner rather than later."

"Yeah." Danny's voice was smaller now, tired. "Soon."

There was nothing else to say after that. Nothing that wouldn't sound like goodbyes or lies or both. So I just stood there in the cold, watching my little brother breathe through a machine we'd built with stolen parts and forbidden knowledge, while outside the city hummed its indifferent song and the temperature kept dropping around us.

Frost bloomed across the metal pipes.

And somewhere in the darkness beyond our chop-shop, something waited.

* * *

I heard the boots before I saw him—three deliberate strikes against wet pavement, the kind of walk that meant business even when it didn't need to. Bram Kovacs pushed through my chop-shop door without knocking, canvas bag slung over one shoulder like it weighed nothing.

"The kid's fucked," he said flatly, shaking water from his beard. Outside, the January wind screamed through Neon Hollow, rattling windows already frosted at the edges where my hexes had been leaking all morning. Every time I thought about what was growing inside Danny's chest, the temperature dropped another degree.

Bram set down his bag and pulled out a pair of those stupid welders' goggles he insisted on wearing everywhere. "Got the diagnostic rig?"

"Back table." My voice came out wrong—tighter than intended. I'd been running on four hours sleep and zero coffee, maintaining the frost-cobalt state because anything less felt like letting go of the last rope holding me above water.

We worked in silence for a minute, unbolting the primary housing of Danny's Iron-Lung. The brass plates came away with a hiss of escaping pressure, releasing a plume of vapor that reeked of burnt ozone and something worse—the metallic tang of necrotic sludge. That smell had been following us since we'd pulled Danny out of the marsh two weeks ago.

Bram hooked up his heavily modded IBM ThinkPad, fingers dancing across keys while a green glow reflected off his goggles. The laptop whined as it booted into some custom Linux distro covered in arcane command prompts I couldn't begin to read.

"Filtration busbars are slagged," he muttered, more to himself than me. "Look at this shit."

I looked. What I saw made my stomach clench hard enough to hurt.

Through the transparent section of the filtration chamber, I could see them—black crystals of Black-Iron Sludge, each one no bigger than a grain of rice but moving with terrible purpose. They were bypassing our filters entirely, riding along the brass channels like parasites finding their way home. And they were close—millimeters from where Danny's pericardium should be, visible through another transparent panel in the chest housing.

"They're adapting," Bram said, his voice dropping to something almost reverent, which was worse than anger from him. "The sludge is learning. This brass rig we built? It's a band-aid on a bullet wound." He tapped the screen, bringing up a schematic overlay. Red zones bloomed across the image. "See here? Here? The crystal formation is fractal-based now. Every time we filter one path clear, three more routes open up. It's not mechanics anymore, Cole. It's biology."

My hands were shaking. Not from fear—I'd burned past that somewhere around hour forty-eight of this nightmare—but from the cold. The shop had dropped another five degrees since we started, frost creeping across the workbench edges. My blood-iron hexes were running hot with stress, bleeding cold into everything around us.

"We need to compress it," I said. The words came out flat, final. "Telluric Core approach. Run the core through a secondary loop, use the magnetic field to crystallize the sludge faster than it can adapt."

Bram finally looked up at me, and what I saw in those eyes wasn't encouragement. "That's theoretical, and you know it. We don't have the containment vessel specs worked out. You try running that much telluric current through untested brass, you'll cook the kid's heart before you slow the sludge down."

"Then what?" The question came out sharp enough to cut. "We watch him drown in his own chest? We built him an Iron-Lung so he could breathe, Bram. Right now he's got maybe—what? Forty-eight hours before those crystals reach his pericardium?"

The welder goggles reflected green light back at me, hiding Bram's expression. Outside, sirens wailed in the distance—probably the Pulaski Skyway, always some kind of accident on that stretch. Normal problems for normal people who didn't have to worry about Black-Iron Sludge growing inside their children's ribcages.

"We build the compressor," Bram said quietly. "But we do it right. Full schematics, test rig, everything by the book." He closed the laptop, unplugging it with practiced efficiency. "I've got blueprints from my grandfather's workshop—pre-war stuff, when Local 405 was doing arcane machinery before anyone called it 'arcano-noir.' There's a compression matrix design that might work if we adapt it properly."

"How long?"

"Fast as possible means six weeks minimum. Realistic is eight." He shouldered his bag again, already moving toward the door. "And Cole? Get control of your hexes before they ice this whole building solid. The kid doesn't need frostbite on top of everything else."

I stood there after he left, staring at the filtration chamber and the black crystals crawling through brass channels designed to stop them. Somewhere in Sterling Manor, whatever had birthed this sludge was still out there, still spreading through the marsh system beneath Newark Bay.

Six weeks. Maybe eight.

Danny only had two days.

My hands clenched into fists, and I felt the frost-cobalt surge harder, faster—the shop windows weeping ice down their panes while motor oil thickened in its cans. The rage wasn't helping. The fear wasn't helping. Nothing except finding another way forward would help now.

I pulled Danny's full schematic off the wall board and spread it across the main table, green diagnostic lights casting everything in an underwater glow. The Iron-Lung design we'd built in Piscataway during those desperate summer months of 2001 looked so clean then, so simple.

Everything looks simple before you see how badly it can fail.

The Black-Iron Sludge didn't care about our timelines or our craftsmanship. It just grew, adapted, pushed forward with the patient inevitability of entropy itself.

I picked up my wrench—weighted brass, union-machinist grade—and got back to work.

* * *

The monitor's sharp alarm cuts through the chop-shop's ambient hum like a blade through meat.

I'm on my feet before I register movement, boots crunching across fresh frost that shouldn't be there on the concrete floor. My breath hangs in the air—visibility low, temperature lower. The copper tang of blood-iron hits my tongue as my hexes lock down cold, dead-silent cobalt.

"Danny!" The name tears out of me raw.

Bram's already moving, his mechanic's hands dancing across the brass valves of the Iron-Lung apparatus. The machine coughs—a wet, struggling *hiss-thump*—that sounds too much like drowning for comfort. Danny's fifteen years old, stretched out on the reinforced medical slab, his chest rising and falling beneath the translucent crystal casing of the 2000-era brass lung.

"Pressure spike," Bram mutters, knuckles white around the pressure gauge. "He's compensating, but the seals are—shit."

The monitors flatline. Just for a second. A microsecond that stretches into forever.

My fingers clamp around the edge of the workbench. Frost creeps up the metal, spreading like veins across steel. A half-drunk cup of coffee sits on the desk—I didn't even see it earlier. Now it's solid ice, frozen mid-ring with the lip prints still visible, condensation crystals catching the harsh fluorescent light.

*Thump-hiss. Thump-hiss.*

The Iron-Lung fights to keep him alive.

"You need to step back." Bram's voice is steady—the kind of calm you only get from twenty years of watching people die in slow motion. He adjusts the main valve, and the rhythmic breathing steadies. "Cole. *Step back.*"

I can feel the frost creeping up my pant legs now, numbness spreading from my ankles upward. My heart hammers against my ribs, each beat forcing more of that metallic cold through my system. The temperature must be dropping ten degrees every time my pulse spikes.

"Tell me he's stable." Not a question. A demand.

Bram straightens up, wiping grease-stained hands on a rag that's seen better days. His eyes meet mine, and I know. I know before he opens his mouth because he's already looking at me the way people look when they're trying to find words soft enough not to break what's left.

"He's compensating," Bram repeats carefully. "But this isn't temporary anymore, Cole. The brass is failing. The crystal matrix is degrading faster than we anticipated."

"How fast?"

"The lungs are 2000-era tech. They weren't built for permanent installation, and definitely not for someone with Danny's... condition." He gestures at the sprawled form on the slab, at the delicate web of brass tubing and arcane crystal that keeps oxygen moving through my little brother's bloodstream while his real organs slowly shut down. "Three months. Maybe four if we're lucky and careful."

My hands are shaking. Frost pebbles off them onto the floor—*crunch crunch crunch*—each shard reflecting the emergency lights.

"You said 'if.'" My voice sounds wrong. Hollow. Like it's coming from somewhere underground. "What's the other option?"

Bram glances at the Iron-Lung, then back at me. When he speaks, there's something different in his tone—a weight he's been carrying and finally deciding to pass along.

"There's military-grade tech out there. Telluric Core Compressors. Pure arcane pressure delivery systems designed for deep-cover metahuman ops." He pulls out a cigarette, lights it with unsteady hands. "The Black-Circuit Syndicate's Inner Council acquired a shipment last month. Rumor is they're sitting on at least six units in their Sterling Manor facility."

I stare at him. At the smoke curling from his lips, at the frozen coffee cup, at the rhythmic *thump-hiss* of my brother's borrowed lungs.

"Military grade." I test the words like tasting poison. "You mean illegal. You mean dangerous. You mean exactly the kind of thing that got us into this mess in the first place."

"The Iron-Lung was supposed to be temporary," Bram says quietly. "Until we found a cure. Until Danny's body could heal itself." He takes another drag, exhales gray into frost-laden air. "That was three years ago, Cole. And now the only thing that can push enough pure pressure to keep those crystals away from his heart is tech so hot it'd melt you if you looked at it sideways."

Silence settles over the chop-shop like snow.

I walk to the workbench, fingers trailing across metal that shrieks under my touch—frost expanding wherever skin meets surface. The coffee cup sits there accusingly solid, lip prints preserved in ice.

"How much?"

Bram knows what I'm asking without elaboration. "More than Local 405 sees in two years of protection money." He pauses. "And even if we had it, the Syndicate doesn't sell to outsiders. They don't negotiate. They don't compromise."

"Then we don't ask." The words come out flat, final. Dead-ice cold.

His eyes widen slightly—the first crack in Bram's professional mask since we started this conversation.

"We buy a seat at their table," I continue, staring at my reflection in the frozen coffee surface—distorted, fragmented, barely recognizable. "We take one."

"You're talking about going up against the Black-Circuit Inner Council." Bram's voice carries an edge of something between concern and disbelief. "Cole, they eat people like us for breakfast."

"They don't know who I am yet."

The frost on the floor spreads wider as my pulse kicks harder, colder. The temperature in here must be dropping into the thirties by now—the oil drums are beginning to glisten with condensation turned white.

Danny makes a soft sound on the slab. Just a whisper of breath through the brass tubes.

*Thump-hiss.*

My little brother, alive because of twenty-year-old tech that's failing faster every day. Three months. Maybe four if we're lucky and careful.

I look down at my hands—they're completely white now, veins traced in cobalt blue beneath skin so cold it almost burns. When I breathe, it fogs more than it should indoors.

"Get me everything you can find on Sterling Manor," I say quietly. "Personnel files. Security layouts. Supply routes. The names of everyone who works there."

Bram watches me for a long moment—measuring something he doesn't like but isn't going to stop anyway.

"And after?" he asks finally.

I pick up the frozen coffee cup carefully, holding it to the light. Through the ice, I can see the lip print clearly—the shape of someone's mouth, preserved forever in cold.

"After," I say, "we go to war."

The *thump-hiss* continues its steady rhythm behind me while outside the chop-shop windows, the winter wind howls across Neon Hollow, carrying the smell of Newark Bay and promises of things to come.

---

## CHAPTER 2: THE SYNDICATE SOLUTION

The Toughbook's screen casts its sickly green glow across my knuckles as they fly across the rubberized keyboard. Each keystroke produces that distinctive *clack-clack-clack* against the metal workbench—sharp, industrial, final. Beneath me, the Undercity tunnels hum with the ghost-rattle of third-rail current.

Stale Marlboro smoke hangs thick in the air of this particular dead-drop, mixing with the metallic tang of machine oil and something darker—something organic and wrong that I've learned to associate with the deeper levels where things that shouldn't exist crawl between the support beams. My breath comes out in visible puffs despite the oppressive heat radiating from the server towers surrounding us.

*"Fuck,"* I mutter, scrolling through another layer of encryption. The Black-Circuit Syndicate doesn't fuck around when it comes to protecting their IP. They're running military-grade scramblers on everything worth stealing, routing their manifests through at least three different dead-satellite relays before dumping them into the public feeds.

But nothing's truly invisible if you know where to look for the shadows.

I find it two hours past midnight—buried in a maintenance log for Sub-Station Seven. A single line item, buried between routine conduit checks and a report about rats chewing through insulation: **TELLURIC CORE COMPRESSOR - UNIT 07429-X - STERLING MANOR WAREHOUSE C**

My heart does that thing where it stops being a muscle and starts being a stone in my chest. It's real. Danny can actually be saved.

The specs scroll across the screen. God-tier tech that shouldn't exist outside black-ops facilities. Capacitor arrays designed to store enough raw electrical potential to power a small city block—or burn one clean to ash. Exactly what he needs to stabilize his core before the feedback cascade tears him apart molecule by molecule.

The motorola Razr on the desk next to me starts vibrating like a man having a seizure, rattling against the cold steel with enough urgency to draw blood. I grab it without looking away from the screen.

"Reyes." The voice crackles through—Grimjaw, calling from somewhere in the sprawl between Kearny and Newark Bay. "You still breathing over there?"

"I'm here." My own voice sounds flat, tired down to my bones. "Got something."

"What kind of something?" There's an edge of interest underneath the gruff exterior. Grimjaw runs the Local 405 coalition—three dozen street crews and independent operators who've decided that the Syndicate's monopoly on high-end tech has gone on long enough. We're talking ex-military hardware, metahuman augmentation tech, digital weapons systems that could punch holes in reality if you knew how to aim them right.

"The good kind," I say. "But we need to move fast. Sterling Manor warehouse district. Tonight."

A pause while he processes this. When Grimjaw speaks again, there's something harder in his tone—the sound of gears locking into place. "How fast are we talking?"

I pull up the manifest cross-references, watching as the data streams across multiple windows. "According to their shipping logs, they've got a military-grade Necro-Thermite shipment moving through the 405 district at oh-four-hundred. Thirty crates. rival cartel trying to muscle in on Black-Circuit territory."

"Jesus Christ." Now there's genuine concern threading through his words. "That shit goes off near any population center—"

"It won't." My hand moves to the Toughbook's trackpad, bringing up the routing information. "They're keeping it underground. Moving it by subway freight car through the abandoned tunnels beneath Pulaski Skyway. It's the only route they can take without drawing heat from the Feds."

Another silence, longer this time. I can hear him breathing on the other end—that wet rasp that comes from too many years sucking factory air in places like this.

"If we hit that convoy..." He's thinking out loud now, running the arithmetic of violence in his head like a priest counting rosary beads. "We'd have leverage. Real leverage. Not just against the Syndicate—against everyone operating in North Jersey."

"You're saying yes."

"I'm saying..." A long exhalation. "I'm saying get your gear ready. I'll start pulling the crew together. Where do you want to meet?"

"The old diner on South Street. The one with the flickering neon sign. Midnight." I pause, staring at the Telluric Core Compressor specs one more time. Danny's face flashes behind my eyes—the way he looked before the accident, before the core went critical and started eating him from the inside out. "And Grimjaw? Bring every heavy weapon you've got stashed away. This is going to be bloody."

"No shit," he mutters, and then the line goes dead.

I close the laptop, plunging the chop-shop into darkness except for the emergency red lights mounted along the ceiling beams. They cast everything in shades of crimson—a preview of what's coming.

The frost-cobalt aura coils tighter around me, that familiar pressure building behind my sternum as I let the cold settle into my bones. Out there in the tunnels, something moves between the shadows. Something hungry.

But tonight, I'm hungrier.

I pick up my gear bag and head for the exit, boots crunching over broken glass and things I don't care to identify. The dark wire stretches ahead of us all—the thin thread connecting this moment to whatever comes after. And we're about to cut it.

* * *

The back alley reeked of grease and stale beer, steam rising from a rusted grate like a dragon's dying breath. I leaned against the brick wall, my frost-cobalt aura coiled tight around me, watching the shadows between the flickering neon signs of the diner. Red. Yellow. Red. Each pulse made the puddles on the pavement look like bleeding wounds.

Grimjaw arrived first, his massive frame filling the mouth of the alley. The Orc enforcer moved with surprising quiet for someone built like a freight train, his leather jacket creaking with each step. Behind him came the others—two Ogre-Kin twins carrying sawed-off shotguns that looked comically oversized even in their meaty fists, a crew of three Goblins with bolt cutters hanging from their belts like badges of office, and finally, three Street-Elves in optical-camo jackets that shimmered like oil slicks under the neon glow.

"Hey, Cole." Grimjaw's voice rolled out low and gravelly, pure South Side enforcement. "Brought your party animals."

I pushed off the wall, feeling the cold radiate through my coat. "You all know why we're here."

One of the Goblin wire-cutters, missing an ear and sporting a jagged scar across her jaw, spoke up fast. "Word is you want to hit cartel armor. That's suicide pay, friend."

"The pay's thirty crates of thermite," I said flatly. "Black-Circuit Syndicate cargo, heading through the Pulaski Skyway at 0400 tomorrow. Their convoy's got three armored trucks and six bike escorts. Heavy weapons."

A Razor-Wire Street-Elf named Knife pushed her goggles up, her eyes reflecting the neon like a cat's. "Sniper positions confirmed along Route 1-9. We can pin the bikes before they scatter. Optical-cam will make us ghosts to their thermal scans."

Grimjaw scratched his tusk with a calloused thumb. "That's a lot of metal between us and those crates. How we cracking the lead truck?"

"Thermite charges on the hinges." I pulled out a folded schematic, spread it against the brick. "Ogre-Kin twins handle security—these two guards won't know what hit them until their doors are molten slag. Goblins cut the comms lines at Sub-Station Seven, blind them for exactly ninety seconds. Elves provide overwatch from the Kearny Marshes elevated roadway."

The larger Ogre-Kin twin, his face half-scarred tissue, laughed—a wet, rattling sound. "So we're supposed to waltz up to three armored trucks and pop the locks? That's heat, Cole. Heavy heat."

"You get paid double if it goes smooth. Triple if it gets messy." I let my aura expand slightly, felt the temperature drop around us. Watched them all instinctively shift their weight, hands moving closer to concealed weapons. "I need you there because you're the best at this. Not because you're heroes."

Knife's partner, a Street-Elf called Ghost, tapped his Nextel pager. The chirp echoed off the brick walls. "We've run harder scores than this. But cartel armor?" He shook his head. "They don't negotiate. They don't warn. They just put bodies in piles."

"They'll be expecting muscle," I said. "Not precision. We move like surgeons, not butchers."

Grimjaw stepped forward, crossed his arms. His jacket strained across his shoulders. "What's your angle here, Cole? Why risk Syndicate retaliation? You building an empire or something?"

"Just evening odds." I watched steam rise from the grate again, thought about County General ER where I'd left that ambulance driver with a pulse but no answers. Thought about Newark Bay and the things crawling beneath its surface. "Syndicate's been running North Jersey tech monopoly since 2001. Time someone reminded them they can bleed."

The missing-ear Goblin cracked her knuckles. "Alright then. What time do we move?"

"2300 tonight. Sub-Station Seven rendezvous point. Come alone, come ready." I folded the schematic back up, tucked it inside my coat. "And leave your personal bullshit at home. This is business."

The group started dispersing, melting back into the neon-lit shadows between the buildings. Grimjaw stayed behind for a moment, studying me with those dark, intelligent eyes.

"You really think thermite charges will crack armored plating?" he asked quietly.

"I think desperation makes good soldiers." I turned toward the alley exit. "Be there or don't. Doesn't matter to me either way."

Behind me, I heard him chuckle—that deep, rumbling sound of someone who'd survived too much to be scared anymore. "Wouldn't miss it for the world, friend. Wouldn't miss it."

I stepped out onto the South Side street, the cold night air biting at my face. Above us, the Pulaski Skyway stretched like a concrete artery, carrying its secrets through winter darkness. Tomorrow would bring fire and thunder and bodies in piles.

But first, I had one more stop to make. One more piece to put in place before the world burned.

* * *

The Undercity tunnels reeked of ozone and diesel fumes, a toxic cocktail that burned my sinuses as I descended the rust-streaked stairs from Kearny Avenue. My boots echoed against wet concrete, each footfall bouncing back through the darkness like a countdown.

"Three blocks north," one of the Street-Elves muttered, her fingers dancing across a cracked PalmPilot. Blue light washed over her angular features, making her look half-mechanical herself. "Convoy hits the chokepoint at 2300 hours. Two modified cargo-haulers, armor plating, rear-mounted plasma cannons."

I didn't need to see the screen. I could feel it—the metallic tang of blood-iron magic coiling in my veins like a spring wound too tight. My breath formed white clouds in the frigid air, and where each mist touched the ground, frost spread in crystalline patterns. The metahumans around me shifted their weight, checking weapons, adjusting armor. They felt it too. That dead-silent chill that meant Cole Reyes was thinking about breaking things.

Grimjaw stood at the perimeter, his massive frame blocking what little light filtered down from street level. His pistol hung loose in one scarred hand, barrel pointed up toward the tunnel ceiling. "You're sure about this, Reyes?" He didn't look at me when he spoke. Just kept his eyes on the shadows. "We're talking Black-Circuit Syndicate. Not some street gang pushing synth."

"Yeah." My voice came out flat, emotionless. Like reading numbers off a clipboard. "I'm sure."

The Elf looked up from her device, her pupils dilated wide in the dimness. "Sir, the arithmetic still doesn't add up. We take the Necro-Thermite, we have leverage. But they'll hunt us. Every crew, every—"

"I know the math," I cut her off, stepping closer. The temperature dropped noticeably as I moved through the group. "We're not keeping it. We're hijacking it. Stashing it. Then we use it to force a sit-down with their broker."

A low growl rumbled from somewhere deep in Grimjaw's chest. "That's suicide. You can't negotiate with those people."

"Watch me."

One of the Ogre-Kin stepped forward, his bulk making the tunnel feel smaller. His respiratory system whistled with each breath—damaged lung tissue from years of factory work. "My cousin works County General ER. Saw your brother last week. Said the kid needs a tube change, might need surgery. That's gonna cost more than any of us make in five years."

He paused, looking down at me with eyes that held too much understanding.

"So why are we doing this again?"

My jaw tightened. The frost spread faster now, creeping across the walls like veins of ice. "Because my brother needs a breathing tube. Anyone who has a problem with that can walk away right now."

Silence. Thick and absolute except for the distant hum of subway trains passing overhead.

No one moved.

Grimjaw exhaled slowly, then racked the slide on his pistol. The sound echoed like a gunshot in the confined space. "Alright, boys. Let's go hijack a war."

The Elf's fingers flew across the PalmPilot screen. "Chokepoint is here." She turned the device toward me. A holographic map flickered to life, showing the transit tunnels beneath Newark Bay. A red line traced the convoy route, stopping where three tunnels converged under an old viaduct. "Single access point. Two exits. If they come in hot, we'll have maybe ninety seconds before reinforcements."

"I can work with ninety seconds," I said quietly.

What I didn't say was what I'd do if those ninety seconds weren't enough. What I didn't mention was how deep the frost could bite when my blood-iron magic really opened up. How bone became brittle as glass when it touched that cold.

They didn't need to know those details yet.

"Move out," Grimjaw barked. "Reyes takes point. Elves on overwatch. Everyone else stays low until we're on top of them."

We descended deeper into the darkness, our footfalls swallowed by the hungry blackness of the Undercity. My breath misted ahead of us all, a ghost leading ghosts toward something that felt less like hope and more like a promise made to someone who wouldn't live long enough to collect.

---

## CHAPTER 3: THE 405 CONVOY RAID

The rain hits different at night in Neon Hollow.

I feel it before I see it—that copper-tang in the back of my throat that means the blood-iron's waking up. Grimjaw leans against the concrete barrier beside me, his mechanical jaw clicking rhythmically as he chews on nothing but ambient radiation. We're sheltered from the worst of it here under the viaduct, but the temperature's still dropping fast enough to make my breath fog.

"Wind's shifting northeast," he rumbles, his voice like gravel scraped across pavement. "Gonna freeze solid within the hour."

I don't answer. My attention's locked on the I-405 on-ramp three hundred yards south, where two stolen '99 Crown Vics sit angled across both lanes like a steel choke chain. Their high beams punch through the freezing drizzle in parallel columns of white, illuminating nothing but rain and the black mouth of the tunnel beyond.

The Razor-Wire Street-Elves are ghosts above us—perched on those concrete support pillars like gargoyles made of light-bending tech and bad intentions. Their optical-camo jackets render them practically invisible unless you know exactly where to look, which means they're already dead if anyone spots them. That's how it works when you're playing for keeps.

My Nextel crackles. The voice coming through is Sharp-Eye, highest up on the northern pillar.

*"Three heavy trucks. Two escort sedans. They’re rolling right into the kill box, Cole."*

I key the mic once. Acknowledge received.

Grimjaw shifts his weight, servos whining softly in his shoulder joints. "You gonna do what you did last month? The County General thing?"

"The situation's different." I watch the southern entrance, counting seconds between raindrops. "This time we actually give a fuck about collateral damage."

That gets a low chuckle from him. "Never thought I'd hear you say that."

The sound reaches us before the lights do—that distinctive rumble of militarized suspensions hitting asphalt at highway speeds. Then the headlights appear around the bend, a wall of yellow-white that swallows the darkness whole. Three transport trucks, each one a mobile fortress painted matte black with running lights the color of infected wounds.

Behind them, two Lincoln Town Cars keeping pace like sharks.

"Here we go," I mutter, feeling the blood-iron surge hot along my spine. It wants out. Always does when there's violence in the air. I can taste copper and ozone, feel my pulse hammering against the inside of my skull.

The first truck hits our ambush zone.

For a heartbeat, nothing happens.

Then the Crown Vics explode.

Not with fire—with kinetic force. Shaped charges detonate simultaneously beneath both vehicles, lifting them six feet off the ground and slamming them back down hard enough to twist their frames into pretzel shapes across the lanes. The effect is instantaneous gridlock, three tons of steel garbage blocking every possible avenue of retreat.

Gunfire erupts from above. The Street-Elves open up on full-auto, rifle rounds sparking off armor plating as they target engines and tires. One escort sedan's front wheel blows apart in an explosion of rubber and steel. The other slews sideways, its driver fighting for control.

I step out from behind cover, Grimjaw moving to mirror position on my left flank.

The lead truck's driver has made the only logical choice—they're bailing. The rear doors burst open and men pour out, automatic weapons already shouldering toward our position. They're cartel muscle, augmented with cheap combat magik, their eyes glowing that sickly green that means necro-tainted.

"Now," I say.

My right hand clenches. The temperature drops twenty degrees in an instant as frost explodes outward from my palm—a wave of supercooled air that catches the rain mid-fall, transforming it into a blizzard of ice crystals sharp enough to cut skin. The effect is immediate chaos; visibility drops to zero within thirty yards as wind-driven sleet scours through everything.

Grimjaw doesn't hesitate. He surges forward through the whiteout, his massive frame barely slowing as he hits the first cartel soldier at full speed. The impact sounds like a car crash—bone meeting metal, wet and final. He's already moving to the next target before the first one finishes falling.

I spread both hands wide.

The blood-iron answers.

Ice erupts from the viaduct surface itself, frozen water javelins punching upward through asphalt and concrete alike. Three more cartel soldiers caught in the open go down hard, impaled by spears of crystalline violence that emerge from solid ground without warning or mercy.

Behind me, Sharp-Eye's voice cuts through the radio static: *"Truck's disabled! Rear doors open—something's coming out!"*

I spin, raising both hands toward the still-moving transport. The driver's trying to reverse, backing up over the wrecked sedan to clear an escape route. But they're too slow, and I've got angle.

"The hell you doing?" Grimjaw shouts over the gunfire.

I don't answer. Instead, I pull deep on the blood-iron magic—the kind of depth that makes my nose bleed and lights up every nerve ending until I'm vibrating with power. The air between my palms starts to shimmer, frost building in impossible geometric patterns as temperature plummets further.

When I throw, it's not just ice.

It's concentrated kinetic force crystallized into a spear the size of a telephone pole, pointed and lethal. It launches with a sound like thunder cracking, its trajectory perfect as it arcs across thirty yards and slams into the lead truck's engine block.

Metal screams. The radiator explodes outward in a geyser of steam and coolant. The entire vehicle lifts two feet off the ground before settling back down, completely dead, smoke pouring from beneath the hood.

"Jesus Christ," someone whispers over comms. Might be Sharp-Eye. Might be one of the Elves.

Grimjaw's already at the truck, ripping the rear doors fully open with his bare hands. Inside, surrounded by padding and restraints, is what we came for—a steel crate roughly four feet cubic, covered in warning labels written in half a dozen languages none of us can read but all recognize anyway.

Necro-Thermite. Enough to level a city block if handled wrong. Exactly what we need to breach Sub-Station Seven and get to those records before the Millennial Consortium burns them.

"The package is secure!" Grimjaw roars, hauling it free with both arms. "Moving to extraction point!"

I cover their retreat, maintaining the ice storm around our position while Sharp-Eye and his team lay down suppressing fire on any cartel survivors stupid enough to still be standing. Bodies are piling up in the freezing rain, blood mixing with sleet to create pink water running toward the drain grates.

Someone's screaming in Spanish, begging for mercy that won't come.

The violence here tonight will attract attention. Already I can feel the ripple through the ambient magik—someone's called down a Hunter, maybe more than one. We've got minutes, tops, before reinforcements arrive.

But we have what

* * *

The first shot rang out like a bell tolling in hell.

Copper tracers arced across my vision—three precise strikes that punctured the lead sedan's front tires simultaneously. The vehicle lurched, rubber screaming against asphalt as it veered sideways. That was my cue.

I stepped out from behind the concrete pillar, rain already soaking through my leather jacket. But I didn't feel the cold anymore, not when the frost-cobalt was singing in my veins. My breath came out white and crystalline, each exhalation hanging in the air like frozen prayers.

"Now," I whispered.

My hands slammed down on the wet pavement.

The shockwave that tore through my blood-iron magic wasn't something you saw coming. It just *was*—an explosion of cobalt winter that crystallized the very rain around us into razor-sharp sleet. The underpass transformed in an instant: asphalt became a battlefield of jagged ice, and every droplet suspended in the humid air turned to glinting needles.

The frost-veins spread outward from where my palms touched ground, racing beneath the transport trucks' undercarriages. I felt their metal frames resist for half a second before my hex-work seized them, freezing their axles solid in blocks of black-cobalt ice that cracked the pavement beneath. The sound was like a thousand wine glasses shattering at once.

Gunfire erupted from the cartel's remaining vehicles—a deafening cascade of automatic weapons fire that lit up the dark underpass like a strobe light show from hell. Bullets sparked off concrete, ricocheted off sheet metal, whined past my ears close enough to taste copper on my tongue.

But they couldn't hit what they couldn't see.

I moved through the sleet-storm like smoke, my boots barely touching the icy ground. Blood-iron sparks trailed in my wake—blue-black residue that sizzled when it struck the frost, sending up small clouds of acrid smoke. A shooter leaned out from behind a sedan door, AK-47 tracking toward where I'd been standing a heartbeat ago.

He never got the shot off.

My iron-gall hex punched into his chest faster than thought, freezing the blood in his veins mid-pump. His face went blank with shock, then his eyes rolled back white as he collapsed. The gun clattered against the ice.

"Push them back! Clear the payload!"

Grimjaw's roar split the night—not quite English, not quite Orcish, but pure street-fighting fury. He charged from the shadows like an enraged bull, wielding a ripped-off car door like it weighed nothing. The metal slammed into two goons who'd been trying to flank around to the transport trucks, sending them sprawling across the ice-slicked asphalt.

The ogre-kin following him was even more direct: twin shotgun blasts that turned the space between Grimjaw and the cartel shooters into a wall of buckshot. Men screamed. Bodies twisted. The wet crunch of bone and meat gave way beneath the punishment.

I didn't watch them work. They knew their job. My focus stayed locked on the transport trucks—their frozen axles groaning under the strain as the drivers tried desperately to free themselves. One had abandoned his vehicle entirely, stumbling out into the sleet-storm with his hands raised.

Bad move.

A cobalt spike erupted from the ice beneath his feet, punching through both boots and shins. He went down screaming, blood mixing with melt-water at his feet. The other driver kept trying, engine whining uselessly against the magical bindings holding him in place.

Three more cartel shooters emerged from behind cover, weapons up, fingers tightening on triggers. They were young—too young—and scared out of their minds. Their training hadn't prepared them for someone who made weather systems out of living frost.

My hex struck all three simultaneously: iron-gall needles that froze the air itself between us. Blood crystallized before it could flow. Lungs seized. Hearts stopped mid-beat. They dropped like puppets with cut strings, hitting the ice with the sickening softness of dead weight.

Grimjaw reached the lead transport truck first, using his stolen door-shield to batter aside another goon. His shotgun fired twice more—*BOOM-BOOM*—the blasts echoing in the enclosed space until they felt physical, like hammer blows against my ribs.

"Reyes! Rear truck's still active!" he bellowed over the gunfire.

I spun toward the second transport, already reaching for the frost-cobalt reserves burning in my chest. The remaining cartel members had learned enough to spread out, making themselves harder targets. Smart. Too late, but smart.

The underpass floor buckled where I directed my focus, ice-spikes erupting in a line that forced them to scatter or be impaled. One wasn't fast enough—I didn't have time to be gentle. My hex punched through his sternum like it was paper, freezing his heart solid in an instant.

The sleet-storm raged around us now, each frozen rain needle glinting cobalt in the flash of gunfire. Steam rose from the heat of discharged weapons meeting the magical cold. The whole scene painted in shades of blue and black, like we were fighting inside a bruise.

Behind me, metal shrieked as Grimjaw and the ogre-kin tore open the rear doors of the lead transport. Chains rattled. Something heavy shifted inside. They'd found it—the Necro-Thermite shipment, right where the intel promised.

I allowed myself half a second to glance back, watching them haul out the crates marked with skull-and-crossbones warnings. Then I was moving again, because two more shooters had crept around from behind the frozen trucks, trying to flank me while I watched my partners work.

They made it within ten feet before my blood-iron magic seized their legs, encasing them in blocks of ice that went up to their thighs. Their screams turned into choked gasps as frost began creeping up their torsos, inch by agonizing inch.

"Clear!" Grimjaw's voice carried over the remaining gunfire. "We're clear!"

The last cartel shooter—a lieutenant by his gold jewelry—made a desperate break for one of the intact sedans. He never reached it. A spike of pure frost-cobalt erupted beneath him, impaling him through the gut and pinning him spread-eagle against the underpass wall. His blood ran down the concrete, steaming where it touched the ice.

Silence fell except for the wind howling through the underpass and the crackle of our breathing.

I stood in the center of my kill-zone, chest heaving, frost still crystallizing on every surface around me. The sleet-storm began to fade as I released the hex-work, rain returning to its normal state—just water, just weather. Just winter in North Jersey.

Grimjaw walked up beside me, shotgun broken open and empty, smoke rising from the barrels. He spat blood onto the ice. "Christ, Reyes. You always gotta make such a fucking mess?"

I looked at the bodies scattered across the underpass floor—twelve cartel goons who wouldn't be getting up. Blood pooled

* * *

The shooting stops all at once.

One second there's muzzle flash and screams cutting through the sleet-storm I've made of this underpass. Next second—silence except for dripping water and the wet gasping of the dying. The rain keeps falling, but it's just rain now, running in rivers off the hoods of frozen cars that look like they've been locked in ice for years.

Grimjaw's already moving, claws retracted, those long fingers working over the electronic locks on the transport truck. Sparks fly when he bypasses them—the cartels don't bother with mag-security on their hauls, thinking they don't need to. Thinking wrong.

"Truck two," he grunts, not looking up from his work. "The other one's yours."

I wipe blood from my cheek. It freezes the moment it leaves my skin, little red crystals scattering in the wind. My left hand's shaking—not from fear, never from that—but from the iron-magic still singing through my veins. Too much output too fast, and now my body's paying the price with tremors.

The second truck's lock gives easier. I pry the doors open and the hydraulics hiss like angry snakes.

Inside: thirty crates stacked neat as corpses in a morgue. Each one stamped with military seals that have been scratched off, replaced with cartel insignias. Necro-Thermite. The good stuff. The kind that burns hot enough to melt through concrete and steel and the wards people use to keep things dead where they belong.

"This is going to cause problems," I mutter.

"Good." Grimjaw doesn't look up. "Problems mean money."

He's right about that.

I pull out the burner Nokia from my jacket pocket—cheap piece of shit, bought with cash from a bodega in Harrison three weeks ago. The screen lights up green, harsh and unnatural in the dim underpass. Rain patters against it.

There's a number burned into my memory from that Toughbook we lifted in Secaucus. A sequence of digits that leads somewhere important. Somewhere dangerous.

My thumb hovers over the call button for a long second.

Then I press it.

The phone rings once. Twice. Three times before it picks up, but there's no voice on the other end. Just static. Then synthesized speech, each word carefully articulated:

*"You have reached the Syndicate Broker's office. State your business."*

"I'm looking for the Syndicate Broker," I say, keeping my voice flat, controlled. My breath fogs in the cold air. "Tell him I'm sitting on thirty crates of cartel Necro-Thermite, and I want a face-to-face. Tonight."

Silence on the line except for that electronic breathing.

*"State your location and security status."*

"I-405 viaduct underpass, Neon Hollow. Security's... handled." I glance at the bodies scattered around us like discarded dolls. Grimjaw's already hauling the first crate down from its stack, muscles bunching beneath his vest. "We're secure."

More silence. Then: *"Bring one crate to the frequency den on 8th Street. Come alone. If you're lying about the quantity or the product, you're dead. If you bring backup, you're dead. You have ninety minutes."*

"You know who this is?" I ask.

Another pause. When the synthesized voice comes back, there's something almost like amusement in its tone: *"Everyone knows Cole Reyes eventually. The question is whether they meet you alive or dead."*

The line goes dead.

I lower the Nokia, staring at the dark screen. Around me, the underpass looks like a crime scene from hell—frozen cars, frozen blood, frozen bodies in various states of dismemberment. Grimjaw hefts his crate onto his shoulder with a grunt.

"Eight Street?" he asks.

"Yeah." I wipe more blood from my face. "Frequency den. We've got ninety minutes to get there and make this deal."

"And if it's a trap?"

I look at the remaining twenty-nine crates. Military-grade necromantic weapons. Enough to level half of Newark if someone wanted. Enough to start a war between the cartels and the Syndicate if we play this wrong.

"Then it's a good thing I don't die easy," I say.

Grimjaw snorts. "You sure about that? Saw you catch three rounds last month. Almost didn't make it."

"Almost being the operative word." I start toward truck two, where my crate waits. My left hand's still shaking, but I can control it now. Push through the pain, the fatigue. "Besides, what's life without a little risk?"

He doesn't answer. Just grabs his second crate and starts walking toward the exit ramp.

I follow, one crate under each arm, leaving behind a graveyard of men who made the mistake of thinking they could stop us.

---

## CHAPTER 4: THE BROKER'S BARGAIN

The tunnel reeks of standing water and worse things. I carry the crate on my shoulder like it weighs nothing—necessary weight for this meeting, and I know better than to show hesitation. Three hundred pounds of Necro-Thermite won't break me, even if what's in that crate could level half the undercity.

The water comes up past my ankles now. Winter 2003 has been kind to the floods, turning the lower sectors into something between sewer and swamp. My boots squelch against concrete worn smooth by decades of machinery and runoff. Somewhere ahead, red emergency lights pulse through the mist hanging close to the ground.

The door appears without warning—a massive slab of steel set into reinforced concrete, painted matte black except for where rust has started eating through at the corners. Two figures emerge from the shadows flanking it, both orcs, both built like linebackers but wearing tailored tactical suits that probably cost more than most people down here make in a year. They move with that unnatural precision that means augmented combat subroutines, their muscles rippling beneath fabric designed to look corporate rather than lethal.

"Cole Reyes," the one on the left says, voice flat as a spreadsheet. "You're early."

I don't answer. Early is never a crime when you're carrying enough explosive to paint the ceiling with the top floor. I shift the crate slightly, letting the movement speak for itself.

Both guards step forward. The one who spoke raises a hand scanner, running it over my torso while his partner does the same with mine. Their fingers are efficient, impersonal—checking for weapons, transponders, tracking bugs. Anything that might compromise the sanctity of this meeting.

"Sidearms only," the second guard mutters, taking my .45 and the backup piece from my ankle holster. They disappear into evidence pockets sewn inside their jackets.

"The Gnome wants the thermite first." First speaker again, gesturing toward a reinforced table set up ten feet away. "Set it down careful-like. He's watching."

Of course he's watching. The Broker doesn't trust anyone farther than his own reflection. I ease the crate onto the table, feeling the familiar vibration of its contents. Necro-Thermite isn't just explosive—it's hungry magic, designed to eat through magical wards and physical barriers alike. In the wrong hands, it could punch holes in reality itself. Which is precisely why the Black-Circuit Syndicate pays premium rates for deliveries like this.

The door groans open, hydraulic hinges hissing. Beyond it, light—the kind of harsh fluorescent glare that makes everything look diseased. A wave of heat washes out, carrying with it the sharp chemical tang of ozone and soldering iron rosin, underneath which runs something sweeter and more nauseating: stale coffee brewed too many times in an office machine that hasn't been cleaned since 2001.

I step through without invitation or hesitation.

* * *

I stepped through the iris-valve into the Den's heart, my breath fogging in air that tasted like ozone and burnt coffee. The space opened up around me—all brushed steel and humming server racks, their LED status lights painting everything in cold blues and greens. My coat was still damp from the rain above, water dripping onto the industrial flooring.

Behind a desk that could've held a Cessna 172 sat the Gnome.

He didn't look up when I entered. His hands were moving across three keyboards simultaneously, fingers dancing over the keys with the kind of muscle memory that comes from decades of typing. Where his eyes should have been, there were these arcane-cybernetic things—chrome and circuit-board, glowing faintly purple at the edges. They clicked and whirred mechanically as they tracked something only he could see.

"Cole Reyes," he said without looking up. Voice like gravel in a cement mixer, accent pure Secaucus. "You're late by seven minutes. I clock everything."

I set the crate down with more force than necessary. It thudded against the desktop, scattering papers. "The Pulaski was backed up. Some jackass flipped his Beemer."

Those mechanical eyes swiveled toward me—*click-whirr-click*—focusing with audible precision. "Excuses are for people who can't deliver. You delivered. That's why you're here instead of floating face-down in the Bay." His hands never stopped moving. "Open it."

I popped the latches on the crate. The Necro-Thermite inside gleamed dully under the overhead fluorescents, its crystalline structure catching the light like black ice.

The Gnome reached out, not toward the thermite but toward some piece of equipment mounted on an articulated arm beside him. A scanner, all brass and crystal lenses that looked older than any tech had a right to be. He ran it over the open crate, those optical implants zooming in close—*whirrr-click*—then pulling back.

"*Mmph.*" He made this sound in the back of his throat. "Genuine shit. Not diluted, not cut. You actually came through, kid."

"I always come through."

"Yeah? Then we'll see." Those clicking eyes fixed on me again. "Thirty crates of military-grade thermite. Enough to level half of Sterling Manor if someone's stupid enough to use it all at once. But you know what else it's good for?" He didn't wait for me to answer. "It's leverage. Big-time leverage with the Inner Council."

My frost-cobalt magic stirred beneath my skin. I could feel it sloshing against the suppression runes tattooed up my forearms, angry and impatient. The temperature around the server racks dropped perceptibly. Frost began creeping along their edges, crystallization spreading across metal casings.

The Gnome noticed. Of course he did. "Easy there, hotshot. Your little weather trick isn't going to impress anyone down here except maybe the rats."

I forced myself to breathe slow, measured. The frost receded, though it left behind these delicate patterns of ice that caught the green light from the servers.

"You wanted the thermite," I said. "Here it is. Now give me the Compressor."

His hands stopped typing. Just... stopped. In the sudden silence, I could hear the hum of the servers, the distant drip of condensation, the mechanical breathing of his ocular implants as they tracked my position.

"Telluric Core Compressor." He said it like he was tasting the words. "That's Inner Council tech, Reyes. Not something you walk away with for a few hundred pounds of explosives, no matter how exotic."

"They're not just explosives. They're *Necro-Thermite.*"

"And?" He leaned back in his chair—it groaned under his weight despite being reinforced steel. "Money doesn't buy what you're asking for. Favor doesn't buy it. Thirty crates of premium black-market military equipment? That's a good start. But the Telluric Core Compressor?"

He stood up then. Even sitting he'd been big, but standing he towered—easily seven feet, broad-shouldered despite the stereotypical gnomish stockiness. His eyes clicked and whirred as they swept over me, cataloging, calculating.

"The Council wants a leash on that frost-cobalt trick of yours," he finished. "They want someone who can punch through reality itself on their payroll. Someone with your particular talent doesn't just get handouts. You *earn* access to the deep-tech. By proving you're worth keeping around."

The air between us felt charged. My magic was doing more than simmering now—it was boiling against the suppression runes, frost spreading across the floor in radiating patterns from where I stood. The server racks were starting to ice over proper, condensation freezing solid.

I could take him. Could freeze this whole room solid, crack every piece of machinery in here like kindling. Could probably walk out with whatever I wanted once he stopped breathing.

But there would be consequences. Always consequences. The Syndicate had eyes everywhere in North Jersey. Kill one Broker, three more would come looking. And they wouldn't send just muscle next time.

"So what's the offer?" My voice came out flat, controlled.

* * *

The Gnome doesn't smile when I step into his den. He never does. His face is all sharp angles and older scars, the kind that don't heal clean under this city's sky. Around us, servers hum like dying bees, their LED lights painting everything in sickly blues and greens.

"You brought the kid," he says. It's not a question.

I glance behind me. Danny's slumped against the doorway, iron-lungs wheezing something that might be "Dad." The sound cuts deeper than any blade. His skin has gone gray, translucent over the blue-black veins spreading from his chest. The compressor he needs—*needs*—sits in the Gnome's medical bay, wrapped in sterile plastic and promises I can't afford.

"Fair trade," I tell him. My frost-cobalt magic coils low in my gut, suppressed but aware. It tastes the place, doesn't like it. Ice crystals spread across the server rack behind the Gnome, spider-webbing down the metal casing. He watches it with flat, patient eyes.

"The compressor will buy your son maybe six months," he says, pulling a blueprint from somewhere in his coat. The paper lands on his desk with a soft thump. "Six months if our surgeons install it right. Six months while you work for me."

I look at the blueprint. It's a Geas Coil, Lead-Bismuth construction. Jagged. Ugly as sin. The kind of arcane hardware they forge in Sub-Station Seven, where the Syndicate keeps their real surgeons—the ones who know how to cut through bone and nerve without killing you.

"A Lethal Myocardial," the Gnome continues. "We'll fuse it directly into your sternum. Break my rules, try to run, and it detonates your heart. Clean. Quiet. Final."

The temperature drops another few degrees. Frost creeps along the edge of his desk.

"I'll be your premier heavy-breacher," I say. Not asking. Telling.

He nods slowly, like he expected this. Like he counted on it. "You'll do what I need done. Wetwork. Breaches. Whatever comes up." He taps the blueprint with one finger. "You belong to us until you're in the ground, Reyes. There's no walking away from this."

I think about Danny's last breath. How thin it sounds now. How much thinner it'll sound tomorrow.

"Where's the operating table?"

---

## CHAPTER 5: THE STERNUM GEAS OPERATION

The fluorescent lights overhead hummed like dying insects, casting everything in that sickly blue-white that made skin look like old hospital sheets. I stood in the middle of the prep room—nothing but tiles, stainless steel, and the smell of antiseptic that couldn't quite cover the metallic tang of blood underneath.

My fingers found the top button of my work shirt. Pop. Second button. Third. The fabric fell away from my shoulders, pooling around my boots. In the full-length mirror mounted on the wall, I caught sight of myself—ribs prominent against pale skin, the old scars looking like raised silver rivers across my torso. I looked like something dug up from the Kearny Marshes after a long winter.

The Nextel in my hand felt heavy as a brick. I pressed send, watching the screen light up with its green glow before the speakerphone crackled to life with static.

"Yeah," came Grimjaw's voice, rough as sandpaper dragged across bone. "Cole?"

"Got ten minutes before they take me in," I said, staring at my reflection. My voice sounded flat, distant—not even my own anymore. Just echoes bouncing off cold surfaces. "You listening?"

"Christ, Cole. You sure about this? 'Cause once you're under their knife, there's no—"

"I'm sure." I interrupted. No point in dancing around it. We both knew what was happening here. What I was trading for Danny's next breath. "The remaining crates are under the old Pulaski overpass. Section seven, third support beam from the east end."

Silence stretched out except for the hiss of static.

"Grimjaw."
