He gestures toward the vault with his free hand, an almost elegant motion considering I'm holding him hostage with a .45 pressed to his brainstem. "...you can accept what you've done was necessary. Accept that some lives are worth more than others. Accept your place as the hero this city needs."

My lungs wheeze, each breath a struggle past smoke-damaged tissue. The static in my blood is screaming—the ghost-chorus of three hundred fourteen voices, all demanding justice, all accusing me of murder, all begging for release from the nightmare I've made real.

But underneath it all, buried beneath guilt and horror and exhaustion, something else stirs. Something cold and calculating that looks at those thirty seconds ticking away and does the math:

If I kill Morvain, Voss will draw on me. I'll take one with me, maybe both if I'm lucky, but the vault stays locked. Thirty-eight children dead because I couldn't control my rage.

Or...

I lower the gun fractionally—not enough that he could escape, but enough to show I'm listening.

"What's the catch?" My voice is barely audible, raw flesh of throat scraped with every syllable. "There's always a catch."

Morvain's smile widens. "Smart girl. The vault code—it requires biometric authorization from two senior commanders simultaneously. Me, and..." His eyes flick to something behind me. "Her."

I turn just enough to see her stepping out from behind the tactical display—a woman in BATC tactical gear, sidearm already drawn and aimed at my head. Dark hair pulled back tight, eyes cold and professional, badge gleaming under the suite's fluorescent lights.

"Commander Elena Rodriguez," she introduces herself, voice steady as rock. "Tactical Response Unit. You're under arrest for the murder of three hundred fourteen civilians at Sub-Station Seven. Drop your weapon."

The trap springs shut around me—thirty seconds to decide whether I die a martyr or live a monster.

Behind me, the timer keeps counting down: `00:28`

`00:27`

`00:26`

* * *

The gun trembles in my hand. My finger rests on the trigger guard—not the trigger itself—I can feel the weight distribution, the cold steel pressed against Morvain's temple. His skin is clammy under the barrel. I've done this before. Twenty-three times. Each one burned into my memory like acid scarring the back of my skull.

But those were clean kills. Necessary evils.

This isn't that.

"Vance," Morvain says, his voice disturbingly calm despite having a .45 caliber pistol aimed at his brainstem. He gestures with his eyes toward the monitors behind him. "You need to see this."

I don't move the gun. "Talk."

He smiles—that same predatory smile he had when he was torturing the techs downstairs. "The yellow tanks. You saw them in the vault. Did you think they were just holding water? Antifreeze?"

My jaw tightens. Behind me, through the glass walls of the Directors' Suite, Newark sprawls in its infinite ugliness—eight million people going about their lives, oblivious to whatever fresh hell has hatched in their midst.

"The children," Voss interjects from somewhere above us, his holographic presence flickering between irritation and amusement. *"Don't worry your pretty little head about it, Vance. They're perfectly safe as long as you're a good girl."*

"Shut up," I snarl without looking away from Morvain.

He chuckles. "As you wish. But you should listen." He nods toward a control panel to his left—a setup I hadn't noticed in the periphery. "Go ahead and look. The switches aren't armed yet."

Against every instinct screaming at me to keep the weapon trained on him, I glance over. There are twelve red LED switches, each labeled with numbers: 1-12. Below them, a digital display reads `00:31... 00:30...`

"What is this?" My voice comes out harder than I intend.

"The Liquid Isfet," Morvain says simply. "Do you know what that is, Commander?"

I do. Every Aegis operative gets briefed on it during their first week. Ancient Egyptian mythology—the concept of chaos made manifest, given physical form. The Sumerian term for "that which causes disorder." In the modern era, the BATC's R&D division weaponized it into a nerve agent so potent that contact with skin causes systemic neural collapse within thirty seconds.

It liquefies the nervous system from the inside out.

"Thirty-one seconds," Morvain continues, watching my face. "That's how much time you have to decide whether those thirty-eight children in Vault Seven live or die. The moment your heart stops beating—"

"I'm not dead."

"—the PalmPilot resets automatically. Or if you pull that trigger..." His eyes flick down to the gun. "...and the biometric reader in this room detects your elevated adrenaline signature, the valves open. Or if you don't press this button every twelve hours." He taps one finger against a screen I can't see. *"Every twelve hours, Vance. Tick-tock."*

`00:27... 00:26...`

I force myself to look at the monitors behind him. There they are—the children. Pressing their small hands against the glass of Vault Seven. Some crying, some staring blankly, others looking directly at me with expressions of mute terror and hope.

"Twenty-six seconds now," Voss purrs. "Tick-tock, Commander. What's it going to be? Your principles? Or thirty-eight innocent lives?"

Morvain leans back in his chair, completely unbothered by the gun pointed at his head. "Here's what happens next, Mara. You're going to put down the gun. You're going to step over here and let me place this collar around your neck. It contains a dead-man's switch linked to the vault's ventilation system. If your pulse drops below sixty, if you try to remove it, if you do anything other than exactly what we tell you..."

He doesn't need to finish.

`00:23... 00:22...`

"The rat, Morvain."

He blinks. "Excuse me?"

"You have a lab rat on that desk. Show me what this shit does."

A flash of something—respect? amusement?—crosses his features. He reaches slowly into a containment tube beside him, pulling out a clear plastic cylinder about six inches long. Inside is a brown lab rat, twitching nervously.

"This little fellow?" Morvain opens a valve I can't see from my angle. A fine mist sprays into the chamber for half a second.

The rat's reaction is immediate and horrifying. Its body convulses violently, limbs splaying outward as if struck by lightning. Foam bubbles from its mouth—not white foam but something dark, viscous. Black sludge oozes from its nostrils and eyes like crying oil. The creature lets out a sound halfway between a shriek and a death rattle before collapsing into itself, its spine contorting at an impossible angle.

Dead. Thirt

* * *

The timer hits `00:05`.

**Five seconds.**

My finger trembles on the trigger guard. The metal is slick with sweat, my palm burning where it presses against the polymer frame of the MP5. Through the scope of my peripheral vision, I can see the red numbers marching backward with the cold finality of a tombstone inscription.

`00:04`

The ash-gray static reaches a new peak inside my skull—a sustained, agonizing scream that drowns out thought, drowns out reason, drowns out everything except the image of 314 bodies cooking from the inside out. My own blood feels like it's boiling in my veins, mimicking the horror I just unleashed.

`00:03`

I'm still looking through the sights, Morvain's head filling my vision, his smile unwavering even as death counts down. But something else pulls at my gaze—the glass partition behind him, and beyond that, the crowd of Orckind refugees packed into the observation deck.

A little girl.

She can't be more than six years old, her green skin almost luminescent against the dark glass. Her yellow eyes are wide, brimming with tears that catch the emergency lighting. She's pressing both small hands against the barrier, her mouth forming words I can't hear but can read clearly:

*"Please."*

`00:02`

The sound cuts through everything—my finger spasms, jerking away from the trigger as if burned. The gun lurches in my grip, and before I know what I'm doing, I'm throwing it.

It clatters across the marble floor with a sound like a church bell tolling doom. The MP5 spins once, twice, then lies there in the silence, its magazine full, its job unfinished.

My legs give out.

I collapse to my knees on the cold marble, feeling each sharp point through my kneepads. My back screams—that wounded, broken thing where Morvain's fire had torn through me—twisting like it wants to split open completely. Hot tears stream down my face, cutting tracks through the soot and ash coating my cheeks.

"God," I whisper, or maybe scream, "god, god, *god*—"

The timer hits `00:01`.

Then stops.

The sudden silence is worse than any sound—a vacuum that sucks all the air from my lungs, all the strength from my bones. Morvain rises smoothly from his chair, brushing imaginary dust from his charcoal suit jacket, that infuriating smile still playing at the corners of his mouth.

"You've made your choice, Commander." His voice is conversational, like we're discussing the weather over coffee rather than the fate of 314 souls and the future of two species. "The clock has stopped. The children live."

I can't look at him. Can't lift my head from staring at the intricate marble pattern beneath my palms—the veins of gray and white stone forming shapes that blur together into meaningless abstraction.

"What do you want?" The words come out hoarse, broken glass in my throat.

Morvain circles around me with the measured steps of a predator inspecting prey. "Want? Oh, Mara. I want everything I've already asked for. Your verbal compliance was... theatrical. Beautiful, really. But insufficient."

He crouches down, bringing his face level with mine. I catch the scent of expensive cologne mixed with cigarette smoke and something else—something ancient and wrong that makes my teeth ache.

"Verbal promises are wind," he continues, reaching out to tilt my chin up with one finger. His touch is cold despite the warmth radiating from his core. "But biological certainty? That's bone-deep. Irrevocable."

My stomach drops. "No."

"Yes." He stands again, straightening his tie with precise movements. "You will submit to the Geas, Mara Vance. Not as an Aegis Commander. Not as humanity's champion. You'll submit as what you are now—a wounded thing who chose mercy over vengeance when it mattered most. Who *failed* when tested."

The word 'failed' lands like a punch to the solar plexus.

"I'm not going to kill those children," I manage through clenched teeth.

"No, you're not." Morvain gestures toward the vault entrance where four heavily armed guards have appeared, their weapons trained on me. They move forward with coordinated precision, boots heavy on marble. "Instead, you're going to guarantee they live by guaranteeing your own absolute obedience. Come quietly, or we can discuss alternative methods of motivation."

One guard grabs my upper arm, fingers digging into muscle already screaming in agony. Another takes my other side, hauling me upward despite my resistance. My knees buckle, but they don't let me fall—not completely. Just enough to make every movement a fresh wave of pain shooting through my back, my shoulders, my ruined lungs.

"We're taking her to Sub-Level Three," Morvain announces, adjusting his cufflinks as if this were just another day at the office. "Surgical bay is prepped. Dr. Chen has been waiting. The procedure should take approximately six hours."

Six hours.

My mind reels at the implications—what he means by 'procedure,' what the Geas really entails when imposed surgically rather than through ritual consent. But beneath that clinical fear runs something deeper: shame.

I'd held the gun. Had 314 seconds to pull the trigger. Could have ended this, could have stopped him, could have saved myself from whatever comes next.

And I chose otherwise.

The little Orc girl's face flashes behind my eyes—that desperate plea against the glass—and I know I'd make the same choice again. Every time. No matter how much it costs.

That's the real failure.

They drag me toward the vault door, away from the observation deck where those children still huddle, alive because I couldn't kill their captor. The marble floor blurs under my feet as consciousness starts to fray at the edges.

"Mara Vance," Morvain calls after me, his voice echoing off the vault walls, "you were the Breach's finest weapon. Tonight, you become its most loyal servant." A pause, then: "Welcome to your new purpose."

---

## CHAPTER 13: THE LEAD-BISMUTH MYOCARDIAL GEAS

The first thing I register is the smell—antiseptic and burned meat, the latter coming from my own body. My armor has fused with my skin in places where the heat was greatest. The medics work with clinical detachment, peeling away synthetic fabric that has become one with my flesh.

"Hold still," someone says. Not asking. Commanding.

I want to tell them it doesn't matter if I hold still or not. I've already lost.

They strap me to the steel table, cold metal against my back. The restraints are unnecessary—I haven't tried to move since they brought me here. What's the point? The Geas is inevitable now. Morvain made sure of that when he signed the authorization forms.

Through the observation glass, I can see him standing there, arms crossed, watching like this is some kind of performance piece. His expression is unreadable. Satisfied, maybe. He got what he wanted—my compliance, my surrender.

The young Dwarf comes in next. Torin Kaelen, his ID badge reads. "Torque," according to the crude tattoo on his forearm. He looks barely out of his twenties, face pale beneath his copper-red beard. His eyes widen when he sees me, recognition flickering across his features even as he tries to maintain professional distance.

He's seen the briefings about Aegis Squad. Knows who I am.

"Calibrate the bismuth-drip, Dwarf," a medic snaps at him, gesturing toward the Panasonic Toughbook wired into the surgical rig. "We need the rune-matrix stable before Dr. Halcyon opens her chest."

Torque's hands shake as he adjusts the dials. He mutters something under his breath in Dwarvish—a prayer, maybe, or a curse. Probably both.

Our eyes meet.

There's revulsion in his gaze. Disgust at what's being done to someone who used to be a hero. But also pity. And something else—recognition that he's powerless to stop it. Just another cog in the corporate machine, following orders because refusing means losing everything.

I offer him nothing. No plea for help that would only make things worse for him. No angry accusation that would waste the energy. Just steady eye contact, acknowledging what we both know: this is happening, and neither of us can change it.

He looks away first, focusing on the screen with desperate intensity, fingers flying over the keyboard as he runs diagnostics on the arcane machinery integrated into my life support systems.

The surgical halogens burn overhead. Every surface reflects their harsh glare—the polished steel instruments laid out on sterile trays, the chrome components of the Telluric generators embedded in the walls, the observation glass where Morvain stands watching like a god overseeing sacrifice.

My heartbeat pulses through me, each beat accompanied by that maddening ash-gray static that started after the Geas was imposed. It's stronger now, anticipatory, waiting for whatever violation comes next.

Dr. Halcyon enters, and I feel my stomach clench despite the anesthetics they've pumped into me. She carries something mechanical and intricate—a silver apparatus etched with runes that writhe in my arcano-sensory perception. The Lead-Bismuth kill-switch, designed to shut down the magical circuits of any metahuman body, to sever the connection between flesh and essence so thoroughly that recovery becomes impossible.

She places it carefully on an instrument tray, then approaches the table where I'm restrained. Her expression is professionally neutral, but there's curiosity in her eyes. Eager interest in what she's about to do.

"Ready to begin," she announces to the room at large, though her gaze settles on Torque. "Is the rune-matrix stable?"

Torque swallows hard, checks his readouts twice. "Stable. But Commander Vance's vital signs are spiking. The bismuth-drip is affecting her cardiovascular system."

"Expected side effect," Halcyon says dismissively. She picks up a scalpel from the tray. "We'll compensate during the procedure."

The blade glints under the halogens as she brings it toward my chest.

* * *

The leather strap tears at the corners of my mouth as I bite down hard enough to feel teeth crack. My body knows what's coming before my mind can fully process it—the arcano-sensory static screaming warnings through every nerve ending.

"Hold still, Commander," Dr. Halcyon says. His voice carries that infuriatingly calm edge, like he's performing routine surgery instead of violating the most sacred boundaries of my being. "This will be... uncomfortable."

The high-pitched whine starts before I see it—a bone saw, its blade glowing faintly with suppressing runes. The smell hits me first: sterile antiseptic masking something older, something metallic and wrong. Blood? No. Something heavier.

My hands are strapped to the operating table. Good. Because I'd kill him if they weren't.

"We're going through the sternum," Halcyon continues, adjusting his glasses with one gloved hand while the other positions the saw against my chest. Right above where my heart should be pounding—it is, actually, hammering so hard I can hear it in my ears, feel it trying to beat its way out of this violation. "Can't risk damaging the pulmonary pathway. Need clean access to the myocardium."

The saw touches skin.

I scream into the leather, but it doesn't help. Nothing could help. The whine builds to an unbearable pitch, and then—

CRUNCH.

Bone gives way like ice breaking on a frozen lake. A sound no human anatomy should ever make. The sensation travels straight through my chest cavity, radiating up my spine, down my arms. My white-lilac magic flares instinctively, defensive wards erupting from my subconscious—

—and immediately dying as something cold and viscous floods my veins.

"Increase the bismuth flow," Halcyon commands. He's already working, surgical instruments making wet sounds against exposed cartilage. "The ward is resisting."

Torque's voice cuts through the haze: "She's burning up from the inside! The static is overriding the matrix!"

The lead-bismuth slithers through my bloodstream like liquid metal, tainting everything it touches. Where it meets my natural magic, there's a chemical reaction—burning, choking, *smothering*. My arcano-sensory perception goes haywire, showing me things I shouldn't see: my own blood vessels turning dark gray, clot by clot forming around the toxic agent.

Halcyon doesn't slow down. His fingers are impossibly steady as he spreads my sternum apart—a sickening crackling sound as bone and tissue separate. Cool air hits surfaces that have never known open atmosphere.

"Heart rate spiking," someone notes. Might be Halcyon himself. Everything's blurring together—the medical bay lights overhead spinning slowly, the smell of burnt copper mixing with antiseptic, Torque's sweating face appearing in my peripheral vision before disappearing again.

Then I feel the probe.

Something cold and metallic pressing directly against my heart muscle. The silver kill-switch, still disconnected but so close I can sense its potential to stop me dead. My body convulses against the restraints, leather straps creaking.

"Easy now." Halcyon's hand presses my shoulder down—not roughly, but firm enough that I understand this isn't negotiation. "Almost done."

The wires come next.

They're woven from something between physical and metaphysical—arcane conduits designed to piggyback on my natural magical pathways. As they touch my flesh, they sizzle. Blue-black residue burns where they make contact, iron-gall scent filling my nostrils. The same stuff that bleeds from corrupted ley-lines when reality itself gets infected.

This is what they're doing to me. Corrupting me from the inside out.

"Torque!" Halcyon barks. "Now!"

More lead-bismuth floods my system in a massive wave. It hits like a fist to the chest—every breath suddenly impossible, lungs burning, vision going white at the edges. My white-lilac magic surges one last time in desperate defense, trying to purge the poison, trying to seal the wounds—

—and dies as the ash-gray static of my trauma overwhelms it.

All those years of training. All that control. Gone in an instant, choked out by heavy metal and dark energy.

The wires drill into my myocardium. Each insertion feels like being stabbed with red-hot needles made of broken glass and bad memories. They burrow deep, seeking connection points, weaving themselves into the very structure of how my magic flows through my body.

And beneath it all, barely audible over the pounding of blood in my ears: Click.

A mechanical sound. Final and absolute.

The silver kill-switch locks into place.

My eyes roll back. Vision tunnels to black for three eternal seconds as a jolt of dark energy—raw, unfiltered, wrong—stops my heart mid-beat.

I'm dying. Again.

For the second time tonight, I die while fully conscious.

Three seconds pass like three hours.

Then my heart lurches back to life with a painful thud, sending shockwaves of agony through every nerve.

* * *

I woke to the smell of ozone and antiseptic, my throat raw like I'd swallowed ground glass. Everything felt wrong—heavy, distant, like I was watching someone else try to remember how breathing worked.

My chest.

The moment I tried to draw a full breath, I felt it: a dull, crushing weight just behind my sternum, like someone had placed their fist against my heart and was pushing inward. Not pain, exactly. More like... presence. A constant reminder that something foreign now lived inside me.

I blinked against the harsh fluorescent lights above, trying to orient myself. Medical bay. Sub-level. The BATC facility beneath Newark Bay. My fingers twitched against crisp white sheets, feeling the raised ridge of fresh sutures along my left hand—the one where they'd taken the blood sample.

Then I saw him.

Morvain stood near the foot of my bed, hands clasped behind his back in that unnaturally still way he had. His dark suit was immaculate despite everything that had happened—the collapse, the breach, the slaughter at County General. He looked like he'd stepped out of a boardroom meeting rather than from a battlefield.

"Commander Vance," he said without looking at me. "You've been unconscious for nearly four hours. Dr. Yatsushiro performed the procedure successfully."

"The children." My voice came out hoarse, broken. I tried to sit up but my body didn't respond properly, muscles sluggish from whatever cocktail of drugs they'd pumped into me.

"They're alive." Morvain's tone was flat, matter-of-fact. "Sedated. Stabilized. But their condition remains critical until you fulfill your obligations."

He moved then, pulling something from his pocket. A small silver fob, no larger than a pack of cigarettes. It gleamed under the lights, innocuous-looking. Harmless.

My arcano-senses screamed otherwise.

That ash-gray static that had been pulsing in time with my heartbeat suddenly *coiled*, tightening around something deep in my chest. I felt the pressure change—felt the new weight shift and constrict.

"What did you do to me?" The question tasted like copper and fear.

Morvain smiled—not quite reaching his eyes. "A necessary precaution. You see, Commander, the lead-bismuth alloy we used to seal your myocardium has some... interesting properties." He pressed a button on the fob.

The world went white.

I couldn't breathe. Couldn't move. Couldn't even scream as my lungs seized, as that crushing weight exploded into agony, as my heart hammered against its metallic cage trying to beat, trying to pump, finding itself suddenly strangled by invisible hands.

Time stretched and compressed simultaneously. I felt every second of those three—maybe four?—interminable seconds where death hovered just beyond reach, held at bay only by whatever black magic sustained this Geas.

Then he released it.

I gasped, coughed, nearly vomited as air rushed back into my burning lungs. Black specks danced across my vision. My heart monitor—that sterile electronic beep—sounded suddenly frantic, syncing perfectly with the rhythmic pulse of the silver fob in Morvain's hand.

"As you can see," he continued conversationally, as if he hadn't just stopped my heart, "your life now depends entirely on my good will. And the lives of thirty-eight children depend on yours."

He stepped closer, leaning over me so I could smell the faint scent of tobacco and expensive cologne. His eyes were cold, calculating.

"You have a press conference tomorrow morning. Nine AM sharp. Channel 7 news. You will smile for the cameras, Commander. You will accept the Medal of Valor they've prepared for you. You will talk about heroism and sacrifice and how the BATC saved Newark from an unspeakable horror."

His grip tightened on the fob, and I felt the pressure increase just slightly—a warning shot.

"And you will never, *ever* look me in the eye with anything resembling disrespect again. Do we understand each other?"

My mouth was dry. The metallic taste of bismuth coated my tongue—blood or residue from whatever procedure they'd performed, I couldn't tell anymore. Couldn't think past the weight crushing my chest, the knowledge of what that small device in his hand could do at any moment.

"I understand," I whispered.

Morvain straightened, tucking the fob back into his pocket. That simple motion made me flinch—made every muscle in my body tense anticipating another activation.

"Good." He turned toward the door, then paused. "Oh, one more thing, Commander. Try not to think too hard about those children in the containment ward. Dr. Yatsushiro has them on a slow drip of lead-therapeutic solution. Very effective. Very... permanent. If your cooperation falters for even a moment..."

He didn't need to finish. The implication hung in the air like smoke.

The door hissed shut behind him, leaving me alone with the sterile beep of the heart monitor and the suffocating weight in my chest.

I stared at the ceiling tiles above me, feeling a single tear cut through the soot still clinging to my face. The ash-gray static that had been pulsing, watching, waiting—it settled deeper now. Not just in my head anymore but wrapping around my soul like chains.

This wasn't recovery. This was ownership.

And as I lay there helpless, possessed by a Geas that bound my very heartbeat to BATC's whims, I understood exactly what Morvain meant when he said I belonged to them now.

The leash had snapped taut.

And I was going to dance on its end until they decided to break me completely.

---

## CHAPTER 14: THE MEDAL OF VALOR

The sodium-vapor lamps transform Neon Hollow Plaza into something resembling a surgical theater—all harsh white light and impossible shadows. I stand behind the podium in my dress uniform, the heavy wool scratchy against the burn scars that snake up my neck like black rivers on pale skin. My hands rest on the polished wood, and even through the glove material, I can feel the phantom ache where my flesh bubbled and healed wrong.

"Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for being here."

My voice sounds like it belongs to someone else. Someone who never spent three weeks in County General's ER watching doctors stitch me back together while Morvain whispered promises in my ear about what happens next. The teleprompter scrolls past my vision in cold green letters.

Mayor Castellano stands beside me, his politician's smile locked in place. Director Voss looms on my other side, his presence oppressive as a thunderhead. Between them, they've built their narrative—a story so clean it could be stamped and sterilized. Aegis Commander Mara Vance, hero of the hour, vanquisher of terrorists, savior of children.

It's all true. Just not in the way they mean.

"The incident at Sub-Station Seven tested us," I read, each word measured, deadpan. "But the spirit of Newark Bay—that unbreakable will—prevailed."

Camera flashes erupt like lightning strikes. Each burst burns itself into my retinas, white-hot afterimages swimming in the periphery. Somewhere in the crowd, a Gnome reporter from the *Tribune* shouts over the din: *"Commander Vance! What was going through your mind when you shielded those kids from the blast?"*

I turn toward him, slow and deliberate. Behind him, I can see the massive LED billboards advertising Sterling Manor's luxury condos. Beautiful people with perfect teeth, living perfect lives in a city that never burns or bleeds or breaks.

"I was just... doing my duty for the city."

The lie tastes like copper and ash. Voss's hand comes down on my shoulder, firm enough to feel through the uniform jacket. His grin widens. *"Brave words, Commander. Truly brave."*

They don't know about the Geas nestled behind my sternum. Don't know how its weight drags at my ribs every time I breathe, or how Morvain's consciousness presses against mine like a thumb on a fresh bruise. They think this medal—gold and heavy as a coffin nail—means something. That it represents victory instead of compromise.

*Smile wider,* the Geas whispers. A sharp twinge of warning, like swallowing broken glass.

So I do. My cheeks ache from the effort.

The Mayor steps forward now, producing the Medal of Valor from a velvet box. The gold gleams obscenely under the sodium lamps—a symbol of everything I've lost and everything I've become. He pins it to my chest, right above where Morvain made his home inside me.

"For valor above and beyond," Castellano intones. "For service that will never be forgotten."

I want to laugh. Want to tell them all what really happened three weeks ago in Sub-Station Seven. How I made a deal with something older than Newark Bay itself. How 38 children survived because their deaths bought me leverage I didn't even need. How 314 others died anyway, casualties in a war nobody in this crowd can even begin to comprehend.

But I don't. Because that would be madness. Because Mara Vance—the real one, the one who still had her magic before Morvain stole it—is already dead.

The press erupts again. Camera flashes. Questions shouted over each other. Someone asks if I'm recovering well from my injuries. Another wants to know my plans for the future of BATC security protocols.

"Yes," I answer the first. "Yes," I answer the second.

Lies. Clean and simple and devastatingly effective.

Behind the podium, I catch sight of Morvain standing in the shadows near the plaza's edge. He doesn't smile. Just watches me accept my reward with eyes that remember what I was before. What I could have been if I'd let those children die instead.

*You're doing fine,* he mouths silently across the distance.

And somehow, despite everything, I believe him.

* * *

The elevator doors hiss shut behind me, sealing me into sterile white light and recycled air. My hand trembles as I press the button for the penthouse floor—level twenty-three—and the mechanism lurches upward with mechanical smoothness that feels obscene after three weeks of County General's grinding elevators and the acrid stench of antiseptic.

The uniform jacket feels like it weighs fifty pounds. I've kept it on since the ceremony. Kept the medal pinned over my heart where the silver node presses against bone and nerve endings still raw from surgery. The white-lilac thread embroidered around the BATC logo has started to fray at the edges. I notice this because I have nothing else to look at in this bright, empty box ascending toward my prison.

My corporate apartment. Seventeen hundred square feet of minimalist furniture and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking Newark Bay. A reward for valor. For saving the city.

For burning alive 314 people.

The numbers won't leave my head. They're carved into my skull alongside the smell—that permanent residue of wet wool burning that clings to the back of my throat no matter how many times I brush my teeth, how much whiskey I pour down my gullet.

The elevator deposits me in a foyer of gray marble and recessed lighting. My keys jangle too loud in the silence as I unlock the deadbolt, the chain lock, the electronic security panel that chimes its welcome in a cheerful female voice: "Good evening, Commander Vance."

I want to smash something.

Instead, I close the door with careful precision and lean against it, sliding down until I'm sitting on the hardwood floor with my knees drawn up. The medal digs into my sternum. Good. It should hurt.

My fingers find the top button of my uniform shirt. Pop. The second button. Third. Fourth. I yank the shirt open, sending buttons skittering across the polished floor, and finally—finally—I can breathe without feeling like I'm suffocating under the weight of everyone's expectations.

But the relief lasts only a moment.

Because now I can see them in the mirror across the living room—a full-length thing framed in brushed steel that shows everything.

My reflection stares back at me, stripped down to my undershirt. And there, where the fabric hangs loose around my shoulders, the scars begin.

They start just below my collarbone, a constellation of angry red tissue where the white-lilac fire licked closest to my skin during the surge. The burn specialists called it miraculous—that I survived burns this extensive without permanent nerve damage. They don't know what they're talking about. Every touch still feels like walking through molten glass.

I turn slightly, watching in the mirror as my hands reach behind me for the zipper of my skirt. The teeth separate with a whisper, and I let the garment fall to my waist, then slide down past my hips to pool at my ankles.

The scars on my back are worse.

They spread like dark wings from my shoulder blades down to the base of my spine—a patchwork quilt of second- and third-degree burns that the healers couldn't fully repair even with their best magic. Because some of that magic came from me. From the same corrupted well that created the breach in the first place.

My fingers trace the worst of them, following the raised ridges of scar tissue. Each one corresponds to someone who died. Each one is a reminder.

The Orc laborer whose screams were cut short mid-roar. The Elven mother clutching her child—both burning, both dying together while I stood frozen, unable to summon anything but destruction.

I close my eyes and I'm back there again. The smell hits first—that goddamn smell of charred wool mixed with roasting meat, with melting rubber and boiling blood—and then the sounds:

*The high-pitched shrieks of a Gnome woman as flames engulfed her children.*

*The deep, bellowing agony of an Orc whose hide was too tough to burn quickly enough, who took three full minutes to die while I watched helplessly through smoke and screaming chaos.*

*The desperate pleas of commuters who'd only wanted to go home, whose last moments were spent clawing toward an exit that wasn't there, reaching for salvation from the very person who'd killed them.*

"I'm sorry," I whisper to the empty apartment. "God, I'm so sorry."

But apologies don't bring anyone back.

And the nightmares won't let me forget.

I push away from the mirror and stumble toward the bathroom, shedding the rest of my clothes until I'm standing naked in front of the shower controls. The node in my chest throbs dully, a constant ache that the burn specialists say will fade eventually.

Liar's promise.

I crank the water temperature all the way to scalding—hot enough that steam fills the small bathroom within seconds—and step under the spray before it has time to fully heat up. The shock of cold gives way to painfully hot, and I welcome both because at least they're real.

At least they're not the memory of 314 bodies burning on platform seven.

* * *

The numbers save me from myself.

I sit on the edge of my bed in the dark, the only light coming from the Panasonic Toughbook balanced on my scarred thighs. The screen casts a sickly blue glow across the burn scars on my face—geometric patterns like circuit boards melting down my left cheek, across my jaw. My hair catches it too, those patches where it won't grow back anymore, leaving behind skin that's pink and tender as an infant's.

The apartment smells wrong. Always has, but worse now. Sterile. Too clean. Like a morgue waiting for bodies that haven't arrived yet. I breathe through my mouth to avoid the scent of antiseptic and nothing-else, that particular emptiness that means human warmth was never meant to exist here.

My chest aches. That constant lead-bismuth weight sits just behind my sternum, pressing down on my lungs with every breath. *One.* The suppressant does its job too well—the white-lilac ward that used to shimmer at my fingertips is gone, replaced by gray smoke that stinks of burning wool when I try to summon it even in the privacy of these four walls.

I pull up the classified files again. The BATC dossier marked EYES-ONLY: VANCE. Inside are the photos of the thirty-eight children who survived Neon Hollow. Thirty-eight out of three hundred and fifty-two.

*Two.*

*Three.*

Their faces stare back at me from the monitor. Some smiling. Others looking confused, scared, drugged into compliance before they were moved to the secure foster homes. The corporate facilities look nice enough on camera—clean bedrooms, educated staff, psychological counseling built into the curriculum. But I know better. I've seen what BATC considers "secure monitoring."

*Four. Five. Six.*

A wall clock ticks somewhere in the apartment. Mechanical. Reliable. Each second marking time I can't afford to waste feeling anything.

Seventeen months old. That's the youngest. A girl named Sophie Chen, dark hair, eyes like her mother probably had before the Breach took her. She's listed as "non-verbal but responding to tactile stimuli." Code for: they don't think she'll ever speak about what happened.

I make myself look at each one. Force my eyes to linger on their names, their ages, their current locations. This is the penance. This is how I survive the fact that I couldn't save them all.

*Seven. Eight. Nine...*

At two hundred and twelve, my throat starts to burn. At two hundred and forty-seven, my vision swims with those gray halos—the hallucinations trying to creep in around the edges. The suppressant makes it worse sometimes, or maybe it just takes away my defenses when they appear.

*Two hundred and sixty-three. Two hundred and sixty-four...*

The dead have no photos in these files. Just numbers. Names cross-referenced with body recovery reports, dental records, DNA samples. Sometimes just "unidentifiable remains fragment K-19" or whatever letter they'd reached by the time they stopped counting pieces instead of people.

But I remember them anyway.

*Two hundred and eighty-nine.*

A boy who'd tried to give me his last candy bar. *Two hundred and ninety.* A woman who'd sung lullabies to children while the walls came down around us. *Three hundred and eleven.*

My voice becomes a mantra, broken and hypnotic in the sterile darkness:

"Three hundred and twelve. Three hundred and thirteen. Three hundred and fourteen."

The highest number. The final count from Neon Hollow after they finished excavating the rubble. After they cremated what couldn't be identified. After they sealed the site and built a memorial plaza over the worst of it.

"One."

I switch tabs now, back to the living. The thirty-eight who made it out.

"Two."

Sophie Chen, seventeen months old. Non-verbal.

"Three."

Marcus Williams, age seven. Night terrors documented weekly.

"Four. Five. Six..."

The numbers lock together in my mind like gears in a machine that can never stop turning. The dead on one side of the equation, the living on the other. If I keep counting, if I keep balancing them against each other, maybe the guilt won't swallow me whole during the long hours between midnight and dawn.

Maybe.

*Seventeen.*

*A clock ticks.*

*Thirty-two.*

The sun hasn't risen yet over Newark Bay. Out the apartment window, I can see the distant glow of the city—Neon Hollow's replacement district already half-built, all glass and steel pretending the ground beneath it isn't still saturated with ash and bone dust.

*Forty-three...*

I repeat the cycle again. Three hundred and fourteen deaths. One heartbeat at a time.

When the sun finally breaks over Pulaski Skyway, Mara Vance—the Aegis Commander who saved thirty-eight children by sacrificing three hundred and fourteen others—is gone.

Only the hollow enforcer remains, staring at numbers on a screen, counting the cost of survival until the mantra is the only thing left that feels real.

---

## CHAPTER 15: THE SNAP TO THE PRESENT

The rain hammers against the corrugated metal roof like a hundred desperate fists. I don't look up when I kick the door in. Don't need to. My boot connects with the lock—once, twice—and splintered wood explodes inward in a spray of wet paint chips and rust.

"BATC! Hands where I can see them!"

My MP5 tracks across the room before I step through the threshold. Water drips from my leather jacket onto the concrete floor. The smell hits me immediately—that familiar cocktail of gun oil, cheap incense, and burnt electronics that marks every wire-runner den we've raided. But underneath it all, threading through like a poison vein, is something else. Wet charred wool. The ghost in my bloodstream.

Three figures scramble behind a wall of mismatched servers—Street-Elves mostly, their fingers moving in practiced patterns as they yank cables. One Goblin, smaller than the others, fumbles with what looks like a Sony MiniDisc drive. His yellow eyes catch mine for just a second before he makes his decision.

Smart choice. He drops the drive and bolts for the side exit.

I'm already moving, finger on the trigger guard. The burst catches him mid-stride—not to kill, never to kill unless ordered, but to stop. Red blossoms across his shoulder and he goes down hard, crashing into a stack of Motorola Razrs. They scatter across the floor like plastic insects, their screens flickering once before going dark forever.

"The hardware!" I shout over the rain drumming on the roof. "Secure it now!"

My boots crunch on broken plastic as I advance toward the servers. The Elves have gone still, hands raised, their pointed ears twitching with nervous energy. I can hear them breathing. Can smell the fear-sweat under their cheap cologne.

"On your knees. Interlace your fingers."

They comply without argument. Good. Makes this easier.

The Geas hums in my chest—a low, constant vibration that's become as natural as my heartbeat. Two years since Sterling Manor. Two years since the ash-gray static burned its way into my bones and rewired every circuit in my brain. I remember being different once. Being... something else. But those memories feel like someone else's. Someone I watched die in slow motion while the Geas rewrote me line by line.

I pull the charging cable from the nearest server tower—an old Dell, probably stolen from some office building up in Midtown—and unspool it methodically. The metal casing is cold against my fingertips. Inside, I know there are terabytes of wire-runner code, encryption keys sold to whoever has cash and doesn't ask questions. Street-Elves running numbers for the Cartels. Goblins pushing corrupted data streams into the city's infrastructure.

All of it illegal. All of it mine to confiscate.

*Crack.* The sound echoes through the warehouse as I slam a panel open with my elbow. Spark shower across my field of vision.

One of the Elves makes a small noise—surprise or fear, I don't care which.

"Shut up." My voice is flat. Empty. I've heard recordings of myself lately, on surveillance footage. Don't recognize the woman speaking. She sounds like she's reading from a script written in ice.

I'm halfway through securing the evidence when the bleeding Elf—the one who went down first—finds his voice again.

"You're a corporate dog," he spits at my boots, blood and saliva mixing on the concrete. "Used to be a cop. Protected people."

I pause. Look down at him. His face is twisted in pain and defiance, both eyes swollen half-shut. Purple bruising already spreading across his jaw where he hit the floor.

"I am BATC Aegis." Each word comes out measured, precise. "I protect corporate interests. I enforce federal mandates. I secure assets."

The goblin whimpers somewhere behind me.

"Zip him," I tell Martinez, who's moved in to assist. "Tag everything. We're done here."

My hand drops to my side, resting on the grip of my sidearm. The weight is familiar now. Comfortable, even. Two years ago, this would have felt wrong. Two years ago, there was something inside me that recoiled at the idea of pointing a gun at someone who wasn't actively trying to kill me.

That something is gone.

Martinez pulls the zip-cuffs from his belt with practiced efficiency. They snap shut around the Elf's wrists with a sound like breaking bones. He doesn't struggle anymore. Just stares up at me with those wounded animal eyes while rain continues its relentless assault on the roof above us.

Outside, November wind howls through gaps in the warehouse walls. Neon light from the street bleeds through in sickly greens and pinks, painting everything in colors that don't exist in nature. My shift ends in fifteen minutes. Then I can go home to my apartment in the Sterling Heights complex—one of the perks of command—and sit in the dark for six hours before it starts all over again.

The smell of wet charred wool intensifies as I exhale slowly.

"Commander?" Martinez's voice breaks through my thoughts. "We're clear. Ready to move out?"

I nod once, sharp. Professional.

"Let's go."

* * *

The rain falls in sheets across Neon Hollow, turning the cracked pavement into rivers of oil-slick darkness. I pull my collar higher, feeling the wool scrape against the scarred skin of my throat. Three years since the breach. Three years since County General burned.

My shoes slap against the wet concrete as I walk. Each step sends small waves rippling outward, disturbing the reflection of the sodium-vapor lights above. They cast everything in that sickly orange glow, making the abandoned storefronts look like something from another world—one where hope still existed.

I pass a row of parked cars, their chrome catching and fragmenting the light. An old Buick with missing hubcaps. A sedan someone's painted to match their gang colors—the faded blue and gold of the Diablos. Past them all until I reach it: my assigned vehicle. A black 1999 Crown Victoria, unmarked, nondescript. Just another government car in a city full of them.

I lean against the hood, letting the freezing rain soak through my hair. The metal is cold even through the fabric of my coat, that penetrating chill that seems to come from deeper than the surface. I close my eyes and do my count.

*Three hundred and fourteen. Thirty-eight.*

Numbers. Always numbers. They're the only things keeping me tethered anymore, the only threads connecting me to whatever passes for reality these days. Three hundred and fourteen days since I woke up in Sub-Station Seven with no memory of how I got there. Thirty-eight souls lost during the Kearny Marshes incident—an incident I can't remember being part of but somehow commanded.

I reach into my pocket and pull out my Nokia pager. The green backlight illuminates my face as I check the time: 11:42 PM.

A group of Orc dockworkers cross on the opposite sidewalk, their laughter cutting through the sound of the rain. One of them uncaps a flask, takes a long drink, then passes it around while they share some joke I'm too far away to hear. Their voices are rough, genuine—alive in a way I haven't been since the ash-gray static settled into my bones.

I watch them like a ghost watching the living. When they pass, I whisper my count into the falling water.

*"Three hundred and fourteen."*

The words dissolve instantly, washed away by the downpour.

* * *

The pager vibrates against my hip like a dying insect. I reach for it without thinking, muscle memory older than thought itself. Two years of carrying this thing around, and still the sudden buzz makes my teeth grind.

I unclip it from my belt. The green LCD screen bleeds light across my knuckles, casting everything in that sickly emergency room glow. Priority One dispatch. Direct from Command. From *his* office.

My thumb hovers over the message button. The ash-gray static in my blood hums its familiar warning, but there's no point in delaying. There never is.

`UNSANCTIONED ARCANE DETONATION. WAREHOUSE DISTRICT. SUSPECT ARMED WITH ILLEGAL TELLURIC HARDWARE. DEADLY FORCE AUTHORIZED.`

Of course they are. They always are.

I stare at those words until the letters blur. Another night. Another mess. Another body count that won't appear in any official report because some things are better left buried under layers of classification so thick they might as well be tombstones.

The rain hasn't let up since midnight. It drums against the Crown Vic's roof in a rhythm that sounds almost mocking—*thwack-thwack-thwack*—like someone trying to get my attention. Like the universe wants me to notice how perfectly it all fits together. The storm, the killing, the orders that come down from on high wrapped in bureaucratic chains.

I unlock the car door. The hinges groan, protesting the weight of water clinging to every surface. The interior smells like stale coffee and leather, and underneath that, something else. Something metallic and sharp that reminds me of gunpowder and old blood.

I slide into the driver's seat. The cold leather sticks to my damp clothes for just a second before releasing. My fingers find the key in the ignition. I turn it.

The V8 engine rumbles to life beneath me—a deep, guttural sound that vibrates through the chassis and into my bones. For a moment, just one heartbeat, I can pretend this is something other than what it is. Just a woman in a car, driving through the rain toward somewhere that isn't here.

But that's a lie we both know.

I put the car in gear. The windshield wipers slap away sheets of water, clearing just enough space to see forward. Forward into the dark. Forward into whatever fresh nightmare BATC Command has cooked up for me tonight.

I reach for the radio mic. The cord is heavy, weighted, pulling at my hand like it's connected to lead ballast instead of plastic and wire. I press the button.

"My name is Vance," I say, and my voice comes out flat, dead, hollowed out by two years of carrying ghosts that won't let go. "I have the page. I'm en route to the Warehouse District."

There's a crackle of static on the other end, then nothing but silence. They heard me. They always do.

I release the button. The mic clicks back into place with a sound that feels final, absolute. Like there's no going back from this. Not that there ever was.

The Crown Vic accelerates into Neon Hollow's rain-soaked streets. The headlights cut through torrential downpour, twin cones of light pushing back against an darkness that wants nothing more than to swallow everything whole.

Warehouse District. Telluric hardware. Deadly force authorized.

Those words sit in my chest like shrapnel, sharp and unignorable. The Lead-Bismuth Geas coils tighter around my heart—a familiar weight, a familiar cage. Two years and it still hasn't gotten any lighter.

I drive deeper into the night.

Somewhere ahead, in the gutters of the Warehouse District, someone's already dead. And I'm on my way to make sure they stay that way.

The rain keeps falling.

The engine keeps rumbling.

And somewhere between here and there—between now and whatever fresh horror waits—I feel something cold settle over me like ash.

The halo of it all.

---

# BOOK #12: THE COPPER POT OF STERLING MANOR
### Prequels Cycle 3 (PB-3)

---

## CHAPTER 1: CHAPTER 1

The basement smells like blood and copper.

I stand over Danny's bed, hands wrapped around the cold brass casing of the Iron-Lung, feeling the rhythmic pulse of the compressor through my palms. *Ca-chunk. Shhhhh.* The sound has been my companion for three years now—the mechanical heartbeat that keeps my little brother alive while the arcane sickness eats him from the inside out.

Amber light spills from the sodium vapor lamp overhead, casting everything in that sickly yellow glow that makes the glass cylinders look like they're filled with honey instead of the black sludge that's crystallizing in Danny's chest. I check the pressure gauges—still holding at 28 psi, right where it needs to be. The brass fittings are tight. No leaks. For now.

"Hold on, kiddo," I whisper, watching his ribs expand beneath the weight of all that machinery. Sixteen years old and hooked up to something that looks like it belongs in a Victorian asylum. "Just hold on a little longer."

The Panasonic Toughbook on the side table blinks green, its screen showing the EKG readout—a steady mountain range of peaks and valleys. Heartbeat normal. Lung function stable. For now. The diagnostic software I pirated from County General runs its scan, and the numbers don't lie: the crystallization is slow, but it's relentless. Like rust, like rot, like every other thing in this godforsaken South Side that just keeps eating away until there's nothing left.

But tonight, I'm not here to watch him die slowly.

Tonight, I'm here to make sure some people die fast.

I turn away from the bed, my boots scuffing against the concrete floor. The workbench is cluttered with tools—wrenches, pliers, a blowtorch, things I've cobbled together over the years. Most of them aren't legal. None of them are safe. But when you're fighting monsters that don't follow the rules, you can't exactly bring a knife to a gunfight.

Except tonight, I am bringing knives.

Three of them, sharpened until they could split a hair. Coated in iron-gall residue mixed with bismuth powder—the kind of alchemical cocktail that burns through metahuman flesh like paper. I found the recipe in an old workshop manual Danny gave me back in '02, before everything went sideways. Before he took a lungful of wrong-air down by the marshes and brought home something that shouldn't exist.

*Ca-chunk. Shhhhh.*

The Iron-Lung keeps its rhythm while I work, each compression forcing sterilized air past the blockages in his chest, keeping him alive even as the sickness spreads. I load the knives into a custom sheath strapped to my forearm, then check the brass knuckles in my coat pocket. Loaded with tungsten carbide spikes. Good for cracking bone. Better for cracking skulls.

Outside, somewhere beyond the sealed basement door, I hear sirens. Not close—maybe a few miles off. Probably Sub-Station Seven burning again. There's always something burning on this side of Newark Bay. Always smoke, always fire, always someone screaming about the things that crawl out of the marshes after dark.

I lean against the workbench, closing my eyes. The cold from the concrete wall seeps through my jacket, but it doesn't touch the frost-cobalt hex humming just beneath my skin. That came after Danny got sick—like my body was trying to compensate for what he'd lost. Blood-iron metallurgy turned to dead-silent zero-remorse. The healers at County General said it wasn't natural. Said I should be dead or transformed.

I told them to fuck off.

"Danny," I say quietly, turning back to face him. His eyes are closed, lashes dark against his pale cheeks. "You remember what I told you about the Threefold Cord?"

His chest rises. Falls. The Iron-Lung *ca-chunks* its answer.

"Penance for what we couldn't stop. Revenge for what they took from us. And a sliver of justice—however sharp we can make it." I tap my knuckles against the brass casing, feeling the vibration travel through the pipes and valves. "Tonight isn't going to scrape the black iron out of your lungs. Won't fix what happened down by Pulaski Skyway when those bastards decided your life was cheaper than their cargo."

The temperature drops another degree around me. Ozone and chilled copper fill my nostrils.

"But it's better than letting them breathe tomorrow."

A sound echoes down from the stairwell above—heavy boots on concrete. Rhythmic. Deliberate. Dwarven steel-toed boots by the sound of them, descending with purpose.

I reach for the door handle, fingers closing around cold metal.

* * *

The basement reeked of machine oil and old sweat. I was elbow-deep in the guts of a disassembled M4 when I heard the familiar scrape of boots on concrete steps. Bram Kovacs descended into my workshop like he owned it—which, technically, part of it he did. Local 405 had fronted me the lease on this South Side chop-shop back in '03.

"Reyes." His voice cut through the whine of my angle grinder. I didn't look up from the trigger assembly I was working on.

"The package is here," Bram said. He dropped something heavy onto my workbench. The canvas duffel hit with a metallic thud that made my teeth ache.

I killed the grinder. The sudden silence rang in my ears, but beneath it, I caught the distant wail of sirens—multiple vehicles, moving fast to the north. Orange light flickered across the small basement window near the ceiling, casting everything in sickly flames.

Sub-Station Seven was burning.

Bram's shadow stretched long across the concrete floor. He lit a cigarette, the flare illuminating his scarred face, the crooked nose from a press accident back in '98. "North grid's lighting up like a Roman candle," he said around the smoke. "Scanner says Sub-Station Seven just blew its primary busbars. You sure we don't pivot?"

My hands were already pulling open the duffel. Inside, nestled in foam cutouts, were rows of depleted-bismuth slugs. Each one gleamed dull gray under the fluorescent lights, etched with armor-piercing runes that would shatter High-Spire kinetic wards like glass. Custom machined. Perfect weight distribution. Exactly what we needed for Sterling Manor tonight.

The ambient temperature dropped ten degrees as my blood-iron hex locked into frost-cobalt. Ozone and chilled copper filled my nostrils.

"Sterling's drinking champagne while the city burns," I said flatly. "We stick to the schedule."

Bram watched me load the slugs into my rune-etched MP5 magazines. His expression didn't change, but he stubbed out his cigarette against the workbench leg. "Grimjaw's team is ready. Just say when."

I racked the charging handle. The weapon hummed faintly, blue-black iron-gall residue coating the barrel. "Signal him. We move in thirty."

* * *

The trunk slammed shut with that satisfying metallic *thunk* that meant weight—serious weight. I wiped the sweat from my brow despite the November chill crawling up through my boots from the concrete basement floor.

"Christ, Cole," Bram grunted beside me, shoulder-checking one of the tactical bags. "You packing lead bricks in these things?"

I didn't answer. Couldn't. My mouth tasted like copper pennies and old blood. The hex was sitting heavy in my marrow now, that dead-silent frost-cobalt state where everything sharpens into brutal clarity. Ten degrees colder than it should be around me, breathing out little clouds that smelled wrong—ozone and iron-gall residue sizzling in the air.

We hauled the gear up three flights of rust-stained stairs, through the chop-shop's main floor with its disassembled engines scattered like mechanical corpses under yellow work lights. Out through the back exit into an alley that reeked of rotting garbage and puddles reflecting neon signs from Neon Hollow six blocks over.

My '99 Crown Victoria sat waiting, black and anonymous under a flickering streetlight. I popped the trunk with the fob, and there it was—my mobile armory. Spare mags stacked neat as cordwood. Breaching charges wrapped in bubble wrap. Zip-ties coiled like sleeping snakes. And that heavy copper pot, gleaming dull orange under the sodium-vapor glow. Foreshadowing something bad. Always is.

Bram whistled low. "Jesus H. Christ."

I started loading. Methodical. Each item finding its place like pieces on a board game where losing meant dying. The weight settled into the springs, making them compress just right. Perfect balance for what we were about to do.

Slammed the trunk shut.

The sound echoed off the brick walls.

I circled around to the driver's side, yanking open the door hard enough to make the hinges complain. The interior still smelled like burnt coffee and leather conditioner—the last honest thing in my life. I reached behind the seats, pulled out the Sony MiniDisc player, plugged it into the cassette adapter with practiced efficiency.

*Click-whirrrr.*

Static. Then Tom Waits' gravel-throat voice crawled through the speakers: *"...walk down the block to the old pool hall..."*

"Christ," Bram muttered again, sliding into the shotgun seat. He had his modified PalmPilot already in hand, thumb flying across the screen as he checked the frequencies hacked by those UnderCity Gnomes. Their code-work was beautiful when you knew how to read it—all those little green numbers cascading like water.

"The Gnome boys got the Watching Party guard codes locked," he said, eyes never leaving the screen. "Perimeter is blind for exactly four minutes. Tops."

Four minutes. Four hundred seconds to get inside Sterling Manor's grounds. To find Vance before she finished whatever hellstorm she'd started at Sub-Station Seven.

I threw the Crown Vic into drive. The engine roared—a deep, guttural sound that made the whole car shake. My knuckles went white on the wheel.

"We're burning daylight," I said.

Tires squealed against wet asphalt, scattering trash and puddle-water in twin sprayers behind us. The speedometer needle climbed past forty, fifty, sixty as we arrowed toward the High-Spire outskirts. Neon Hollow fell away behind us, its garish glow replaced by the sick orange reflection of Sub-Station Seven in the rearview mirror.

Burning.

Always fucking burning.

I pushed harder on the accelerator.

The road ahead was dark now—no streetlights out here where the money lived. Just blacktop and the occasional flicker from a distant security light. Then the trees started appearing, manicured and perfect lining both sides of what became a private road. Wrought-iron gates up ahead, barely visible through the windshield.

"Three minutes," Bram announced.

I killed the headlights with one flick of the stalk.

The Crown Vic rolled forward into darkness, engine still roaring, carrying us toward Sterling Manor like a steel coffin full of bad intentions.

---

## CHAPTER 2: CHAPTER 2

I killed the Crown Vic's engine three hundred yards out, letting the sedan coast into the drainage culvert beneath the High-Spire ridge. The November rain hammered against the roof like machine-gun fire—cold, relentless, perfect for what we had planned.

"Down," I said to no one in particular, sliding out into the ankle-deep water pooling at the culvert bottom. Ice crystals formed along the concrete walls, frost-cobalt magic bleeding from my fingertips without conscious thought. The temperature dropped another five degrees around me.

Grimjaw was already there when I emerged, a mountain of green-skinned muscle wrapped in black tactical gear. His tusks caught the ambient light filtering down from above, making them gleam like polished bone. Behind him, twelve members of Local 405 materialized from the shadows—goblins, ogre-kin, street-elves, dwarven sandhogs. All of them carrying more firepower than most city blocks could handle.

"You're late, Reyes," Grimjaw rumbled, his voice like gravel tumbling through a cement mixer. He extended a meaty paw toward me.

I ignored it and looked past him at the assembled crew. They were good—their body language tight, controlled, faces smeared with grease paint that turned them into shadows with eyes. Weapons clicked as safeties came off. Magazines checked. Loaders seated with soft, wet snicks.

"They know why we're here?" I asked, pulling out my PalmPilot.

"The Sterling Manor contract." Grimjaw's expression didn't change. "The union vote last week made it official. We take back our people, or we take back their lives."

I watched the rain run down his face, mixing with the war paint. Twelve years since I'd pulled him out of that High-Spire cage, but he still remembered what they'd done to his family. What they'd *tried* to do.

"Sterling's got eight High-Spire retainers on the outer ring," he continued, dropping his voice another register. "Elves. Fast, but they rely on the Telluric wire to do the heavy lifting. Cut the wire—"

"We cut their throats." I finished the sentence for him, my breath pluming in the cold air. The frost-cobalt magic pulsed stronger now, responding to the violence already building in my chest. "No noise."

A younger goblin near the back—couldn't have been more than seventeen if he was a day—shifted his weight. Made a sound low in his throat.

Grimjaw's head snapped around so fast I heard vertebrae crack. "Problem?"

"No problem, boss." The goblin's yellow eyes went wide. "Just... you sure about this?"

"I'm sure the Telluric Perimeter Wire is going to make very interesting music tonight," I said, holding up the wire-cutters I'd taken from Sub-Station Seven. They were heavy steel, industrial-grade, and already beginning to frost over at the jaws. My magic had other ideas about how this operation would go down.

Grimjaw grunted approval and handed me an IBM ThinkPad, ruggedized and waterproof. The screen glowed green in the darkness, showing Sterling Manor's active security grid. Red dots marked guard positions. Yellow lines traced camera coverage. A blinking blue icon showed the Watching Party's current location inside the manor grounds.

"Bram's team spoofed the perimeter sensors ten minutes ago," Grimjaw explained. "We've got a four-minute window before the system recognizes the false data."

I stared at the screen, watching the seconds tick by. My palm was sweating despite the freezing rain. This was it—the point of no return. After this, there was no going back to being just Cole Reyes, machinist from the South Side.

"There's a loading dock on the east side," I said, tracing a route with one finger. "Less visible from the main house. We can get in clean if we move now."

The crew tensed, weapons coming up. Eyes gleaming in the dark. Ready for blood.

"Remember what we talked about," I said, raising my voice so everyone could hear. "Tactical discipline first. Emotional payback second. We're here to free metahumans, not start a war we can't finish."

"You keep saying that, Reyes." Grimjaw checked his rifle magazine—full, locked, loaded. "But wars have a way of starting themselves."

My PalmPilot buzzed.

The encrypted message appeared: **WATCHING PARTY GUARD CODES SPOOFED. PERIMETER SENSORS BLINDED. FOUR MINUTE COUNTDOWN COMMENCING.**

Grimjaw looked at me. I looked at him.

"Let's make some music," I said quietly.

And then we moved into the rain-soaked darkness toward Sterling Manor, armed and ready for whatever waited inside those walls.

* * *

The wire hummed—a low, angry vibration that made my teeth ache behind the safety goggles I'd stolen from the machinist's locker at Sub-Station Seven. Telluric perimeter wire. Old magic married to new tech, running hot enough to cook a man who didn't know how to read its signature. I did. Three years maintaining the power grid for PSE&G had taught me which wires sang death and which ones whispered warnings.

This one sang death.

I knelt in the muddy shoulder of the Kearny Marshes access road, hidden behind a rusted chain-link fence that probably hadn't kept anyone out since the Carter administration. Fifty yards ahead, past manicured hedges that cost more than most people's mortgages, Sterling Manor rose against the November sky like a tombstone carved from limestone and old money.

Frost-cobalt magic pooled in my palm—my inheritance from a mother I never knew, a gift I'd spent twenty-five years trying to control. The cold bit into my skin, familiar and hungry, racing up my forearm toward the heavy bolt cutters gripped in both hands. The steel handles began to sweat ice crystals, frost spreading across the metal like a creeping disease.

Behind me, Grimjaw stood silent as a monument, his massive frame blocking what little light filtered through the pollution-choked air. He'd been quiet since we left County General, watching me prepare with those dead-eyeballs that saw too much and said nothing. Around him, fifteen Local 405 members checked weapons, comms, and the nervous tics that came before a job like this. Street-Elves adjusted their rifle scopes. Ogre-Kin flexed fingers the size of baseball bats. A human medic I didn't recognize—a woman named Singh according to Grimjaw's briefing—checked her trauma kit for the third time.

"Telluric wire carries a signature burst when it breaks," I muttered, not taking my eyes off the glowing thread barely visible in the darkness. "Standard security response is seven seconds minimum. We have five."

"That's your problem now." Grimjaw's voice rumbled like distant thunder. "Cut it clean or we're all dead inside those walls."

I pressed my freezing hands tighter around the bolt cutter handles. The frost-cobalt hex surged down the steel, racing along the joints and blades until the entire tool shimmered with impossible cold. Temperature dropped below zero, then below absolute zero—the magic eating away at the fundamental heat of the metal until the bolt cutters became something colder than physics should allow.

The Telluric wire pulsed ahead of me, glowing faintly with trapped lightning. Standard security said it would explode into an arc-flash the moment any significant current drew from it. Electric fence on steroids, designed by High-Spire engineers who thought the South Side was full of stupid laborers who couldn't read schematics.

They were half-right.

I lunged forward, clamping the frozen jaws onto the humming wire. My heart hammered against my ribs. One second. Two. The frost-cobalt magic hit the superheated Telluric line and...

Silence.

The wire stopped humming. Stopped glowing. In the space between one heartbeat and the next, it turned brittle as glass, frozen solid by magic that shouldn't exist outside of theoretical physics. Ice crystals spread across its length, spiderwebbing the structure.

I squeezed.

*Tink.*

The sound was tiny—a small, delicate breaking like a wine glass dropped on carpet. The Telluric wire shattered, fragments falling to earth in a cascade of frozen light. Dead-silent. No explosion. No alarm burst. Nothing but the sudden, gaping darkness where security had been moments before.

"Go," I hissed, already moving toward the breach point in Sterling Manor's wall. Grimjaw pushed past me, his bulk carrying him through the gap without slowing. Local 405 members poured through behind him—flooding into gardens lit only by distant streetlights bleeding over the estate walls.

A Street-Elf sniper mounted up on an Ogre-Kin's shoulders, clearing the twelve-foot barrier with practiced ease. His rifle came up instantly, sweeping the garden grounds below.

"Outer grid is dark," he whispered into his throat mic, voice tight with adrenaline. "We're in the garden. Smells like expensive fertilizer and dead men."

Mud squelched beneath tactical boots. Someone stumbled over an ornamental fountain. A curse muttered in a language older than English. I wove between the hedges, bolt cutters still gripped in my frost-numbed hands, scanning for movement ahead.

Flashlight beam.

Sweeping across the garden path, maybe twenty yards ahead, accompanied by the crunch of gravel under heavy boots. Two silhouettes materialized from around a marble statue—High-Spire elven guards in full tactical gear, their weapons already rising toward the breach point they'd just discovered.

They saw us.

We saw them.

The distance collapsed to nothing in my peripheral vision as I dove sideways, hitting the damp grass hard enough to knock the breath from my lungs. Bullets stitched the air where I'd been standing milliseconds before. Grimjaw roared—a sound that shook loose leaves from nearby trees—and charged forward like an avalanche.

My hand found the bolt cutters still clutched in my grip. Frost-cobalt magic flared again, desperate and wild, pouring into the steel jaws.

* * *

The Telluric wires sang—a high-frequency whine that set my teeth on edge even through the rain-soaked air. November cold bit through my jacket as I crouched beside Grimjaw near the topiary sculpture, watching the perimeter guards make their patrol pass.

"Two more minutes," I whispered, feeling the familiar cold gather in my fingertips. The wire-cutters hung heavy in my left hand, their steel jaws already beginning to glaze over with frost-cobalt condensation. The magic came easier now, after all these years working the night shift at County General's machine shop—long hours with metal and compression had taught me how to make tools obey.

Grimjaw grunted beside me, his bulk barely contained by the shadows. His yellow eyes tracked the guards' movement, calculating angles and reaction times with that Orcish precision that made him worth every penny of the retainer I couldn't afford. He was borrowed time, dangerous company, but tonight we needed someone who didn't flinch when things got messy.

The guards paused at the junction point, their corporate-tactical armor gleaming wet under the security floodlights. Elven High-Spire, if the pointed ears and expensive equipment were anything to go by. One of them knelt, running a gloved finger across the grass, then looked up sharply at his partner.

Frost.

My mistake. Should've been more careful with the temperature manipulation. The first guard reached for his radio, his expression shifting from confusion to alert concern.

That's when we moved.

I exploded from the darkness like a frozen blade, my hand clamping down over the nearest elf's mouth before he could draw breath to speak. My frost-cobalt magic surged through the contact point, racing along his neck, freezing the blood in his carotid artery with such sudden, violent efficiency that his body went rigid, then slack within a heartbeat. His eyes went wide, then glassy as the ice crystals formed beneath the skin, turning it a pale, sickly blue.

Behind him, Grimjaw was already on the second guard. No finesse, no magic—just pure, brutal physics. He stepped forward as the elf turned, one massive hand shooting out to grip the back of the guard's head while the other clamped around his chin. Then came the sound—a wet, sickening crunch that echoed through the garden despite the rain, the distinct pop-pop-pop of cervical vertebrae separating.

The corpse dropped like a sack of meat.

I dragged my kill into the bushes without looking at his face, my expression flat, clinical. This wasn't about anger or revenge—not yet. This was reconnaissance, elimination, preparation. The guards had made their choice when they signed contracts with people who hired out execution squads. Their deaths weren't on me any more than the rust was on the iron I worked with every night.

Grimjaw wiped a drop of arterial spray from his knuckles with his thumb, then sucked it clean. "Too slow," he rumbled, his voice like grinding gears. "High-Spire soft. All show, no substance."

"Three minutes." I checked my watch, the luminous dial cutting through the darkness. The BATC emergency channels were probably already screaming about Sub-Station Seven by now—that distraction we'd carefully engineered to pull resources away from Sterling Manor. "Move to the terrace."

We crossed the manicured lawn in bounds, the grass crunching under our boots, each footfall careful and deliberate. Through the driving rain, Sterling Manor loomed ahead—a monument to old money and newer corruption, its facade lit against the night sky. And there, just visible past the decorative hedgerow, the massive glass terrace doors glowed warm and golden.

Classical music drifted out through the cracks—some baroque piece I couldn't name, all strings and harpsichord. Inside those doors was everything we'd come for. Inside was Visible Head #1, and the answers he owed me for what happened to Maria at County General last spring.

Inside was first blood in a garden that would soon run red.

I raised my hand, signaling Grimjaw to halt as we reached the hedge line. The glass doors were perhaps forty feet away now, close enough to see movement inside—shadows passing across the light, the silhouette of someone moving between rooms.

Time slowed down to the rhythm of my heartbeat, each pulse another second closer to whatever came next.

"Ready?" I asked quietly.

Grimjaw's grin was all teeth in the darkness. "Been ready since you hired me, machinist."

---

## CHAPTER 3: CHAPTER 3

The night air bit at my exposed skin as I crouched behind the manicured hedges of Sterling Manor's west terrace. November cold, but it was nothing compared to what was building inside me—the frost-cobalt pressure that wanted out, that always wanted out when my psychogenic bleed got too thick in my bloodstream.

"Locks are solid," whispered Mika from where she knelt beside the French doors, her gloved fingers working over the deadbolts with practiced precision. Her breath plumed white in the darkness. "Three internal bolts, two external. All magnetic-kinetic sealed."

I didn't need to see the locks to know they'd be tough. Sterling Manor belonged to Vincent Moretti, and Moretti had more money than sense when it came to security. The kind of money that bought things that went *chunk-chunk-chunk* when you tried to pick them normally.

But normal wasn't something we dealt in.

I pressed my palm against the cold glass, feeling for the resonance frequencies of the locking mechanisms through the doorframe itself. My 4th-Law awareness let me taste the iron-sweet flavor of the electromagnetic fields holding those bolts in place. Too easy. Like plucking fruit.

"Stand back," I muttered, drawing a rune-etched blade from my thigh holster. The metal sang its harmonic frequency as I scored three quick passes across the threshold—blood-iron geometry, old magic married to new physics. The hex wouldn't break the locks. It would make them break themselves.

The sound was like someone snapping steel cables inside a coffin. Three sharp *CRACK-CRACK-CRACK* echoed through the empty terrace.

Mika's eyes widened in the dim light filtering from the manor's interior windows. She pulled the doors open without another word, revealing a corridor of such opulent excess it made my teeth hurt. Imported marble flooring, mahogany wainscoting that probably cost more than Bram's apartment building, recessed lighting casting everything in warm amber glow.

That warmth lasted exactly three seconds after I stepped through the threshold.

The temperature dropped like I'd walked into a meat locker. The air crystallized around my face with each exhalation. Frost began creeping up the walls immediately, spreading like a living thing along the expensive woodwork. Behind me, I heard Kovacs curse softly.

"What the fuck, Reyes?"

"Don't ask." I kept moving, MP5 raised and ready. The bismuth-depleted slugs in the magazine felt heavy in their casings—good weight, good balance. Mika slid in behind me, her own weapon covering our six. Bram took up position at the front door we'd just breached, watching for any movement outside.
