Julian's eyes fly open at the sound of the ignition. Wide. Perfect circles of brown iris around dilated black pits. He tries to scream but only manages a choked gurgle around the rag.

"Shhh." I move closer with the torch, letting him feel the radiant heat against his cheek. "Almost done here."

The rats inside the inverted pot are going insane. Their shrieks echo off the copper walls, bouncing back and forth until it sounds like hundreds instead of dozens. The steel plate rattles slightly as they throw themselves at it again and again.

And underneath it all, that constant scratching.

*Scritch-scritch-scritch.*

Blood on copper. Copper on flesh. Flesh under assault.

I adjust the flame regulator, feeling it cool against my iron-gall stained fingers. The frost-cobalt chill has retreated into my bones, replaced by something hotter—purpose, maybe, or just plain old-fashioned rage.

"Last chance," I tell Julian, though we both know what comes next isn't about chances anymore. It's about answers.

---

## CHAPTER 9: CHAPTER 9

The torch catches with a sharp *whoosh*, a column of blue flame that screams like a jet engine even at low pressure. I adjust the valve slowly, deliberately, watching as the needle-thin stream expands into something more aggressive—hotter, angrier. The hiss fills my ears as I step toward the table where Julian lies bound.

The copper pot sits upside-down on his exposed stomach, its rounded base flat against his pale skin. Even in the dim light filtering down here, I can see it beginning to darken slightly around the edges where the heat first kisses the metal.

"Cole!" Julian's voice cracks, desperate. "COLE! Don't fucking do this!"

I don't answer. Can't answer. Not yet. My hand remains steady as I bring the torch closer, the blue flame dancing in my peripheral vision like some malevolent spirit hungry for its due. The frost-cobalt ward keeps the ambient temperature brutal, crystalline, but right here—right where the flame meets metal—I'm creating an inferno.

*Click.*

The igniter sparks once, twice, and then the flame stabilizes into a focused point of absolute white-hot fury.

I press it to the base of the pot.

For a heartbeat, nothing happens except the sound—that god-awful roar of propane burning clean and hot. Then the copper begins to drink the heat. It's like watching sunrise concentrated into metal. The dull brown coloration bleeds away from where the flame touches, revealing orange beneath, then red, then deeper shades I can't name because they're beyond naming—they're just *heat*, pure and unfiltered.

Inside that inverted bell, the rats feel it immediately.

Their squealing starts as confusion—a few experimental chirps turned frantic. Then the first true shrieks of panic as their tiny bodies register what their simple brains cannot process: every surface is becoming hostile. The walls are still cold from my ward, but the bottom of their prison is turning into a griddle.

"NO NO NO NO—" Julian's scream tears itself apart on the words, his back arching against the zip-ties holding him down. He pulls hard enough that I hear something pop in his shoulder, but he doesn't stop thrashing. "Cole, you fucking psychopath! You've already won! You've already fucking WON!"

The copper glows brighter, now showing distinct patches of orange-red spreading across its surface. I keep the torch steady, feeling the vibration travel up my arm. The smell hits me next—not yet the roasting flesh, but the copper itself beginning to off-gas something metallic and sharp, mixing with the acrid tang of burning propane.

Inside the pot, the chaos escalates. I hear it clearly now—the rats' high-pitched terror giving way to something more primal. They scrabble against each other, against the sides, their claws scraping frantically for purchase. And underneath all that noise, fainter at first, then clearer:

The wet sound of teeth breaking skin.

Julian's screams become wordless, animal sounds of pure agony as the panicked rodents, cornered by heat they can't understand or escape, turn on the only soft thing left in their world. Their bites are shallow at first—desperate, not malicious—but even through the metal I can see the way his stomach muscles spasm and contract, feel the vibrations in the table beneath my feet.

I don't move the torch. Can't move it. Not yet.

The base of the pot is cherry-red now, almost glowing in the darkness of this vault. Steam rises where it touches Julian's skin, his flesh literally cooking from direct contact with metal hot enough to cauterize as it burns. But that's secondary, incidental. What matters is what's happening inside—that pressure cooker of heat and panic and razor-sharp desperation.

"Please!" Julian sobs now, all pretense of defiance evaporated. "PLEASE, Cole! I'll give you anything! Everything! Just make it stop! MAKE IT STOP!"

I watch him twist, watch the zip-ties bite into his wrists until blood beads up dark in the cold air. Watch his face contort in ways that go beyond simple pain into some territory where the mind breaks under stress.

And still I hold the flame steady.

Because I know what comes next. The rats are realizing there's nowhere left to go—the walls too hot, the bottom too hot, the space between them and Julian's stomach shrinking as his body convulses and heals and bleeds simultaneously. Physics is a bitch like that. Heat transfers. Pressure builds. And biological organisms trapped in enclosed spaces start making choices based on pure survival instinct.

They're going deeper now.

Julian's new scream—a wet, bubbling thing—confirms it.

I adjust the torch angle by a fraction, moving the blue-white point across the copper's surface methodically, systematically spreading the glow. Creating zones of increasing temperature. Making sure every square centimeter of that inverted prison becomes an oven.

"Tell me about Sterling Manor," I say quietly, my voice barely audible over the torch's hiss and Julian's ragged breathing. "Tell me everything."

His answer dissolves into another shriek as something inside him tears loose.

* * *

The copper pot glows now—a living ember in the frozen air, pulsing with that deep, arterial red that welders call cherry. I hold the torch steady, its flame licking across the bottom of the vessel with hungry precision. The metal groans under the heat, expanding, contracting, singing that high-pitched metallic hymn that means we're past the point of no return.

Julian's body goes rigid beneath it all. His spine bows upward off the concrete slab, muscles standing out like steel cables, vertebrae cracking audibly as they compress. The clamps bite harder into his cheeks, tearing skin, but he doesn't scream anymore—not with his voice, anyway. What comes out is a wet, bubbling shriek that froths pink at his lips, spraying droplets that freeze mid-air before hitting the ground.

The rats are going insane.

Their high-pitched chittering rises to a fever pitch inside the copper prison. I can see them through the thin metal—shadows writhing, pressing against the walls, their fur beginning to smoke where it touches the heating surface. The smell hits me then, that god-awful cocktail of burning hair, scorched flesh, and something else... something chemical and sweet that must be the Sludge itself cooking in their bloodstream.

They start digging.

Not toward the opening—they're too smart for that, even mutated. They go downward. Their tiny claws scrape frantically against Julian's stomach wall, leaving furrows in the pale skin. Then the teeth come into play.

*Rip.*

It sounds like someone tearing through wet canvas. Julian's entire body convulses, a full-body seizure that nearly bucks him off the table. Blood—so much blood—wells up around the rim of the pot where it sits flush against his abdomen. It pools quickly in the frozen air, steaming, sizzling as it hits the cherry-red copper.

The first rat breaches.

I don't look away. Can't. My eyes track every detail as those yellowed incisors sink into the abdominal fascia, tearing through muscle fibers like they were tissue paper. The sound is obscene—a wet, enthusiastic chewing punctuated by the tearing of tissue, the popping of capillary bundles, the slick squelch of organs shifting beneath the violation.

More join. Dozens. A mass of needle-teeth and clawed paws working in a frenzy, driven by nothing but primal survival instinct. They gnaw through fat deposits, through the rectus abdominis muscles, creating a maelstrom of destruction that spreads outward from the central point of heat. Julian's screams return now, wordless and animalistic, vibrating through the clamps until I'm afraid his jaw will shatter.

"Holy fuck," Grimjaw mutters, his thick fingers unconsciously scraping at the scarred flesh of his own torso. "That's what the Sludge felt like, Sterling. Eatin' us from the inside out."

I keep the torch applied. The copper radiates heat now, baking the area immediately surrounding the breach while my frost-cobalt ward holds back the encroaching cold just inches away. The contrast creates this bizarre effect—the flesh around the wound sears black while the rest of him glistens with ice crystals. Steam rises constantly, carrying that stench of cooked blood and roasted meat.

The rats tunnel deeper.

Through the transversus abdominis. Through the peritoneum. Into the visceral cavity itself. Their movements create visible bulges rippling across Julian's stomach, shadows moving beneath translucent skin. He's losing consciousness now, his thrashing growing weaker, more convulsive. His eyes roll back, hemorrhaging blood from the strain, the optic nerves themselves rupturing.

I nod to the Ogre-Kin waiting in the corner—Brick, if memory serves, though they all blur together sometimes. Six feet eight of raw muscle and malice, his hide marked with burn scars from years of work in the foundries before the Sludge got him.

He steps forward with something in his hands: a set of crude metal hooks on chains, heated until they glow dull orange.

Time to see how deep these bastards can go.

* * *

The copper pot gleams like a captured sun in my frost-cobalt warded air, its surface already beginning to blacken at the edges where the welding torch's flame licks hungrily. The smell hits me first—that metallic tang of heating metal mixing with something organic, something wrong. Burning hair. Roasting flesh.

Julian Sterling makes a sound around the duct tape over his mouth. Not words. Just animal noise. His eyes are wide enough that I can see white all around the irises even from here, clamped open with the spring-loaded clamps I'd modified from shop tools. He's watching the vault door.

I'm watching it too.

The door groans open, letting in a rush of warmer air that immediately begins to battle against my ward. For a moment, the temperature in the vault spikes, and I smell the sudden release of trapped scents—blood, sweat, fear, and underneath it all, that chemical sweetness of Sludge-mutated flesh.

They drag her in like a sack of broken dolls.

Victoria Sterling doesn't come in quietly. Her scream starts before she fully crosses the threshold, high and sharp enough to crack glass if this were any normal room. But these aren't normal walls, and we're past caring about noise complaints.

"Let go! JULIAN!" She fights like she thinks she's still got power, kicking out with designer heels that have lost one stiletto somewhere between the manor and here. "You can't—my husband will—"

A heavy-handed Ogre-kin slaps her across the face. Not playfully. Not as warning. Just... efficiently. The sound is wet meat meeting brick wall.

Her scream changes pitch.

They drop her in the center of the floor, right in Julian's line of sight. She lands hard on her shoulder, bone crunching audibly beneath the silk blouse. Even through the fabric, I can see it bend wrong.

"You signed the papers, corpo-bitch." A Goblin steps forward, his voice like rusted metal scraping concrete. South Side accent thick as sludge in summer. "You bought the cages. Now you're in one."

He pins her arm down with a hand that could crush granite. His fingers are too long, joints bending at angles they shouldn't, yellowed claws scraping against the marble floor.

Victoria twists, trying to pull away. Her other arm flails wildly, connecting with nothing but empty air. Then another pair of hands clamps onto her free leg—a smaller set, belonging to a Sludge-Goblin barely four feet tall but built like an overcoiled spring.

"I don't know what you think you—" Victoria starts, blood already trickling from her nose where the Ogre hit her.

The spring-loaded clamps on Julian's eyes click louder as he struggles against the chair restraints. He makes that noise again. Deeper this time. More broken.

I watch them work.

There's no artistry here. No finesse. This isn't my show anymore—I'm just audience now, holding the torch steady so its blue-white heat keeps the copper pot cooking. My frost-cobalt ward pulses around me like armor, keeping me isolated in my bubble of frozen air while the rest of the vault becomes a furnace.

They tear her clothes first. The expensive stuff—a Chanel suit that probably cost more than most people make in a year. Ripping it away in strips and handfuls until she's exposed beneath it all, skin pale and perfect and soon-to-be anything-but.

The Ogre-kin doesn't bother with words. He just kneels down and takes hold of her leg with both massive hands.

The snap echoes off those soundproof mahogany walls.

Victoria's scream reaches a new octave entirely.

Julian convulses in his chair hard enough that I hear wood splintering. His sobs come muffled through the tape, wet and desperate.

*Watch*, I think at him silently across the vault. *This is what your money bought. This is what Sterling Manor was built on.*

The Goblin machinists have moved forward now, dragging something behind them. Iron chains that rattle against the floor, and blowtorches whose flames dance orange and hungry in the superheated air.

Behind Victoria, another figure enters—Grimjaw himself, his massive frame filling the doorway before he has to duck under the frame. His eyes glow amber in the torchlight as they fix on Mrs. Sterling.

"She funded the experiments," Grimjaw says simply, his voice carrying over the sounds of breaking bones and tearing fabric. "Signed off on every sweep. Every 'cull' of expendable slag."

He looks at Julian then. "Your wife broke bodies in her labs. Now we break hers."

The first chain lands on the marble floor with a heavy clang.

I keep the welding torch steady, watching its flame reflect off the copper pot's increasingly blackened surface.

The temperature in the vault keeps climbing.

---

## CHAPTER 10: CHAPTER 10

The vault reeks of copper and burning flesh.

I stand over Julian's writhing form like an architect surveying a half-finished project. His abdomen has become something grotesque—a wet workbench where my razor-rats perform their ugly surgery. Through the gaping wound, I can see the glistening coils of intestines, the yellowed fat, the pink muscle fibers twitching in agony.

He's making noises. Wet, choking sounds that bubble through the blood pooling in his throat.

"Cole..." Victoria's voice cuts through the carnage, hoarse and broken from somewhere near the vault entrance. "Please... no more..."

But I'm not looking at her anymore. My attention has shifted entirely to Julian—his face contorted in a rictus of pure suffering, eyes clamped shut behind swollen lids, veins bulging purple-black against skin gone deathly pale. The zip-ties bite into his wrists deep enough to leave permanent scars. Not that it matters. He won't need wrists much longer.

The copper pot on his stomach has filled completely now. Dark red fluid sloshes against the metal sides as his body convulses—the sound obscene, rhythmic. Each spasm sends fresh rivulets cascading down his hips onto the concrete floor.

My blood-iron hexes pulse through the steel table beneath him. I can feel his heart stuttering, trying to quit, to mercy-kill itself into oblivion. The hexes force it to keep beating. Thump-thump. Thump-thump. A mechanical drum keeping time with this symphony of suffering.

Grimjaw towers over Victoria's crumpled form. She's curled protectively around her torso, one arm wrapped around her shattered ribs. Her expensive dress is torn and mud-stained, streaked with dark blood that matches the stuff seeping from between Julian's legs.

The goblin brings his boot back and drives it into her side.

I hear the crack of bone. See her body lift an inch off the ground before crashing back down, gasping for air she can't seem to draw properly.

Julian's scream becomes something primal, animalistic.

"Look at them," I say, stepping into his field of vision. The welding torch in my hand casts dancing shadows across my face—across the dead expression I've worn since we began. "This is what you built. This is your legacy."

His clamped eyes fly open.

The sclera are shot through with broken blood vessels, turning the whites a mottled crimson. Pupils dilated so wide they're almost entirely black. He stares up at me with the hollow terror of a man watching his entire world collapse into this single moment of absolute horror.

Behind him, on the vault floor, Victoria's body spasms again. Grimjaw plants another kick, this one to her thigh. Not lethal. Never lethal yet. Just pain. Excruciating, compounding pain.

"You wanted power," I continue, my voice flat as machinery. "You wanted control. You thought money meant immunity." 

The razor-rats inside Julian's abdomen shift position. He arches violently against the restraints, making those wet tearing sounds as they scrape against ribcage, against liver, against whatever organs they haven't hollowed out yet.

The copper pot sloshes again.

Somewhere in the chaos, Victoria sobs.

* * *

The air in the Subterranean Trophy Vault turns thick with the stench of industrial solvent and old money. Two figures in tailored suits—younger versions of the patriarch who'd already been reduced to screaming meat on the other side of this chamber—they're dragged forward by Goblins with yellow eyes that gleam like headlamps in the dim light.

I stand at the periphery, arms crossed, watching. My breath comes out in frost-white clouds even though the temperature should be sweltering down here. It isn't. My aura keeps a pocket of winter around me while hell itself erupts in the center.

"Put them in the puddle," Victoria's voice cuts through the damp air. She stands beside me now, her crimson eyes reflecting nothing but satisfaction as she watches her father's legacy unravel. "Right in the fucking center."

The Goblins don't hesitate. They haul the two heirs—probably mid-forties, both of them, the ones who'd signed off on the Telluric Pylon blueprints, the ones who'd stood over spreadsheets calculating profit margins while sandhogs died underground—and shove them into the middle of that spreading pool of solvent.

One of them stumbles, falls hard on his ass in the chemical slurry. His brother catches him, steadying himself against his sibling. They're looking around now, confused, scared. Not yet understanding what's coming.

A Goblin steps forward from where they'd been waiting in the shadows. Matches between his teeth. He flicks a lighter.

*Whooooosh.*

The ring ignites in an instant—a perfect circle of fire surrounding them, maybe fifteen feet across. The heat washes over everything immediately, making my frost-cobalt chill feel like the only sane thing left in this room. The flames climb higher, bright orange and hungry, licking at the edges of their expensive suits without quite reaching them yet.

They're trapped inside it now.

"You know what happens next?" Victoria asks me quietly. Her gaze never leaves her cousins. "What Dad did to the sandhogs who complained about safety violations?"

I do. I've read the files. All three hundred pages of testimony from the collapsed shaft in Kearny Marshes.

The first Dwarven sandhog emerges from behind a support pillar, dragging something heavy. An iron pipe, thick as a man's thigh, dented and scarred with old use. He hefts it onto one shoulder like a baseball bat.

"Which one first?" he grunts.

Victoria points. "The one who fell."

The Dwarf nods once. Steps up to the edge of the fire-ring. For a moment, the flames part around him—they don't burn through whatever mystic shit lets these creatures exist in our world—but then close again behind him as he walks into the center.

The heir who fell is trying to get up, slipping in the solvent. His brother reaches for him—

*CRUNCH.*

The sound is wet, heavy, final. The Dwarf brings that pipe down on the kneecap with all his weight behind it. Bone fragments audible even over the roar of the flames. The heir screams—a high-pitched, animal sound—and collapses sideways into the burning ring.

His leg bends wrong where it shouldn't bend.

"That's for Tommy Mendez," the Dwarf spits into the fire, then swings again—this time at the elbow. *Crunch.* Another scream joins the first.

"Tommy Mendez was nineteen years old," Victoria says conversationally beside me. Her voice doesn't waver. "He had a daughter."

The second Goblin comes forward now, carrying something more complex than a simple pipe. A pneumatic bolt-gun, the kind used for driving rebar into concrete foundations. He racks it—a sharp metallic *CLACK*—and aims at the other heir, the one still standing, holding his shattered-brother.

"Wait!" the standing one screams. "Please! We didn't know! The reports said it was structurally sound!"

"You read them?" another sandhog asks, stepping into view. This one's got a wrench the size of a crowbar. "You actually fucking read them before you signed off?"

"I... yes! Of course we read them!"

The pneumatic gun fires.

*SNAP-CRACK-BOOM.*

A steel spike, three feet long, slams through the heir's left knee and embeds itself in the concrete floor beneath the solvent puddle. His leg gives out immediately. He goes down hard, his brother's head cracking against the edge of the flaming ring as he falls.

Now they're both screaming together.

"You docked my brother's pay," the Dwarf with the pipe growls. He shifts his weight, swinging at the jaw this time. *CRUNCH.* Teeth shatter. Bone breaks. The heir's head snaps sideways, lifeless eyes staring at nothing. "For the delay. While he bled out underground because your Pylon collapsed on him."

"Twenty-three men died that day." Victoria's still talking to me like we're discussing the weather. She pulls out her phone, scrolls. "Forty-seven more lost limbs. Your father approved the budget cuts that removed the support struts. These two signed off on the final inspection report knowing full well those numbers were faked."

The Goblin with the bolt-gun racks it again. Fires twice in quick succession—both knees this time. The second heir's body jerks like a puppet with cut strings.

The screams merge into a single deafening choir, bouncing off every soundproof wall in this vault.

I watch it all without blinking.

Mechanic's eyes.

Just watching gears turn.

My frost doesn't melt even as the heat makes sweat bead on my forehead—cold sweat from what I'm seeing rather than any physical temperature change around me.

This is retribution.

This is machine logic applied to human sin.

And I am simply here to observe how the system processes its input.

"Should we continue?" Victoria asks, tilting her head toward where there are more tools laid out against the far wall. More sandhogs and Goblins waiting their turns. More bones to break. More teeth to shatter.

I don't answer.

She takes my silence as assent.

The symphony of suffering continues.

* * *

I stand in the center of the slaughterhouse, my breath coming out in white plumes against the cobalt chill radiating from my chest. The vault reeks—copper steam thick enough to taste, mixing with the acrid tang of charred flesh and boiling blood. Victoria's body lies crumpled near the table where her father died, limbs arranged at angles that defy nature.

Julian Sterling is still breathing. Barely.

His rats have already begun their work, gnawing through the soft tissue around his eyes while he shudders on the floor, lips pulled back in a silent scream. Blood pools beneath him, dark and viscous, seeping between the cracks in the stone. The ring of fire has collapsed inward, leaving only smoldering embers and blackened bone fragments scattered across the marble.

Grimjaw wipes a swipe of someone else's blood across his heavy jaw, his tusked face grimaced but satisfied. "It's done, Reyes," he growls, his voice echoing off the vault walls. "They're meat."

I don't respond immediately. Instead, I raise two fingers to my own neck, pressing them against the carotid artery. My pulse beats steadily beneath the skin—a metronome counting down the seconds like any other night. Sixty beats per minute. No acceleration. No tremor. Nothing.

Just the calm, flat rhythm of a man who just finished a job.

The frost-cobalt aura flickers once around me before retracting entirely, leaving goosebumps on my forearms as warmth creeps back into the air. But there's no heat anymore—not real heat. Just smoke and dying coals and the wet, sucking sounds of Julian Sterling's final breaths.

"You want me to finish him?" Grimjaw asks, nodding toward Julian. "Mercy killing. Quick."

"No." My voice comes out hollow, detached. "Let nature take its course."

I turn away from the carnage, scanning the walls with mechanic's eyes looking for loose threads, incomplete circuits. That's when I see it—a painting shattered by the chaos, its frame now hanging at an odd angle. Behind it, barely visible, is a dark rectangle cut into the wall. A safe. Hidden.

"Pack it up," I tell Grimjaw, already moving toward the hidden compartment. "We're burning the house."

My hand finds the cold metal edge of the safe door. It's locked—electronic keypad, probably biometric. But the housing is old, pre-2000s installation. The kind of thing they put in walls before everything went smart and stupid-proof. I can feel the wiring through the paint, trace the connection points with fingertips that still remember blueprints better than names.

Behind me, I hear Grimjaw dragging bodies toward the center of the vault, preparing them for the fire we'll set before we leave. Julian makes one last gurgling sound before falling silent.

Sixty beats per minute.

No remorse. No sadism. Just the quiet satisfaction of a job completed according to specifications.

The safe clicks open under my ministration, revealing a slim drive encased in what looks like lead shielding. On the side, scrawled in permanent marker: *THREE-HEAD LEDGER - VISIBILE #2*.

I pocket it without ceremony.

Time to find out who's next on the list.
